incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
Executive summary: Does very well what it is supposed to do.

The details: I have a moderate-size house with a lot of wall-to-wall light brown / beige carpeting which was laid down about 10 years ago and had never been cleaned (other than the occasional vacuuming). Ugly dark patches had developed in high-traffic areas. After a thorough cleaning with Hoover Max Extract 77 the carpet looks as close to new as a 10 year old carpet can get. The improvement exceeded my expectations. I am very happy with the results.

The assembly of the machine was a cinch. The usage was quite straightforward, but be sure to _read_ and _follow_ the instructions. The suction is impressive -- it leaves the carpet practically dry to the touch.

The most demanding part of the job is the moving of the heavy furniture -- you will have to clear the floor in order to make room for maneuvering the machine. I piled up all the furniture into one half of the room, cleaned the other half, then on the next day, after the cleaned part was dry, I swapped the furniture into the cleaned part and did the other half.

The amount of the detergent used depends on the speed at which you move. If you take twice as long to clean the floor, you will use twice as much detergent. I cleaned somewhat slowly because I felt the carpet was being cleaned more thoroughly that way. Because of that, I ran out of my initial supply of two 32 oz bottles of detergent. I went out and bought a 64 oz bottle of Hoover 2X CleanPlus at my local Target for about $18, which, by the way, is substantially less expensive than what it would cost buying it here. I assume that this is because the shipping cost is actually built into the "free shipping" deal.

I haven't used the machine's hand tools yet so I cannot comment on those.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text: The feature that I most wanted with this vacuum, was the ability to use a disposable bag.  Amazon bundled the vacuum with a package of 15 disposable bags.  Great!  Problem 1) They arrived days apart. Problem 2) The product manual makes no mention of the use of disposable bags, or how to use them. 3) The bags themselves are JUST paper sacks with no rubber dam to seal it or hold it in place.  I inserted it into the cloth bag, not knowing what else to do.  The dirt and hair completely bypassed the paper bag and collected in the cloth bag.  Not surprising.  I sat down to do further research and then I discover that there is an adaptor that is necessary for use with the disposable bags.  Amazon - you sell it, but it is priced higher.  Wish I could have gotten it as part of my bundle.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: Cleans great but has a tiny cleaning solution reservior
text:
I have used several different models before, I have also used professional carpet cleaners in the past. It does clean well and the accessories preform well. It does it's main functions as you would expect. I found that it works better than the lower level Hoover Steam Cleaners. I have worn a few of them out, I have an older model in my basement still. I would saw that the professional carpet cleaners do better at deep deep cleaning than any of the standing home models but this does a great job on surface dirt. Which is what you see. The suction is pretty good, better than my last one.
The big problems I have with it are the plastic wheels for starter. Ours squeaks all the time. These carpet cleaners are loud and you can hear the high pitch squeak of the wheels over the blower motor. Could just be ours, it pretty much happened right out of the box. My wife wouldn't let me return it but I really wanted to. I can live with it, but man does it annoy me.
Second is the reservoir for the cleaning solution...it is tiny. This is the only design problem I have with it. You can go through 3 loads of cleaning solution before you are out of water or before the waste water bin is full. It is very annoying to run out of just the cleaner that fast. They could have made the other compartments smaller and save on weight and bulk, or they just could have made the cleaning solution container larger. The pictures made it look like it took up half of the water reservoir but really it is just a narrow tube inside of it.
It really should only get 3.5 stars because of the added time it takes to fill up the cleaning reservoir all the time. Other than that it works great and is very comparable to other steam cleaners in this form factor.

review_title: Tank fails. Machine is decent, but probably not worth the price.
text:
The tank that held the water and cleaning solution failed. There are 2 spring loaded plugs on each tank that are depressed by sitting it on the platform. This allows the fluids to leave the tank.

After 6 months, the solution tank plug no longer stays closed and it leaks everywhere. My machine is now worthless unless I can get this tank replaced. Looking at it now, this is a very bad design choice on their part.

As for the performance of the machine?

Carpet 4 stars

Pergo/Laminate 3 stars

Stairs 1 star - [the suction powered attachment has to build up speed but then stops the moment you put any pressure on it. It has that motor that requires movement to get it going, like a childs toy car that they run across the floor a few times and then release it to watch it go.]

Upholstery 5 stars - [the attachment has no moving parts, but the suction is great and it cleans micro fiber couches like a champ. The trigger gets stuck and requires manually pulling it back out so it stops spraying. It was like this even new, so it's more of a minor flaw than anything.]

review_title: This is the carpet cleaner you're looking for!
text:
Wow! This machine really impressed me. I have 3 dogs, one of which we've had almost 4 years and have just now been able to house break her. Our carpet was so bad that we were planning on ripping it out and just use the subfloor until we could afford the vinyl plank flooring we want.
My mom had a Hoover SteamVac that's probably close to 10 years old but still worked pretty good. Although it didn't work as well on my carpet because I have Berber. A few months ago I loaned it to a friend and we all know how that goes... never saw it again. Sooooo, I had to replace mom's carpet cleaner. I did a lot of research, checking many stores and brands, but chose this one because it cleans hard floors too and since we planned on at some point replacing our carpet with hard flooring, I thought this would be perfect. I also liked this machine because it has 11 spinbrush scrubbers rather than the usual 6 on other Hoovers.
I'm having Thanksgiving at my house so I thought I'd try this carpet cleaner out on my nasty carpet. WWWOOOWWW!!!! My carpet has never been so clean in the 7 years we've lived here. I am sooooo happy I bought this!! It worked so well that I don't even plan to replace the carpet any more. I've included pics to show how nasty my carpet was before and how it looks now. (It's really gross, no judgment please!)
So, about the machine:
I like that it has separate compartments for water and solution. The "rinse" option is where its at! I could tell a huge difference from the "wash" passes to the "rinse" passes. The water was black every time after "wash" and still dark brown after "rinse." I will probably be going over it again in the very near future to get more up.
This machine did a great job of getting water and dirt of my Berber carpet. No other carpet cleaner, SteamVac or rented machine, has ever been able to pull so much out of my carpet. It still took over night for the carpet to dry completely but I could tell a difference in dampness after just a couple hours.
I made good use of the easy drain spout for the dirty water. It makes emptying the dirty water so much easier and less messy.
I never used the clean surge button. Didn't need it. I thought it used plenty of solution regularly and if it needed more I just went over the spot again.
I used Hoover Platinum Collection Pet Plus solution from Amazon, Hoover Pet Plus, and Rug Doctor Oxy-Steam solution. My living room is very large and very dirty so I used ALOT of solution. 5 bottles to be exact. I really liked the Platinum Pet Plus. The scent was great. I didn't notice a big difference in the cleaning power of the different solutions though.
I also used this on my hard floors. Even on linoleum it did great! I wasn't ever able to get the squeegee to stay on, but it really didn't need it. Sucked up the water just fine without it. My hard floors felt and looked really nice, and the nice smell was a bonus.
Cleaning: This machine has to be cleaned when finished using! I clean out the dirty water tank. I remove the brushes, take off the brush cover and spray everything out with the sink sprayer. I also take off the nozzle and clean that up. While shampooing, I have to keep an eye on the filter going into the dirty water tank. It doesn't take long to get clogged with gunk. This machine would be clogged with dog hair in no time if I didn't clean it after every use.
Some reviews said their machine leaked. I have not had this trouble at all. I've used it twice since I got it 3 days ago and haven't noticed any leaks at all. I can't speak to the longevity of it yet but hope it lasts as long as the old SteamVac did.

The shampoo constantly leaks into the clean water, which means you cannot rinse your carpet.  If you clean your carpet and leave shampoo residue, your carpet will be dirty again within days.  Dirty likes sticky surfaces and your carpet will attract and hold the dirt.  Not only that but you will be wasting expensive shampoo.  The only way you can rinse your carpet is to totally empty the shampoo out of the tank and use only water.  I'm currently waiting for yet another tank or a refund for the cleaner from Hoover. review_title: great for pet hair...use the floor brush nozzle
text: I have used Hoover portapower vacuum cleaners for over 20 years. They are great for picking up dog hair on solid surface floors (hardwood, linoleum, etc.). This portapower vacuum gives you two main floor nozzles. I always use the floor brush nozzle...the one without wheels. I have always prefered the floor brush since it does not have those little wheels that get tangled with dog hair... and it always seems that nozzles with wheels will scratch my wood floors.  The floor brush option with this Hoover portapower has only brushes, no wheels to scratch the floor. This is the only vacuum I have found that gives that wonderful floor brush option. If you purchase this, put the floor brush on and the nozzle will go smoothly over your hard wood, etc. floors. Works great on hard wood, ceramic, etc.. I use a regular upright vacuum on carpets, but I love, love, love this one for hard wood floors. I have a lot of hard wood. It comes with a reuseable bag, but you can purchase an attachment so that you can use disposable bags if you wish...Hoover type N. Since this is a canaster type, I just usually carry the canaster in one hand and the wand in the other while I vacuum...or put the canaster down to vacuum an area then move the canaster. Being a canaster with a long wand, the wand reaches under beds, etc. where uprights can't get. This is a great price, I ordered another one, since the one I have now I have had for many years... and I hope they don't stop making this.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
First things first, I started off with an expensive "brand name" a while back. The stuff was super thick and hard to work with, and mysteriously either cured too fast, or not well enough. One time it didn't cure at all! Either way, when fully cured, it never really seemed as hard as it should be...

Some of it was inexperience, but not all. I watched YouTube videos, bought a scale, etc.

Right off the bat, this is better priced, comes with a nice lower l little kit, and all Nelly packed in a box.

Leap of faith, I poured 2 boards 18 x 12. Measured everything, did everything right, and everything works well! Even though I had my doubts (being that both parts seemed much, much more fluid than the "brand name").

Because this stuff was more fluid, it was SO much easier to mix, so much easier to pour, & seemed so much easier to get the bubbles out!

It seems so much harder when fully cured than that "brand name" that I originally had bought.

I'm going to stick with this for a while as I'm very happy so far, and you can see the results!

incident_description: early april 2021, i purchased an led neon sign from yellow pop usa.  hello@yellowpop.com . i found the general quality of the product poor (made in china) and the electrical power component supplied potentially dangerous to children, adults and pets. my concern about the safety issue was presented to two individuals at yellow pop and brought no results. i was told by both individuals (i have emails) that my issue of high voltage electrocution is of no concern as the led power supply is "low voltage".  well the 120 volt ac power cord terminals (directly from the wall outlet) are completely exposed and the owners manual for the power supply (online power supply manufacturer) states specifically under "hazards" that the component is to be mounted in an enclosure. obviously the power supply manufacture understands this high voltage unit is to be shielded to avoid an electrocution hazard. yellow pop scoffs at the concern and so far has refused restitution to me. i have photos of the power supply and a link to the power supply owners manual posted below. the power supply that came with the sign by yellow pop (to lay openly exposed on the floor or mount exposed on the wall) is a model lrs-150-12 at www.meanwell.com . the warning to shield this unit is on the meanwell website. since potentially thousands of these power supplies were supplied to u.s. customers for their led signs, i believe this is a potential hazard that needs to be addressed due to the exposed high voltage wires creating a shock hazard. i emailed the underwriters laboratory may 7, 2021 and they informed me by telephone today, may 12, 2021 that this is a serious hazard issue and yes, that this power supply is designed to be covered and installed as part of a component. they also mentioned that my complaint is out of their jurisdiction however as the yellow pop product is not "ul approved".  they recommended that i contact saferproducts.gov.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: Does a much better job than I expected
text:
I really like this cleaner. I've used it on carpet, tiled floor, a couple of chairs, and just about every flat surface in the bathroom, and I've got almost nothing to complain about. But since I like to complain, here's my one gripe:

The dirty tank is much smaller than the clean water tank. (It doesn't look smaller, but it holds less than half as much as the clean tank.) This means that I make many more trips to dump dirty water than I do to fill the clean tank, especially on hard floors. So far I've never had both need attention at the same time. This is a minor complaint and isn't worth taking a star off the review.

Otherwise, this thing is great. I started on the kitchen floor. I'd recommend starting on hard floor before cleaning carpet, because this gave me a much better idea of how the solution is sprayed and what it takes to pick it up again. I cleaned tile floors with the squeegee and without, and it seemed to do a much better job without the squeegee. This might not be true on all types of floors, especially floors that don't have deep grout lines.

It did a great job on the tile. A three day old coffee spill (yes, I'm lazy) took about four passes to clean, and high traffic areas also took three to four passes. Everywhere else took one pass to clean and one or two passes to pick up the solution in the grout lines. Since it puts down cleaning solution as you push, and clean water as you pull, I got in the habit of holding the trigger when pushing and releasing when pulling back, until spills were cleaned up, then holding the trigger when pulling back to rinse. It sounds complicated, but I do it without thinking now.

Tile floors are dry within minutes, because the water is picked up so well and probably also because of the hot air this cleaner blows on the floor as I clean. (Yay--warm feet.) The kitchen and (small) front entryway took one tank of cleaning solution for a serious cleaning, but I suspect that one tank will do all the tile floors in the house when doing regular cleaning.

It's also done a great job on carpet. So far I've only cleaned high traffic areas. The dirty water was... well, yuck. The carpet looks clean again. Dirty areas like armrests on furniture also cleaned up well and look new again. I haven't found any carpet or fabric that is damaged by the cleaning solution that came with this cleaner. (Everything in my house is pretty ordinary, though, so I'd still recommend testing the cleaning solution on a hidden spot before trying it on carpet or upholstery for the first time.)

I was cleaning the floors in the bathroom and had plenty of solution left, so I turned the hand tool on the shower and bathtub. The tool is quite large and doesn't get into curves and corners, but it still cleaned most of the surfaces very well. Hard water stains that I usually have to scrub at lifted off very easily. Scuff marks on the outside of the tub that I haven't been able to remove came off after a minute of just holding the brush tool in place. I rinsed the inside of the tub with running water, so the dirty tank never filled up there. The hose is very flexible, and bending it to get the tool to reach all angles is very easy. I've still got to clean the tight places with some elbow grease, but the job just got a whole lot easier.

Cleaning the cleaner is pretty easy, too. The dirty tank has a pour spout to empty it quickly, and a large lid that lifts off, so at the end of the day all the dirt can be rinsed out of all the funky corners and hidden places in there. The hand tools rinse easily. The filter that really gets clogged with carpet fibers is easily accessible and can be scraped clean every time the dirty tank is removed. The other filter is a bit more of a pain to get at, but it doesn't need to be cleaned very often.

Sometimes I try tools that I think were designed by people who have never tried to do the task at hand. That's not the case here. It seems like someone put a lot of thought into how this works and how it's used and maintained, and so far I don't have any serious complaints. It works. I'm happy.

Update: The more I use this, the more I like it. A few things I've noticed today:

1) When you stop for a while (to empty or fill a tank, to answer the phone, whatever), park the cleaner on a hard floor. It does leave a small puddle behind.

2) When rinsing (not just dumping) the dirty tank, leave the small pour spout open. Most of the water will exit that way, and leaving it open speeds the job up a lot.

3) I'm finding that when I clean low-traffic areas of carpet, I hold the trigger to push and pull once, then release the trigger and go back and forth over the same spot twice more. This seems to extract much of the water. With fans and ceiling fans running, the carpet dries fairly quickly. High-traffic areas require more attention.

4) For very heavy pieces of furniture, I use [[ASIN:B001W6Q4W4 carpet sliders]]. I clean next to the furniture, then slide the furniture to the clean (wet) area and clean where the furniture was. The furniture stays on the sliders for the rest of the day, then it's moved back into place and the sliders are removed.

text:
We have used this machine twice since we ordered it, and will do another room in 10 days. That in itself is the main advantage of purchasing a rug cleaning machine; no longer the necessity of conducting a rug cleaning marathon as there is with a rental.
We chose this model because it has 11 spinning brushes, (as opposed to the 5 brushes of the model 66), and the consumption of cleaning fluid appears to be less with the Hoover than reported by Bissell users.
So far, so good.
We are only cleaning carpet with this machine, not hard floors.
Patience is a virtue with this machine. The manual describes wet strokes and dry strokes. Briefly, this means wet stroke number 1, forward, dispenses the cleaning fluid. Wet stroke number 2, reverse, is a rinse stroke. The manual recommends 2 dry strokes to pick up the liquid. I have tended to use four dry strokes. You can see the liquid still being sucked up on the third and fourth dry strokes. As a result of the extra dry strokes, the drying time seems to be greatly reduced. So as to give the machine a chance to do its job, all strokes should be relatively slow. This is not a vacuum cleaner. title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: I couldn't be more pleased with how easy it is to use!
text:
I used this on heavily soiled carpets in my kids rooms. I used the carpet cleaner with Hoover platinum collection pet plus carpet detergent. It was so easy to get set up...the clean water container has one opening for the hot water and one opening for the detergent. It is so easy to remove the container from the machine and connect it back. The dirty water container is below the clean water container and it is even easier to remove and put back. The handle makes it so easy to carry the containers too the sink to fill/empty and the dirty water container had a latch to open it up completely too clean it out when done. The brush strip on the bottom of the machine takes no effort to remove for thorough cleaning of the machine after use.
Now, for the cleaning of the carpet, like i said it was heavily soiled in my kids rooms, the carpet hadn't been in a year so there were some pretty dark stains. I did put a stain pretreatment on the bad spots before but the cleaner really did well in cleaning the dirty carpet. I will have to goo over the really bad spots one more time but over all it did really well.( I took before and after pictures but don't know how to post them)
I also hard wood floors in the majority of the house and the squeegee tool that you add to the machine for floors snap on and off the bottom of the machine with just one hand with ease. I cleaned the floors with the hard floor solution that came with the machine ( it came with a 16 oz bottle of the multi floor plus cleaner solution and a 32 oz bottle of 2x proplus professional strength carpet cleaner solution) there was an old spill on the floor in the living room that had dried and it took the machine just a minute to clean it right up...
If the carpet cleaner keeps up working as good as the first time I'll be ecstatic! So far I would definitely recommend this cleaner too anyone who would benefit from having a multi floor cleaning machine ( wish I had tile too see how it would clean that)
Btw the machine is a little larger than a vacuum but not so big it doesn't fit in my hall closet with my vacuum cleaner.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water.

text:
I have owned Hoover Steamvacs for over fifteen years. The first two models I owned were the old school Steamvacs with the square-type bucket receptacle for dirty water. This receptacle had one clamp on each side to create suction for uptake of dirty water; i.e., because the receptacle tank was forced down onto the rubber-covered uptake hoses, there was no air or room for a leakage of suction. A vacuum.

I bought this a great while ago because of my great love of the Hoover products but used it only recently. I did not think to keep my receipt, because I love Hoover products. What could go wrong? Well, this is what went wrong: I did not keep my receipt, it is too late to return the Steamvac, and I am out of luck because of it.

This model's design is different than the other designs in that the dirty water uptake tank is not clamped down onto the operating unit; instead, some genius designed it so that it rests on top of the base. The only way I could create suction was to push down on the dirty water uptake tank with one foot while precariously moving the Steamvac toward me. I am positive that somewhere, in an alternative universe, Lucille Ball fights this piece of crap in an episode of I Love Lucy. Paw-see-tive. I can see her, just as I saw myself, fumbling for balance while I crow-hopped on one foot backward, with my other foot pushed down on the dirty water uptake tank. All I needed was a few glasses of Meatavitavegamin to leave me good and sloppy drunk, in which case I would have fallen backward and into my china cabinet, and the picture would have been complete.

To top it all off, on the second usage of this product the little switch than controls the brush speed snapped off, and the little spring-thing inside of it flew across the dining room, where I was haplessly attempting to eradicate my son's dachshund's mini-puddles. (The dog is almost housebroken.)

I have no idea why the Hoover company would screw with such an excellent design. In review after review, I have seen that the old Hoover Steamvac beats Bissell and the Rug Doctor in actually cleaning and what is left behind on the carpet. Those days may be gone. This Steamvac does not reclaim a good deal of the water, soap, and dirty material (in this case, puppy peepee); instead it leaves the carpet wet and sopping in refuse water. What good is a steam cleaner that does not reclaim the water?

I am genuinely disappointed in Hoover.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: The first time I used the machine I thought it did a very good job of cleaning
text:
I had a Bissel floor cleaner for MANY years and when that unit finally died I did the research and decided to get the Hoover Max Extract 77 Pro cleaner. The first time I used the machine I thought it did a very good job of cleaning. Nice spray power, good extraction and easy to work with. Used the machine a couple more times for spot clean ups such as a spiled glass of white wine and cat hairball. These are the kind of reasons I bought the machine, quick clean-ups for small messes. The last time I attempted to use the machine I was going to do a full room clean, remove all the furniture and clean wall to wall. Set the machine up and started to shampoo the carpet. The full few pulls of spray and vac I watched the water and suds being extracted and continued to clean the room. Noticed the machine wasn't doing a very good job, check the machine and discovered no water was spraying, just vacuum running.Spent the next twenty minutes trouble shooting the machine for possible reasons/solutions to failure to spray. No success. Contacted Amazon and asked for recommended next action as the machine was less than eight months old at this time. Amazon did respond and gave the number for Hoover Customer Service. After MULTIPLE attempts to contact Hoover at different times on different days I finally got a hold of a live person. I was given the name of an approved repair shop to take the machine to. I made an appointment and dropped the machine off for repair. Now it gets interesting. The owner of the repair shop informed me Hoovers were junk as the company wasn't really Hoover anymore. Company sold, employees let go, change of personnel, etc.. Company hard to work with. I left the machine for repair and waited for the promised call when done. After three weeks I called the repair shop wanting to know status of the repair and when ready. I was informed the computer circuit board (?) was defective, Hoover would not honor the warranty and the repair shop was still trying to resolve the repair. Not other info available regarding time.
For an alleged $300 floor cleaner to last three uses after eight months and be informed Hoover won't honor the warranty, I'm agreeing with the service tech, Hoover use to be good but not any more.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

Took me some time before deciding on this unit. Had a quote from the steam cleaning company for a 2 bedroom, hallway and a living room carpeted condominium for $100. Tried it one time but after only 3 weeks, our carpet is back to its dirty self.Having kids didn't really help also. I don't have the budget to have it done every 3-4 weeks so after reading the reviews, took the risk and purchased this from another online retailer which is cheaper than Amazon at that time.

The Good :
- It really cleans the carpet. My wife also admits that it almost is the same as cleaning with the steamer company less the cost, of course. Some problem areas like the door entrance and hallway will need a few passes.
- It was on sale a few months ago for around $220, a real steal if you would ask me.
- It can save you money. I used it every 2-3 months. On the 3rd month, I have already recuperated the cost of purchase. I used it for about 6 times now and had we still gone with the steam cleaning company, it's like $600 down the drain. I saved almost $350 and will continue saving until the life of the machine
- It's pretty durable. I was surprised by the negative reviews here of its durability. The only thing that I can say is, if you take care of it and use it well, it will also take care of you. Please read the instructions before using this unit for proper care of this machine.

The Bad :
- Heavy. It can be a workout while cleaning, but for me this can be a good thing
- Hand detailer is worthless, suction is bad that it blows the water instead of sucking it. Tried to use it on fabric chairs, that was my big mistake.
- It can consume a lot of carpet shampoo especially when you are trigger happy with the Cleansurge button. What I did was to buy from Home Depot a generic brand of premium carpet shampoo. It is very much comparable with Hoover cleaners less the cost.
- This unit, though multi-surface, is more suitable for carpets. I tried it with tile cleaning, a total failure. It only made the tiles wet but didn't really clean it like conventional handscrubbing.
- With the steam cleaning company, dry time was around 3-4 hrs. With this unit,longer around 6 hrs with the fans on but can be quicker during summer, around 4 hrs. That's why I make it sure that the family is out during carpet cleaning time.
- Cleaning can be a pain especially the spinscrub brushes as dirt/gunk sticks to it. You also have to dry it before storing to prevent mold buildup and to extend it's life.

Overall, we found this to be a good purchase . Saving money while having our carpets clean is the real reason we got the Hoover Maxextract77 and we are hoping that this unit last more years to keep our carpets clean the way we like it.

I will start out by saying, I use to work for a cleaning company that used these vacuums in every home. We would clean 5 houses a day, some with animals and some without. I absolutely loved this vacuum then. It made my daily work life so much easier and faster. It's been a few years since then and I decided to buy this vacuum for my home (purchased March 28th, 2019). With all that being said, I will write my review.

We recently bought a house with all wood floors. Soon after, we got two dogs. One is short haired, and the other is an extremely floofy 80 pound dog. With winter coming to an end and an installation of a doggy door... our floors have been covered with clouds of dog shed and dirt. I absolutely haaate the feeling of dirt on my feet, it's one of my biggest pet peeves. I had to sweep every single day and even than, dirt and hair would build up in hard to reach areas. Standing there, debating on shaving my dog bald, I remembered this vacuum that I use to love! So I ordered it.

The package arrived on time while I was at work and I was so excited to open it up that I rushed home on my lunch break. I'm not sure if it's written somewhere, and to be honest I didn't look.. but I was fully expecting to receive a black vacuum with black attachments(which is what I thought was pictured). This vacuum is grey with white attachments. The floor attachment is much smaller than I remembered, so it doesn't cover as much floor as it use to and the bristles use to cover the entire edge so that your floors wouldn't be scratched and suction would stay strong throughout the attachment (they switched it up for some reason). The larger attachment (which I assume is for carpet) is useless if you have shedding animals. The smaller attachment (which I assume is for stairs) has rubber bristles(may work ok with dog hair but I don't have stairs so idk). The corner attachment is much shorter than the previous version and the furniture attachment is what you would expect. The cord is very long compared to my regular vacuums. And everything did arrive in perfect shape.

I bought this vacuum for my hardwood floors so it was important to me that that specific attachment work. I waited two days before vacuuming so that dirt and hair would build up enough so I could see how this vacuum really works. Having a shorter attachment makes the job take a little bit longer but as long as your vacuuming correctly, this vacuum works really well! The suction is great! No scratches so far and I can get under, behind, in between and more with this vacuum!! It sucks up hair really well and after vacuuming my entire 3 bedroom house, my feet feel clean walking around barefoot!!

I used this vacuum with the cloth bag it came with because the paper bag adapter is taking longer to get here, but I do suggest getting the paper bags(bags and adapter sold separately). The cloth ones collect everything fine but hair and dirt gets stuck in it and dirt flies everywhere when dumping it. Wearing the vacuum can be a little bit uncomfortable. Walking around with it isn't so bad, but bending over is where it gets the most uncomfortable. I made the strap as long as it could get and it's much more comfortable that way. They do sell a bag that goest with this vacuum and it makes it all much more comfortable if you wanna spend the money. Over all, I really like this vacuum and I think it works great! I wouldve given a 5 if I had received what I was expecting and if the attachments were what I use to use. I'm not really sure why some of the reviews were so bad. It might be that this vacuum works great at first and slowly declines. But for 100 dollars.. this is a great deal. If I do have any issues I will update my review. Otherwise.. enjoy your clean floors!! :D

text: I have never tried this before. I had many problems but no complaints about the epoxy, it worked perfectly. I ignored the "mix for several minutes" instructions because I am not an idiot and realize that instruction is an attempt to get people to make sure it's mixed well. I used a cordless drill, 20-30 seconds. This caused a lot of bubbles. I learned a trick by just trying it... A heat gun is a magic bubble destroyer. Heat over the surface, the epoxy gets thinner from heating, and they disappear  quickly. My mold leaked, It got rained on, everything was wrong, but I fixed it. This stuff takes a long time to dry and setup, they all do. It's not like fiberglass resin. I used it to repair a section of my driftboat with carbon fiber cloth. It looks amazing, and is very strong. I don't see how anyone that can read could find anything wrong with this so remember when reading reviews that  "Some of the tools in the shed are not very sharp" . You really shouldn't leave a negative review without reading the instructions and following them. All the problems I had were my own fault. I Love this stuff & I will buy it again soon. I will try to add a photo later.

text: I've read reviews after reviews of various types of carpet cleaners on Amazon.com for weeks now and couldn't really decide whether to get a Hoover or a Bissell.  Finally today, I just couldn't stand our carpet anymore so I decided to go to a local store to pick up a carpet cleaner.  I opted to pick up the Hoover Maxetract 77 at the store because I've had my Hoover regular vac for years and it hasn't failed me yet.  I rushed home to try it right away.  Please note that this is my first carpet cleaner purchase so I really wasn't expecting any professional carpet cleaning results.  After following instructions to a "T", I have to say that this machine got the carpet decently cleaned.  Light stains were removed easily and the darker left in pet stains seem to appear lighter than before.  The carpet felt softer and overall just cleaner.  I think I would definitely keep this machine were it not defective.  The hose and dirty water tank leaks.  At first I thought I  wasn't "dry vacuuming" correctly as it seems that it would get wet again.  I kept running the machine on dry vac mode over and over an area and it appeared to be sucking up water but it still felt soaking wet as if it was just newly rinsed.  That's when I noticed that liquid was dripping from the back hose.  Basically, the machine sucked up water and simultaneously leaked out water (or possibly solution) in the rear.  I also noticed that the dirty water tank leaked.  It appears that the plastic corners are not sealed properly as it would leak when tilted a certain way.  Yup I found out the tank was defective after I saw a trail of dirty water from my family room to the restroom.  I guess this can be remedied by just being careful not to tilt the tank a certain way but the hose on the other hand is hopeless.  Just utterly frustrating.  Liquid was pouring out that even the electric cord was wet.  Were it not for those issues, I would say it does the job.

incident_description: early april 2021, i purchased an led neon sign from yellow pop usa.  hello@yellowpop.com . i found the general quality of the product poor (made in china) and the electrical power component supplied potentially dangerous to children, adults and pets. my concern about the safety issue was presented to two individuals at yellow pop and brought no results. i was told by both individuals (i have emails) that my issue of high voltage electrocution is of no concern as the led power supply is "low voltage".  well the 120 volt ac power cord terminals (directly from the wall outlet) are completely exposed and the owners manual for the power supply (online power supply manufacturer) states specifically under "hazards" that the component is to be mounted in an enclosure. obviously the power supply manufacture understands this high voltage unit is to be shielded to avoid an electrocution hazard. yellow pop scoffs at the concern and so far has refused restitution to me. i have photos of the power supply and a link to the power supply owners manual posted below. the power supply that came with the sign by yellow pop (to lay openly exposed on the floor or mount exposed on the wall) is a model lrs-150-12 at www.meanwell.com . the warning to shield this unit is on the meanwell website. since potentially thousands of these power supplies were supplied to u.s. customers for their led signs, i believe this is a potential hazard that needs to be addressed due to the exposed high voltage wires creating a shock hazard. i emailed the underwriters laboratory may 7, 2021 and they informed me by telephone today, may 12, 2021 that this is a serious hazard issue and yes, that this power supply is designed to be covered and installed as part of a component. they also mentioned that my complaint is out of their jurisdiction however as the yellow pop product is not "ul approved".  they recommended that i contact saferproducts.gov.
