incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: Just as good as they were decades ago!
text:
I just purchased my second Hoover PortaPower, the first one being bought second hand about 25 years ago from a thrift store. The old one came with no attachments, but I used it for furniture, stairs, along baseboards, and cars for all this time. We still have it and it is still working, although missing a switch (you have to now plug and unplug it to turn it off and on)and didn't even have its crevice tool any longer (it broke after 25 years...........can't complain!)
Decided to get a new one, but figured that nothing is made like it was in the past, and would probably be a cheap imitation of the original. I was wrong. The new one is as good (better with all the great attachments) than the old one! Very few differences, (color went from old white to new black)but the most notable changes are the increased cord length and the new hose is shorter and a little harder to manipulate than the old. The best thing is that the old parts (like the hose and the dust bag) fit the new machine. LOVE THAT! I love the reusable dust bag, hate buying bags for something like this. Just take it outside and empty it. Can be washed and line dried too, if you wanted to do so. One of my main concerns was that the suction power of the new unit wouldn't be as strong as the older one, but it seems to be just as good. I can't say enough about this unit. I still have a good full size Oreck for deep cleaning carpets, as I don't feel this unit would get deep down dirt from carpet on a regular basis, but I couldn't get by without my PortaPower! Will be ordering another one for my mom soon.

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

review_title: Two cleaners that I never tried because of tank cap leaks.
text:
I had borrowed a Hoover carpet cleaner (not this model) from a friend and was impressed by the job it did so I decided to buy one to keep. The first cleaner I received leaked water from three areas. Both the freshwater and soap dispenser caps would not seal and the solutions drained out the caps when I tilted the handle back to start cleaning. The tanks were not overfilled. The third leak came from the back of the machine's handle but I'm not sure of the source.
I completed a return request with Amazon and typical of their wonderful service, they responded immediately with another cleaner that arrived the next day. I removed the new tank and filled both freshwater and soap dispensers with water to test for leaks. Same problem, maybe worse. These leaks are not a fluke but are a design flaw. The molded tank openings are so poorly done and rough that the double-lipped gaskets on the caps cannot seal the tanks. As a result, this one is going back as well. I hope Amazon has recourse with Hoover because I'm sure Hoover is aware of this problem already.

I can't comment on the unit's ability to clean because I never got that far but can say that the well used Hoover unit I borrowed worked very well and certainly did not leak. I will contact the owner of the unit I borrowed to get a model number and see if that model is still available from Amazon

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
We owned an older Hoover which lasted about 13 years -- sure a few pieces broke off here and there but the thing ran and did the job longer than you'd expect.

Finally we replaced it with this new one (Max Extract 77). After using it approx 10 times, I have found it be far inferior to the old one I owned. While there are some bells and whistles (and adjustments) that my older unit did not have, this unit is very hard to use and it's very easy to not get any suction at all. When emptying the dirty water tank, it's very easy to somehow incorrectly re-install it, or not "seat it" properly in the unit, or end up with a little dirt on one of the gaskets. The result is no suction. It is very frustrating to have to have to check multiple times whether it is sucking or not.

Another poor feature is the hand piece with the rotating brushes. The brushes don't rotate fast enough to do any good. The unit also includes a simple hand attachment with a fixed brush -- with this you can really scrub the carpet hard and fast and do a much better job than with the rotating brush attachment. The attachment is not worth the money. In fact, this entire Hoover unit was a poor buy.

Don't think me a fool that doesn't know how to put together a vacuum. I am a design engineer with many years of experience and know a thing or two about design usability. Hoover needs to get its act together and make products that work more robustly and don't require an engineering degree to troubleshoot every time you use it.

text:
Really well made. Easy to clean. A much better design than some of the older models, especially the waste water holding tank, which is much easier to remove and replace now.
I was amazed at how dirty our carpet and rugs were; not any more.
Be sure to read the manual and watch the You Tube videos about the Max Extract 77 so that you are really familiar with the ins and outs of operation. Something seemingly as simple as how long it should take to make one pass is put into perspective as one watches others do it.
I did not see one important process discussed, though: how to remove, disassemble, and clean the rotating brush, brush-block unit. Carpet fibers become trapped in the brush-block's plastic case and in the brush bristles. After removing the brush-block (I used a dull dinner knife to pry open the plastic case) I was able to clean the whole assembly with running water and my fingers. With care, the case snaps back together. You may need to rotate the brushes by hand to allow the bristles to clear the brush-block holes.
Be aware: the brush-block brushes do not rotate unless the Max Extract is on a flat surface or carpet, the grey, the handle release pedal has been pressed, the handle has been brought back to be used, and the power has been turned on.

text:
Epoxy countertops/tables are nothing new to me. I have been doing it for a few years now, and used many different brands. My overall experience was awful with this particular brand. I am hoping it was just a bad batch. This kit ruined a nice table top. I prepped the top with 220 sandpaper like usual and wiped down with 91% isopropyl alcohol, letting it dry over night. Wiped down one last time with a dry cloth. The epoxy poured thick and layed down smooth and I got as much of the air bubbles out as possible. (I used a paddle attachment for my drill in a cheap $1.25 bucket for easy clean up and mixing.) Woke up the next morning and the epoxy cured in a peculiar way. It cured all spotty throughout the table top. The epoxy like shrunk up and left spots throughout the top and you can feel the dips in the surface. If I had epoxy left over it wouldn't be a big deal, I would just mix and fill in the gaps. But considering a 1gal kit was already overkill and I ended up needing all of it because the mixture was so thick, it's a little disappointing.

Amazon atleast refunded me my money so I can at least attempt to finish my table top. On this experience alone I would not recommend this epoxy kit. I could have gotten a bad batch but who knows.

text:
I'm a woodworker and make a lot of custom pens with wood & acrylic. I ran out of epoxy resin and decided to order this. This was shipped, very well packed in 1/2 gallon jugs along with a pair of nice plastic beakers, stir sticks & disposable gloves (epoxy resin gets very sticky). I found this very easy to work with. It poured well, mixed well and casted well. When these jugs are empty, I know where I'm going to get the next batch. Great product, very well priced and easy to work with.

I'm casting blanks at 3/4" square by 6" long, sometimes up-to 1" square. After I mix and pour the product, I tap the molds a bit to get the air bubbles to surface and pop them with a mini torch. The molds then go into a pressure pot for 3-hours minimum at 60psi. Once they sit in the molds for a day, they are removed and turned upside down to finish curing. 2-days and the resin is set and can be cut, turned, shaped, whatever. Finding decent resin at a good price is challenging. I'd say this one is a winner.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

- Separate water/detergent tanks make fill-ups way easier.
- Rinse mode eliminates leftover detergent on the carpets.

text:
We remodeled our home this summer, replacing the 20-year old carpet with solid hardwood throughout. I bought a Hoover Cyclonic upright, but while it is a good vacuum, it wasn't very handy at picking up the dustballs and dog hair along the baseboards and under furniture. My Spousal Unit (S.U.) was not happy, which is a situation I try to avoid at all costs...so I looked for a low-cost supplemental vacuum.
I got S.U.'s tentative approval to give the Hoover Commercial Portapower Vacuum Cleaner a tryout. It arrived in a record 4 day's time, and we have just now tried it out. This is a superb appliance for our housecleaning mission! It is indeed lightweight, with all needed attachments, and a nice, long power cord. Everything connects intuitively, with strong and secure connections. For us geezers, this Hoover model uses the same kind of connectors that Hoover models have employed since the 1950s, which REALLY suits my retrophile S.U. Best feature? Metal extension wands/tubes. They do NOT telescope, so when we are sucking up rogue dustbunnies from under the beds, we have a Kareem Abdul-Jabbar-like reach...Very nice! The suction is not overwhelming, but it is more than adequate for our needs.
One small negative: The S.U. isn't used to having equipment slung from a shoulder strap, so she was banging it into walls and doorways. (Of course, this may have been her clever way of getting me to take over the role of Portapower operator, but I'm cool with that.) Oh, and I have to really concentrate so as not to refer to our new vacuum as the "Hoover Porta-pottie"

We highly recommend this vacuum for folks with hardwood or vinyl floors, especially if you live in a relatively small home. I expect it to perform well when vacuuming out our vehicles, but I saved that bit of excitement for New Year's Day!

review_title: Almost full-proof and can be used as an ICU
text:
I've used this incubator for the last 1.5 years and have had great success. There is a way to manually adjust the temperature by as little as a tenth of a degree.

It doesn't seem loud until you are done and then realize how loud it was. I did have some issues with the cord pulling out but luckily it resumes to the previous setting once power is restored.

I use a paper towel over the hatching tray during lockdown. It would be too slippery and cause leg issues if you only used the supplied plastic insert. I also add a moist paper towel to add additional humidity on hatch day (even though they are on lockdown).

I consider this incubator almost fool proof. I now use this as my high-risk bator. I transfer any eggs to this that don't have good air sacs or look like they may need help. This keeps me from having to open the larger incubator and putting the other healthy eggs at risk.

I've also used it as an ICU for a newly hatched chick that kept stargazing. The headroom was low enough to prevent her from throwing her head back and spazing. I kept her in it for a couple of days until the extra vitamins kicked in and eliminated the issue.

review_title: Does what it says on the tin
text:
I bought this, then read all the negative reviews and got worried. I'm a proud dog mom of two big girls in a decent sized apartment, and my carpets take a beating. I just used this for the first time over three high-traffic areas and I must say I'm impressed. An old pet stain that survived a visit from Stanley Steemer came out, and a spot where I stepped on a packet of hot sauce also came out (don't judge me, I'm in my 20s). More than anything I'm amazed at how dry my carpets are after use. Barely damp to the touch. It works as it promises to, easy to assemble, easy to take apart and clean. It is heavy as heck, but for the great job it does I don't mind. I'll update when I use the upholstery cleaner.

Upholstery cleaner gets an A++. Took out a couple embarrassing mattress stains from my nearly new mattress. Being a girl sucks sometimes.

Edited to add: As time goes on and I'm able to tackle more of my apartment, I'm more impressed with this machine. I started out with carpets that a professional would probably advise replacing. I vaccuumed thoroughly, then used a rubber broom to really remove all the dog hair and little "numies" that hide in carpet fibers- then gave it a few passes. incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

So I put about 1/4 cup and the rest water in the soap dispenser and it works great without too much foaming. (I have heard to never put soap in steam cleaners and instead pre-treat and just use water, but I like the fresh scent).

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
Despite some concerns from the negative reviews here, I went with the majority (positive reviews) and bought a MaxExtract77 cleaner. Here are my observations, based on using this cleaner with my white wool carpet:

1. Best feature of all is that you can use this cleaner in the rinse mode or wash mode. To test the rinse mode, I first cleaned several rooms in rinse mode. Despite using no soap application (only filled the soap container with plain hot water, just to be sure), this cleaner pulled an incredible amount of pre-existing soap residue (suds) and dirty water out of two large rooms. Apparently, previous professional cleanings left a lot soap residue on my carpets. After two complete "rinsings" the removal of previous soap residue was much reduced and the dirty water container was no longer jet black, just a light brown.

2. In wash mode, the MaxExtract77 is easy to operate and the multiple rotating scrub heads do a great job of removing embedded pet hairs. Yes, I vacuumed my carpets several times prior to cleaning them, using a high suction Dyson vacuum. It was amazing to see the remaining amount of embedded pet hairs that the rotating brushed pulled up from one of my three long haired resident dogs. The cleaner is easy to operate and control, with a trigger action to apply soap mix into the carpet. Following instructions, I used one or two passes on the same area with the cleaning soap spray engaged. Following these cleaning passes, I used one rinse pass in each direction to verify that most of the soap residue had already been removed. Leaving a soapy residue on your carpet is a key reason for the carpets not remaining very clean over time, despite your best cleaning efforts. I liked the fact that the motor noise changes its sound when you are no longer spraying any cleaning solution into your carpet, alerting you to clean and refill the unit's fluid chambers.

3. I used the handheld hose attachment and its single rotating brush for small carpet areas and tight spots. It seemed to offer a powerful spray and clean path, similar to that of the multi-brush unit, but was very useful for under furniture and small area cleaning. Again, I was amazed at how much pet hair the rotating brush assembly collected and how much hair and dirty water were in the main dirty water container. The design of the handheld hose length and its rotating attachment head is ideal for cleaning carpeted stair runners.

4. The three tank design is a nice feature, as is the use of transparent plastic for certain parts to monitor what is going on (depth of water, cleaning solution, removal of soap from the carpet, amount of dirt retrieved, etc.) One tank is for cleaning solution; one tank is for rinse water; one tank is for suctioned up dirty water.

5. The unit is very easy to clean and appears to be well designed. Because of the plastic components, you just have to be a little bit gentle with disassembly cleaning and re-assembly. It is a heavy unit and is somewhat tiring to use, but that is really what you want in a heavy duty carpet cleaner.

Overall, I would rate this cleaner as much better than my commercial Rug Doctor cleaner. The MaxExtract77 has better suction, better brush action, more maneuverability, and a selectable rinse mode. With the Rug Doctor, you can use it in rinse mode; but you have to choose to do that by not mixing any soap compound into the fresh water tank prior to starting your cleaning process. The rotating multiple-brush action of the MaxExtract77 also appears to be more efficient than the side to side brush pad action of the Rug Doctor.

So far, I am highly pleased with the MaxExtract and I look forward to avoiding future $1000+ commercial carpet cleaning bills for my 8000+ square foot Victorian house. I have some white and black marble floor areas to experiment with, but I will have to report back on how well or how poorly the MaxExtract does on these stone floor and grouted areas.

text:
I've bought two this year: one had a motor fail,and the other a broken hinge on the dust bin lid. The warrantee only covers the motor, not the other parts, which you have to buy, which was a surprise. If you complain and the purchase is very recent, they'll give you a 50% discount. Shipping is always on you. Amazon stepped in and refunded the charge for the new lid. But that was Amazon, not Shark.

The hose is much too short once you detach the motor from the base. You can't get under a bed, or even a coach, for example.

Plus the air pathway is prone to clogging, which will easily overheat the motor. Finally, the included upholstery brush is too skimpy for my taste, so you need a larger one for most tasks. Plan on buying some accessories to make the machine properly functional.

It is very inexpensive. I would have paid more, had I known what my $ got me, which was 2/3 of a good machine. Very good on floors and rugs, challenging on everything else.

review_title: It sucks, but it's supposed to
text:
When you get down to it, despite all of the marketing hype a vacuum needs to do two things well. It needs to have great suction to pull up dirt and, depending upon your needs, must have the flexibility to deliver that suction conveniently and consistently. This Hoover, if the form and function fit your needs, delivers on both counts!

We own a Dyson upright for most things and love it. But as easy as the Dyson is to get around, it, like all uprights, is not the thing to reach under beds or low furniture. The Dyson has the flexibility to pull out its handle and configure it to do some of this with a bit of work, but for some things it is inconvenient, at best. (Again, this is not a knock on the Dyson, but a reality of uprights.)

We really didn't want another 'regular' vacuum like a canister, so after researching things we settled on the Hoover Portapower unit to give it a try. What is the verdict? Highly recommended, as long as you understand that it is not a canister on wheels or an upright! If what you need is something that is relatively lightweight and very easy to move where it is needed, can reach under the furthest reaches of your furniture, including beds or cabinets, and can suck with the best of them, this unit delivers.

Also, the build quality is far above most products that it might compete with. It really feels solidly built, all the way down to the heavy duty and long power cord. Some have commented on the hose, but we have had no issues with any attachments or with the quality of the overall unit.

The only reason that I gave it 4 stars instead of 5 is that the cord is not retractable, which would be nice. But having lived with this for more than a year now, that is an easy trade-off to make for this level of product quality!

review_title: Hoover MaxExtract77 Multi-Surface Pro Carpet & Hard Floor Cleaner
text:
My first carpet cleaner. Used it on the floors also. Does a great job. Wouldn't use it on the floors again as it leaves too much water, and too much trouble for the 2 small floor areas in my apartment, and I had to use as towel to dry because it doesn't get up the water good enough even with the squeegee attachment. But the floors were sparkling clean. Live an apartment, have 2 Chihuahuas and pretty sure the previous tenants had pets. Carpeting was installed in 2007. My female Chihuahua smelled something and kept urinating on the carpet near the door. Since I have cleaned with the Hoover, she doesn't smell anything and has stopped peeing on the carpeting and the look and feel of the carpeting is almost like new.

Pros: Cleans great, easy to fill and empty tanks, quick and easy to use. Cleaned the carpets in my whole apartment in about 1/2 hour. Fast drying time for carpet.

Cons: Have to refill tank too much (but easy to do), leaves floors too wet, don't like having to hold in the lever.

Yes, I would recommend this for carpets only. Great carpet cleaner, but a pain for floors. If you just want something for floors, I would buy something else. I intend on buying a Haan Steamer for the floors.

text:
Plenty of suction, I bought it to use with a Neutripure backpack as a portable shop-vac. Although the hose is a small diameter I've been surprised what it will pull thru, dry small leaves etc. Some of the reviews seem confused about this thing, it's a wet/dry shop-vac, intended for outdoors or garage/workshop use, not a domestic Dyson/Miele/HEPA type vacuum cleaner.
1. It comes with a coarse foam filter installed in the top part, which would require taking screws out etc if u had to get at it.
2. It also comes with 2 other filters, a clothy one for normal use and a foam one for wet use. In the box they put the foam one inside the cloth one, just to amuse themselves I guess. These are mounted over a plastic filter frame that sticks down from the top part of the machine. Either of these filters are held on by an non-stretchy plastic band, when this breaks I guess you use blue tape or an ~8" hose band.
3. It also comes with a paper disposable type bag, like domestic vacuums used to.
You use it with either the clothy filter (dry stuff) or the foam one (wet), and the contents accumulate in the metal canister and you empty it when full, OR you put the paper filter over the inlet nozzle inside the canister, it wraps around the canister and is held in place by the filter assembly of the top part when u clip it back on. When it's full I guess u throw it away, then work out why u bought a shop-vac if u really wanted a house vacuum cleaner.
4. It comes with no manual or instructions whatsoever so u have to use Amazon etc for that information.
5. It comes with the wheels in a bag that you would pop into the slots in the base, if u want to use it that way.
6. It comes with the base attached but the base is easy to remove, it's held on by 4 little springy bits and u lever them off with a screwdriver
7. The hose & attachments are cheapo plastic, the only thing that fastens together "properly" is where the hose screws onto the canister. The other pieces all push together, but they stay together ok, and if not u could always use blue tape.
Other than all that, u turn it on, use it then empty it. If the clothy filter gets blocked when using it for sheetrock dust etc then u rinse it, like u would the canister filter for the fatter type of vacs, ie buy this for what it is, not what it isn't.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: Wish I Had Known About This Years Ago!!!
text:
After lots and lots of research on the best "portable" vacuum cleaner for a house full of wood and tile floors (and stairs), I finally broke down and ordered this one.

Wow, is all I can say. I love that it's portable (not super lightweight, but not overly heavy either), and the cord is nice and long (yes, it will still wrap it's way around the edge of the sofa, or under the corner of something, making you have to back-track and untangle it before moving on). I love the heavy duty METAL extensions, and the attachments that come with it (I still haven't tried them all).

I've used it on my wood floors and stairs, and YES IT WILL suck the dust and dirt out of the tiny cracks (where boards meet) in the wood floor using the wide attachment! WOO HOO!! No more vacuuming each individual crack with a slanted nozzle attachment. That alone makes this vacuum worth having! It works great on tile too. I am impressed completely, and I am hard to impress. I do not have pets, but I do have a busy household with a moderate amount of foot traffic in and out. I like floors that are dust and dirt free, and the swiffer just doesn't cut it. I absolutely hate using an upright vacuum nozzle period. Most of them are useless, and I end up wanting to drop kick the whole unit out the front door every time I try. Keep your nice upright for carpets and rugs, but for your solid floors I wholeheartedly recommend the Hoover Portapower.

I was able to find this model for $20 less plus free shipping and no sales tax by doing a little research online, but the Amazon.com price is good too.

Oh, I did not order the carrying case, and I am still not sure if I will. It would probably make carrying all your attachments easier, as this vacuum does not come with any way to carry those with you. Just keep that in mind when you order!

I am off to vacuum!!

review_title: The Hoover Max Extract 77 does an excellent job of cleaning
text: This is my 4th carpet cleaner over the past 15 years, as we own rental property and use them a lot.  The Hoover Max Extract 77 does an excellent job of cleaning.  Having said that, it is by far the heaviest and hardest to use of any machine I have owned or rented.  It doesn't maneuver well, and the caps to the water resevoir tank and shampoo compartment do not seal.  I would give it a 5 for cleaning, but a 1 for ease of use and a 1 for spilling water everywhere if you aren't super careful.  The "clean surge" is so hard to use while actually running the machine it takes both my hands on the trigger to hold it down.  I am exhausted after cleaning one room with this machine, and I used to be able to do a whole house or apartment with my old Hoover.  The dirty water tank on this one does have a much superior design to the old one, and is easier to empty.  It does have good suction.  However, it's just very hard to push on carpet with any pile at all.  It might be good for Berber or an extremely low pile.  Using it for hard floor cleaning is so loud I can't stand it, and water goes everywhere!  Not a good design at all, and the hard floor rubber brushe squeegy tends to fall off a lot if you are cleaning a floor with grout lines.  You have to stop every few minutes to re-attach it.  I thought maybe I had it on wrong, but I had someone else look at it and its just a bad design.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

text: In order to use in hard floors, you have to attach a squeegee for it to extract The dirty water off of your floor. The problem is that this squeegee attachment falls off very very easy. With a perfectly level floor with no bumps you probably would not have any issue, but if you have a tile floor like myself that is a complete nightmare.  With a perfectly level floor with no bumps you probably would not have any issue, but if you have a tile floor like myself With a little tiny bumps where the grout line is then this attachment will continue to fall off time and time again. Also, it uses an extraordinarily large amount of water and detergent. When you press the trigger down and move forward it sprays out so much liquid so quickly I found myself going through a bottle of detergent just to do one level on my home. I figured out that I need to squeeze the trigger, release it, squeeze it, release it and just intermittenly Spray out liquid as I slowly move forward. I’m going to have to get some gorilla glue so I can try to glue the squeegee attachment on, but once I do that I will not be able to remove it to use the machine on carpets.  That attachment comes off so easily that it blows my mind that a board room full of overpaid executives and engineers somehow approved this product. Also, if you have laminate or hardwood floors do not use this product. The one enemy to laminate or hardwood is moisture. This machine will sprout so much liquid that it will reach into the seams and make your hardwood or laminate and warp. Don’t even use steam. Use a regular mop or you can use a reasonable amount of moisture and it can dry quickly before the moisture seeps into your seems.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
This is the second carpet cleaner I've tried to keep our beige carpets from turning black under the relentless onslaught of tracked mud and grime brought into the house by our large dog. It compares well to the [[ASIN:B000RPTV62 Bissell Proheat 2x]] in some respects, and falls short in others.

Where the Hoover excels is in its water extraction. The cleaner seems to form a good tight seal with the carpet, and is able to pull enough liquid back out of the fibers to allow the carpet to fully dry in a five or six hours (on a dry day). The water it pulls up is remarkably dirty, which gives me confidence that it's agitating the fibers well and making a good dent in the amount of ground-in dirt. One drawback to its water extraction, however, is the small screen filter (underneath the dirty water tank) that must be kept clear to maintain good suction. Even though I vacuum thoroughly before using the cleaner, this filter still clogs up very rapidly with dog hair and loose carpet fibers. So frequently, in fact, that I have to clean this screen more often than I have to empty the dirty water tank! Part of this may be due to...

Where the Hoover falls short is in its cruelty to the carpet. Unlike the Bissell, the Hoover has flat discs for scrubbing the carpet, that spin while pushed flush against the fibers (the Bissell has a rotating bar, like a vaccuum). These flat scrubbing discs do a good job agitating the fibers, allowing the cleaning fluid to pull up lots of ground in dirt. The discs also leave a pleasing whorl pattern on the carpet that indicates where you've already passed the machine, so you can be sure to rinse in the same track as you've washed. Unfortunately, this cleaning action seems to be pretty hard on carpet - occasionally a strand of carpet will get caught in the disc and pulled up from the carpet - leaving a frayed hole behind. In cleaning a few hundred square feet of carpet, this happened two or three times. If the cleaner keeps pulling out carpet strands at this rate, the carpet will need replacement far, far sooner. Whether this is a function of the quality of our carpet, its age, or the aggressiveness of the machine, I can't say for sure. Only that it didn't happen with the beater-bar-style cleaning action of the Bissell.

Other things worth knowing about the cleaner:
It automatically switches from dispensing cleaning solution to dispensing water. When the trigger is depressed, the machine dispenses cleaner if it's being pushed forward, and dispenses cleaner if it's being pulled backwards. Two more passes without depressing the trigger (one forward, one back) will extract the moisture from the carpet. This approach lets you break the cleaning of a large carpet into discrete chunks, rather than soaping a large area, rinsing a large area, then drying a large area, as you might be tempted to do if switching modes required turning knobs and the like (looking at you, Bissell).

It has a button for dispensing extra cleaning solution for especially dirty areas. Be careful with it. I held it down while doing a single forward stroke over an area with a food spill. Several rinse passes later, it was still pulling up frothy foam. I think it may dispense WAY more soap than it needs to in this mode.

text: Just finished using my Hoover cleaner on both carpet and tile.  First, let me say...I have no pets.  I have owned Hoover carpet/hard floor cleaners for several years and have gone through several models.  I was always happy with them and they actually were used on some very hard jobs...filthy carpet.  My last model finally gave out so I ordered this one (for much less than the previous models).  I must say that the improvements on this model are substantial.  The product engineers must have listened carefully to user feedback.  First great change:  the dirty water receptacle is much improved, making it easier to clean.  I was always frustrated by not being able to access the dirty buildup.  Second great change:  insertion of the clean water receptacle is super easy now.  Before, I was often frustrated by my inability to insert the container on the first try and it often leaked.  Now it just clicks in.  The cleaner is very heavy which I hope will help it last longer.  I wish I could have given this only 4.5 stars since the green tile attachment does not stay on.  This was a problem on my old models and continues to be a problem on this one.  I finally taped it on since you need it to ensure that you pull out a maximum amount of water.  And I am also puzzled by the tanks:  why aren't they able to hold the same amount of water.  I often filled the dirty water tank before the clean water tank was empty. Logically, I couldn't pull more out than was put down???  In spite of these two issues, I love this cleaner.  It is perfect for residential use...not perfect but it certainly gets the job done and is cheaper than paying others to clean your floors or than renting machines at the grocery.  Love it.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
We had a hoover carpet cleaner previously for six years...and it saved us from ever replacing our light beige carpets in our last house despite the abuse of multiple kids and dogs. Our old hoover still cleaned like a champ however it was impossible to really clean!
So I chose to stay loyal to Hoover and went with the Max 77. A main attraction was the apparant ease of keeping it clean.

Heavy? yep
Easy to clean ? yep
Good size containers ? yep
Cleans well? appears to
Sucks? NO! It lays down a LOT of water, and the dirty water reservoir is fairly empty. Therefore our carpet stays wet.
Note: our old hoover left it almost entirely dry immediately!

So moral of this story...consumer loyalty doesn't pay off these days

Helpful hint to pet owners...you never really know what your pets are really doing to your carpet until you use a black light in the dark. Use a black light to locate piddle stains...use your cleaner over the spot..and only when that spot disappears under the black light can you be certain, its gone.

Another 411: DON'T USE SOAP ON YOUR CARPETS! soap will ruin your carpet! The professionals will tell you this. We tried and tried different soaps to reduce /eliminate pet odors and they added to the smell problem. The soapy water is going down into the pad along with whatever you're trying to clean up, possibly to the subfloor and never quite extracted out fully (that grosses me out!). So....get in touch with a water softener company and get yourself an RO system. Water treated through an RO systems breaks down dirt and stains WITHOUT SOAP! Promise! We use our cleaner several times a week on off white berber carpets and you can't tell we have a dog with a bladder issue and a puppy still in training.
