review_title: NO Extraction of Water -- This SUCKS (not!)
text:
I have an older Hoover steam carpet cleaner that I had for almost 3 years before its nozzle broke and the handle on the receiving tank broke, affecting the suction and operation. Also, the hose hook was broken. Coincidentally, I found out that for once I purchased a 3 Year "Purchase Protect" (via Sears) on this machine which supposedly would give me a freebie if it's broken. ALAS, the policy required it to be fixed instead.

Two weeks later after dropping off the machine at Sears for service, it still wasn't back from Service. I was getting a new mattress delivered that day, and so I neeeeeeeded to clean up old BAD DOGGIES' pee spots around the old bed frame. So I bit the bullet and bought a Hoover MaxExtract 77 blindly but being assured it's "top-of-the-line." Took it home, assembled it easily and took it out for a test spin before the mattress delivery ....

I noticed I used two tankfuls of water and two of detergent as well, but my dirty water tank was still near-empty. I mean, I'm talking 2 Tablespoons of water to the 2 gallons dumped on it! It cleaned well, and the brushes spun fine ... but where was all my dirty water? And why is this called MAX-EXTRACT when it really was a MINIMUM extract? And again, where's all my dirty water?! Ummmm-- in the rugs. GROSS.

Figuring the first time was a fluke and operator error, I read the instruction manual again, cleaned all the tanks and filters, loaded it up to clean a less plush rug in my living room today. Same thing -- two tanks of water, no ... I mean NO ... uptake. I ran the machine on FULL SUCK ONLY and got a wee bit of water but nohwere near what there should have been.

I returned this (non) sucker to Sears today for a full refund ... and found that my old cleaner was now back (FINALLY!) from Service. On the way out the door, I found that it was returned without the water/detergent tank!!! GRRRRRR. Even though I know this part can be ordered, I am just entirely and thoroughly peeved with Sears (non-)service.

Looks like I'll be buying a Bissell ... and not from Sears!

review_title: The only vacuum I’ll use for non carpeted floors and stairs
text: I’ve been a professional house cleaner for over 15 years, I’ve always used this vacuum to clean non carpeted areas and stairs, as well as hard to reach areas (also great for vacuuming your vehicle). A few tips- do not use the large floor attachment for floors (does not allow the vacuum to suction well because the hole is small) Instead, use the second largest attachment with soft bristles for all hardwood or vinyl floors. Another tip, use the attachment that has “teeth” without bristles for carpeted stairs.- this is what I used in the picture (use a up and down motion to create a pattern) Another tip, if you get a clog- remove the hose from the canister and attach the hose to the rear or of canister (open the flap in the rear and a filter and hole will be there). Turn the machine on once you’ve attached the hose to the rear of the canister and this will blow in reverse and unclog anything that was stuck in the hose. I admit the “new and improved “ models do not last as long as they used to- but still is a great machine if you know how to use it.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
Carpet Cleaning Excellent. Cleaned an extremely soiled carpet at the top of my stair landing, my foster dog was apparently trained to urinate on carpets, it's been a struggle(for the past 9 months). The carpet was so soiled, even after using my other carpet cleaner that I was ready to remove it. Even after cleaning with the other manual cleaner and quality soap it still smelled like urine. I cleaned this once with the Hoover and stains are barely there (keep in mind this was extemely filthy) all of the smell is gone. It fully dried in about an hour. It felt mildly damp when I was done vacuuming, so it didn't oversoak the carpet and did pull the water. I like that I can see the dirty water container as one can conveniently see the filthy water being pulled out. I like that the unit will stop running if the filthy water container is at capacity. ***This has made a positive improvement in the quality of my house - my whole family was happy that I could finally clean this area***

***NOTE - Keep in mind Hoover recommends to use only their soap products with this unit to not damage the plastics fo the unit. More than likely to ensure that the plastic containers are not damaged or fogged which some soaps can create. Their 2x soap product was excellent. I haven't tried the Pet product but my local Home Depot rep said they have had excellent feedback. The soaps are decent prices.

Ease of use. It is literally easy and quick to use, it is literally like vacuuming except it is cleaning the carpet. I prevacuumed well first, then cleaned the carpet, carpet cleaning was same time as vacuuming.

Hand scrubber-good. I'd like more scrubbing power on the hand tool although the scrubber this is a good addition. The hose for the manual device is long so I could reach half my stairs with the unit at the top and half from the bottom. The scrubber speed did not seem to change when I changed the speed selection on the Hoover.

Lanolium - Good - I placed the squeege on and used for lanolium but it didn't seem to pull the water as much as I'd like it to. . . however, I may have not carried out the proceedure correctly.

Convenient logical tool storage - excellent. The unit carries all of the tools they snap on somewhere on the body for ease of use, no having to go back to the vacuum closet.

Easy set up / Easy clean up - very convenient set up. I found also very logical ability to figure out how to assemble and unassemble. The soap and water are stored on the unit during cleaning, the container does unattach easy to fill at the sink - however filling when it is on the unit is easy too. The dirtly water retention is easy to remove, easy to disassemble with one click to clear out rug fiber. Also there is a screen behind the cleaning area, very convenient to access. The bottom scrubber is easy to remove if needed with one click. As a self test, I wanted to see if I could figure out the system without reading the instructions, I found I could figure out all assemblies without issue, items are well marked and snap in securely, the items user friendly to assemble.

Transportation - This unit is designed to be carried by the waste container handle, it is well balanced. It is a little heavy but for me worth the trouble. If someone had back issues, they'd need help (I'm a 120lb female - so may have felt a little more heavy for me.)

Quality of parts - excellent. The quality of containers seem to be thick plastics the hose for the eternal tool is also durable. The parts snap in and out firmly so the assembly does keep its integrity.

I wish I had this 8 years ago when my beagle started having urinary issues. This would have saved me having to remove my downstairs carpet - which is now all wood. It is well worth the price to improve quaility of living and also save time in having to try to spot clean areas or manually clean areas with my old unit.

Upon arrival is looked exactly like our original except the color is different (grey versus beige).  I used it for the car and it is in little quieter, but seems to have just as much suction.  We will see if this one lasts as long as the other one, assuming we are still around in 40 years.

incident_description: early april 2021, i purchased an led neon sign from yellow pop usa.  hello@yellowpop.com . i found the general quality of the product poor (made in china) and the electrical power component supplied potentially dangerous to children, adults and pets. my concern about the safety issue was presented to two individuals at yellow pop and brought no results. i was told by both individuals (i have emails) that my issue of high voltage electrocution is of no concern as the led power supply is "low voltage".  well the 120 volt ac power cord terminals (directly from the wall outlet) are completely exposed and the owners manual for the power supply (online power supply manufacturer) states specifically under "hazards" that the component is to be mounted in an enclosure. obviously the power supply manufacture understands this high voltage unit is to be shielded to avoid an electrocution hazard. yellow pop scoffs at the concern and so far has refused restitution to me. i have photos of the power supply and a link to the power supply owners manual posted below. the power supply that came with the sign by yellow pop (to lay openly exposed on the floor or mount exposed on the wall) is a model lrs-150-12 at www.meanwell.com . the warning to shield this unit is on the meanwell website. since potentially thousands of these power supplies were supplied to u.s. customers for their led signs, i believe this is a potential hazard that needs to be addressed due to the exposed high voltage wires creating a shock hazard. i emailed the underwriters laboratory may 7, 2021 and they informed me by telephone today, may 12, 2021 that this is a serious hazard issue and yes, that this power supply is designed to be covered and installed as part of a component. they also mentioned that my complaint is out of their jurisdiction however as the yellow pop product is not "ul approved".  they recommended that i contact saferproducts.gov.

review_title: Flawed design. Poor water extraction. Weak 10amps
text:
[[VIDEOID:15750bedb91770ebe9fe7d0b4eac5c3b]] Based on my recent experience with this used unit in good condition (Model FH50230 manufactured in 2010) I suggest anyone who
owns this Hoover devote 60 seconds to determine if their unit has suction diversion issues. According to the manual (and customer service) when the handle is in the upright position all the suction should be diverted to the hose. Conversely, when it is being used to clean carpet (handle unlocked) all suction should be applied to the carpet head.

1) Turn the unit ON and leave handle locked in the upright/vertical position. Slide a piece of newspaper under the carpet head suction strip and cover the entire length of the suction channel to determine if any suction is present. My unit grabbed the newspaper. After the newspaper blocked the head the suction at the hose was significantly greater.

2) With the unit still ON unlock the handle and lean it against the wall or table. Remove
the hose from the cradle to determine if any suction is being diverted to the hose. My unit had some suction at the hose when all suction should have been at the carpet suction guide.

I typically rescue and refurbish abandoned units from the sidewalk before they meet the trash masher, like the DYSON vacuum last month, but this Hoover was spotted at a Goodwill. The first observation was the good condition of this unit. It wasn't clogged with lint or debris and wasn't abused. Why was it dropped off? It sounded OK and all the attachments were there so I risked $20. It didn't take long to confirm the Amazon comments regarding poor water extraction. Within twenty minutes of toying around with the unit I noticed the issues involving suction loss. I assume this unit is performing as designed, so I am at a loss to explain why anyone could be pleased with this model if they paid over $200, if it has the same symptoms. This 2010 model, FH50230, appears identical to the one currently for sale on Amazon except for minor wheel design difference. I believe the current unit is FH50240 and that newer model got poor reviews at the HOOVER site. 2 star average with 130 reviews.

Try the simple duct tape modifications shown in the video to enhance suction. You will have to remove the duct tape patch blocking suction to the hose before using the hose, and also remember to block the suction at carpet strip with duct tape when using the hose. To achieve maximum suction for carpet cleaning cover that square outlet with duct tape to prevent suction being applied to the hose when you are cleaning carpet.

This unit received ONE star despite modest $20 cost. I intend to return this useless device. The Maxextract77 has abysmal reviews at WMart site, managing only 2.5 of 5 stars. Even AFTER the duct tape modifications on this unit it only managed to remove 1.5 quarts of 4 quarts applied to the carpet, a paltry 40 percent. I expected a minimum of 2 quarts/50 percent. The results of this type of test depends on the users expertise and technique. I did two or three suction passes after each application pass using the rinse cycle only. High quality units can extract 70 to 90 percent but those are probably professional grade.

My older Hoover Legacy model has a design which avoids the apparent pitfalls of "automatic suction diversion". I am referring to the position of the handle automatically determining where suction is being applied. The Legacy has a design which requires users to insert the hose nozzle into a port in order to divert the suction. The MaxExtract77 boasts a few design refinements (emptying and filling tanks, screen cleaning) which the Legacy lacks, but the Legacy received a glowing 4 star review. I believe the Legacy managed to extract 50 to 55 percent if memory correct. Perhaps that was due to the fact the older Legacy model (F7227900) is 12 amps and the newer MaxExtract77 are 10 amps. Once again we see newer isn't always better, and frequently cheaper/inferior. The older Legacy model achieved FOUR stars with over 1,000 reviews at the Hoover site and I concur with that rating.

A call to the Hoover toll free line was disappointing. That rep indicated she has been on the job for two years but was unable to tell me what the best result which can be expected, in regards to water extraction, if the user is doing everything right. She seemed to think 40 percent was OK. The rep could not explain why I was getting suction at the hose when the unit was in carpet cleaning mode OR why there was suction at the carpet in upholstery cleaning mode.

I made one other minor modification using clear silicone to make certain the unit was not losing suction at the gasket on the suction guide. I am referring to the yellow gasket between the two pieces of plastic held together by 10 screws, with the channel at the tip that contacts the carpet. That piece snaps off easily and comes apart for cleaning, but I use an large plastic wire tire dislodge debris rather than take it apart. I opened it up by removing the 10 screws and put a small bead of silicone on the yellow gasket. That gasket looked like hard rubber rather than foam, so it could have been losing a little suction, but I did not confirm any loss there before taking the precaution of the silicone. The older Hoover Legacy model has a suction guide which is one piece and lacks lacks the gasket and screws, but it does have small round door to clean out the suction guide, which I keep covered with duct tape to prevent any suction loss. I also noticed the gasket between the top half of the dirty water tank and the bottom was worn. Since I only use the cap to empty the tank I put a strip of duct tape on the outer seam of those two components to prevent any suction loss.

I am now under the impression any HOOVER product that garners a favorable review from users (4 stars or more) indicates they created a good product by accident. There is NO excuse for older models to perform better than newer designs.

WHY EXTRACTION IS SO IMPORTANT. Leaving behind 60 to 70 percent of the liquid applied to a carpet means washing solution residue remains on the carpet. Even with a unit capable of extracting 50 percent (or more) I never use these devices to apply cleaning solution. I prefer to use a pump-up garden sprayer to apply cleaning solution, paying extra attention to high traffic areas or spots, and use these units only for hot water rinsing. After applying cleaning solution with the garden sprayer I use a shag rug rake, scrub brush or nylon broom. Leaving cleaning solution in the carpet will result in dingy, matted down carpet.

text:
I purchased this to replace a Bissell that I have never been too happy with - heavy, weak performance, awkward tank system. I researched cleaners on Consumer Reports and saw that Hoover did consistently better than Bissell. I liked this one because of the low weight and so many reviews that lauded the suction power. My cleaner arrived last week and I have used it twice already on heavy-use carpets in my family and bedroom. Both rooms have been the recipients of recent dog illnesses (from a large dog) which I have spot treated, but still were obvious to a casual observer.
Assembly was simple and the instructions were easy to follow. The tank system is easy to use with very easy caps that secure nicely for the water and cleaner. It comes with a small bottle of concentrated cleaner so I didn't have to run out to the store to buy a bottle.
I used in both rooms and was amazed at how much dirt came up and how easy it was to re-fill and empty. I had used my Bissell on my bedroom only 3 months ago yet I was dumping black water with each use. I went over the pet-soiled areas 2-3 times in different directions. When I was done, I couldn't find the stains anymore. Equally impressive was that the carpet was dry to the touch in less than 6 hours. I cleaned it at 4PM and was walking barefooted by bedtime with no concerns for slipping or wet feet. The family room went similarly well. This was more impressive since we had this room professionally cleaned 3 months ago. Both carpets look great and are fluffier - I'm thrilled. My only complaint is that I had to predict how much cleaning solution I would need since I can't re-use the concentrate after I have dilluted it in the tank. Not so much a complaint about the cleaner as about the cleaning solution (or my lack of foresight).
My only concern, based on Amazon reviews, is the machine's longevity. Hopefully that will not be a problems, since I don't use my cleaner often.

With the 7412, I'd have to replace the roller after every 5 uses or so because the plastic pin would shear off the roller if it got the slightest built clogged with hair - this one doesn't seem to clog up as easily, and pin that turns the brushroll is a different design and appears to be much sturdier. incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

Note - for low pile carpets/area rugs (i.e. outdoor/indoor types) use the hardwood floor attachment. It worked great on our living room area rug which is technically an outdoor/indoor but with the dog we didnt want to take chances on expensive area rugs.

text:
At the recommendation of my son's physical therapist, I got these and the Hape Put-Stay Rattle set to help encourage my kiddo to pull up to stand by his mirror and for some fine motor stimulation. Both sets of toys are excellent, so if the cost is a concern I would actually go with the other set.

We like that each of the toys is a different shape for him to manipulate and that they are made from dishwasher safe silicone. The rattles are more of a dull sound, which I find to be pleasing. The kiddo loves to chew on the pink one. All three suction very well and it does take him some effort to get them off. (A good thing!)

After reading the other reviews, I was careful to tell my husband not to suction them to his head. At first he was a bit indignant, but realized that I was probably right to warn him. :)

text:
I bought this in 2013, along with an extra cloth bag. It is the handiest vacuum cleaner I have ever used. It is light, easy to move around and easy to store. It is not fancy - no wheels, no super filters, no extra options, nothing but a small vacuum cleaner. However, I love that I can pick it up and bring it anywhere in the house. I swap between two inner cloth bags.I always have one in use and one clean. It has a super long power cable so that I can plug it in and vacuum the kitchen and bathroom without needing to change the power source. The suction is good. Like any vacuum cleaner, occasionally larger items like pieces of paper get sucked in and block the hose. However, it is simple to undo and clean.

The suction hose comes in sections that clip together, making them secure. The various head attachments also clip onto the suction hose.

It is also easy to remove/replace the bags. Remove the hose by twisting and unlocking, open the little door and viola! the bag is right there, easy to remove/replace.

My only quibbles are:
1) the strap for the cable: it had a snap clasp for closure... an impossibly hard clasp to snap. Also it was loose, not attached to anything and so always in danger of being misplaced. Had hoover not heard of velcro? I swapped the original strap for a velcro cable tie that attaches to the cable and keeps the cable organized when not in use.

2) The afore mentioned clips that make the suction hose and attachments clip together so securely also prevent you from using other parts from other vacuums you may have as they do not attach. If you are like me, you have lots of those pieces and usually they are fairly interchangeable. Not so with this vacuum.

Overall, I am very pleased with it. I use it far more often than our dyson vacuum cleaner!

text:
I have cleaned living room , 3 bedroom carpets, my 2) 5' x 7' area rugs that are in my entry which has hardwood floors.. my cars' floor mats, the carpet in my car., my tile, my carpeted steps , my living room couch and love seat..
I absolutely love this multi surface cleaner..
I've had no issues what so ever .
Here's the best things about this machine...
There's one canister you fill with Just water.. There is a cylinder inside that canister for your cleaning solution..
So you can spray your solution going forward and there's these tiny brushes that circulate to scrub your surface.. Then once you have cleaned it... When you go backwards you spray just water to rinse .. That way your carpet is cleaner and feels better because you've rinsed the cleaner out of the carpet.. So it's not stiff.. ❤️❤️❤️
There is a dirty water container too...
I have another steamer made by a competitor that has a heater on it.. That's it..
But this Hoover is not only a steam cleaner with the hot water you put in it.. But a shampoo'er too...
So if it heated the water too.. That would be great..
I seen others have had issues with the little green scrubbers.. They are replaceable.. They come off easily to do such.. But I've had no issues with them..
One thing that's a must...
When you go to empty your dirty water .. There is a little screen .. It's red.. And is held in place by a yellow rubber casing.. This needs to be cleaned often.. Just check it when you empty the dirty water...

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
One improvement that have not seen many people mention is that the dirty water tank has a fully opening top With a convenient handle. This allows cleaning the tank much better than in previous models. The seal and cover shape are designed so that the cover is removed and replaced very easily.

Another excellent improvement over other Hoover models I have owned is that there are removable screen filters which can be cleaned after each use. This lessens the likelihood of lint buildup throughout the system.

I am really glad they got rid of the foot operated power switch from previous models which can be easily confused with the upright release lever. The power switch is located half way up the upright body within easy reach.

Another positive is that most of the parts are removable and can be cleaned after each use, including the brushes nozzle and filters

My carpets have never looked fluffier or cleaner this is an excellent piece of machinery. I can't believe the amount of dirt this thing pulled out of my fairly new carpets; absolutely amazing. Also I love the smell of the new Hoover Cleaning solution. The scent is of roses and Geraniums.

One criticism I have is that the instruction sheet is really not well done. I thought they could have done a better job at explaining the cleaning process. I don't think the physical build of this machine is as durable as in previous model, s however I do not think that it is a performance hindrance.

One thing I have found with floor cleaning machines such as these is that you have to be careful the way you store them or else you'll shorten the life of the machine significantly. Always store the tanks with any of the seals free from any contact with the other parts. In other words do not reassemble the tank lids and caps while the machine is in storage. This will help ensure that the seals remain dry and in better shape. It is extremely important to thoroughly clean and trying the machine each time after use before storage. I have a feeling people who are having problems with these machines are not cleaning drying and storing properly.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: One slight detail, works great otherwise.
text:
The machine was simple to put together, pretty much already assembled and easy to figure out. It cleans really well and the water system is really simple compared to my last cleaner.

The one detail that is annoying is the hole in the back of the machine. The hole is not a mistake, it was put there as part of the design to relieve water if it builds up where it should be going into the rest of the machine by the release valves below the water tank. Typically the water wont even need to go out, but it does a lot for this one. The dripping comes out when tilted back, but goes away quickly when it's turned on and moving. The dripping is mild and not bad considering I am just going to be cleaning it anyways.

Other than that the machine is as described and works great.

i bought one after i kept seeing pro hotel staff using them. we have 1200 sq ft of concrete floors, about 150 sq ft of loop carpet. for that i bought a Hoover rug attachment. for carpet, buy a carpet tool. whatsa problem?

it's a lovely tool, not a consumer feel good product.

review_title: Hose is too brittle and too short.
text: I was impressed by the power, efficiency and its easy portability but unimpressed by its ergonomics. The flexible hose is far too short and the metal extension tube much too long, with the result that it's difficult to manoeuvre, especially in tight corners, up above head-level and on stairs. However, it's fairly manageable. My main complaint is that the said hose-part ruptured at the joint where it attaches onto the machine—after six months!. The result is that I have had to order a new part and have been without a vacuum cleaner for two weeks! The material used for the hose is far too brittle for the amount of stain it has to undergo, thanks to its disproportionate length. The old model we had, purchased in 1983 continued to work very well for 30 years, when at the end of last year the hose ruptured in the same place as the new one did. No doubt materials were made better in those days. We are still using an old upright Hoover that belonged to my mother-in-law and which has been in constant use since the sixties! Those were the days!

text: I was impressed by the power, efficiency and its easy portability but unimpressed by its ergonomics. The flexible hose is far too short and the metal extension tube much too long, with the result that it's difficult to manoeuvre, especially in tight corners, up above head-level and on stairs. However, it's fairly manageable. My main complaint is that the said hose-part ruptured at the joint where it attaches onto the machine—after six months!. The result is that I have had to order a new part and have been without a vacuum cleaner for two weeks! The material used for the hose is far too brittle for the amount of stain it has to undergo, thanks to its disproportionate length. The old model we had, purchased in 1983 continued to work very well for 30 years, when at the end of last year the hose ruptured in the same place as the new one did. No doubt materials were made better in those days. We are still using an old upright Hoover that belonged to my mother-in-law and which has been in constant use since the sixties! Those were the days!

text: I am very impressed with the Hoover MaxExtract 77 Multi-Surface Pro Carpet & Hard Floor Cleaner.  I used it for the first time and my hard floors are sparkling clean and my carpets have been revived.  I am impressed with the way that the cleaner brought the pile back up on my carpet.  Areas where there is no traffic (behind and under furniture) now blend in perfectly with the high traffic areas.  The cleaner is easy to use and pushes back and forth smoothly.  My hard floors were dry in no time.  I did learn that you need to check the screens each time you empty the dirty water tank for any lint/debris buildup, otherwise the carpet will remain very damp because the suction deminishes tremendously when the screens are full. this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,

I brought out this vacuum cleaner and attempted to vacuum up the dust in and around my appliances and water heater. I set the vacuum cleaner down on the dryer and began stretching out the hose when it suddenly snapped back together suddenly pulling the vacuum cleaner off the dryer. It landed with a great bang right on the faucet at the bottom of the water heater and snapped it right off causing water to gush into the room with terrible force. Understand, the vacuum cleaner is rather heavy, but the hose is so tight and contracts with such force that it jerked that heavy object right off the dryer in an instant! If anyone is willing to deal with that, I wish you well, but I curse this thing. Dealing with that hose while cleaning an entire house would be exhausting. For me, it is like wrestling a large reptile!

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: Strong suction for a mid-size vacuum
text:
My vacuum arrived today and I am pretty happy with it. It was certified refurbished and it appears to have all the parts and instructions. It wasn't in an original box and it had a couple of scratches on the lower section but otherwise in nearly new shape. I tried it with the roller on carpet and with the hose on bare floor. It has nice strong suction either way. In fact, the instructions tell you to adjust it for lower suction for use with the hose and attachments, which I did.

The biggest pros are the power and suction for the size and price, and that is isn't too loud for its size and power (I've had 2 Bissels that were louder and didn't clean as well). The suction was almost as good as my old Kenmore canister vacuum that was 3 times the price. There are a few minor downsides. The place where the hose detaches from the body of the vacuum is a little awkward and mine slipped apart a couple of times when I was using it as an upright until I made sure it was firmly connected; then it was fine. The on/off switch is not is the most convenient place. The old Kenmore had the switch right in the handle and that was very convenient. A few other uprights I have used had the switch near the bottom so you could use your foot to turn it on and off. This one has a switch on the body about halfway down so you have to reach down to turn it on or off. But this is minor. Several other vacuums I looked had other, more awkward design features. The model has a hose that is off the floor and not stretched when it isn't being used. The attachments are supposed to all store on the vacuum but I haven't got the last 2 on right yet. But the ones I tried worked fine.

Time will tell how well this machine lasts. (I paid for a 2 year warranty). But I am optimistic since I have had other Shark vacuums that have lasted well. I still have a little dustbuster style cordless Shark that runs great after 2 years. I liked it so much I got my mom the same one and she likes it too.

incident_description: early april 2021, i purchased an led neon sign from yellow pop usa.  hello@yellowpop.com . i found the general quality of the product poor (made in china) and the electrical power component supplied potentially dangerous to children, adults and pets. my concern about the safety issue was presented to two individuals at yellow pop and brought no results. i was told by both individuals (i have emails) that my issue of high voltage electrocution is of no concern as the led power supply is "low voltage".  well the 120 volt ac power cord terminals (directly from the wall outlet) are completely exposed and the owners manual for the power supply (online power supply manufacturer) states specifically under "hazards" that the component is to be mounted in an enclosure. obviously the power supply manufacture understands this high voltage unit is to be shielded to avoid an electrocution hazard. yellow pop scoffs at the concern and so far has refused restitution to me. i have photos of the power supply and a link to the power supply owners manual posted below. the power supply that came with the sign by yellow pop (to lay openly exposed on the floor or mount exposed on the wall) is a model lrs-150-12 at www.meanwell.com . the warning to shield this unit is on the meanwell website. since potentially thousands of these power supplies were supplied to u.s. customers for their led signs, i believe this is a potential hazard that needs to be addressed due to the exposed high voltage wires creating a shock hazard. i emailed the underwriters laboratory may 7, 2021 and they informed me by telephone today, may 12, 2021 that this is a serious hazard issue and yes, that this power supply is designed to be covered and installed as part of a component. they also mentioned that my complaint is out of their jurisdiction however as the yellow pop product is not "ul approved".  they recommended that i contact saferproducts.gov.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

incident_description:
the submitter said he installed 80 units, 1 on each condo porch, at the address below. the submitter said he began installing them in september 2016 and stopped in early january 2017.

the submitter said approximately 25 units have burned up or stopped working. he said the first incident occurred in september and then a few weeks later a few more burned up.

the submitter then contacted the firm and informed them of the incidents. the submitter said the firm was unresponsive.

in early january a firm local sales rep., [redacted] witnessed the submitter remove one of the units that had burned up. the submitter said the rep. advised him the unit was properly installed. the rep., sent he unit to their testing lab and received notice that the unit was too damaged to determine a cause of failure. 

(april 2017) the submitter said he filed a complaint with national fire protection association (nfpa) regarding the defective units. he said shortly after he filed the report the firm contacted him to obtain more information and denied receiving a complaint about the issue. 

the firm asked the submitter to send them the units but the submitter only sent 5, some that were burned and others that just stopped working. the firm advised the submitter that their findings showed the units had been excessively wet and caused the failures. however, the submitter states these units are water resistant and are intended to be used in outdoor outlets. the submitter believes the firm is denying that there is a defect with the units. the submitter believes the units should be tested by cpsc and recalled. the submitter said he removed all 80 units and has 5 in his possession. 

the submitter said he installed another brand gfci receptacles on the condo porches approximately 5 weeks ago and there hasn't been an incident.

text:
DON'T BUY THIS PRODUCT !!!!!!!!! I purchased this vacuum about 5 years ago and liked it so much I ordered another recently. Hoover must have changed the design on the lever that holds the main vacuum hose to the unit and the same lever is supposed to keep the bag door from opening. The new vacuum that I just received has a lever that does not perform the two functions. it either keeps the hose in place or it keeps the bag door closed. The failure of this lever to perform both functions means you need to keep a third hand available (if you have a third hand) in order to keep the vacuum together while you're vacuuming. Really bad design change. Never had this problem with the same vacuum purchased 5 years ago. Thinking this was an anomaly, I contacted Amazon and they graciously send me a replacement vacuum. I received it today and it has the same problem. The issue is not an anomaly. It seems to have been a very bad design change by Hoover. I contacted Hoover customer service and have yet to hear from them on how they plan to address this issue, or if I need to purchase another supplier's vacuum. I'll update this review once I hear from Hoover. In the meantime, stay away from this vacuum cleaner.

UPDATE - Hoover did not respond to my email, so I called them and spoke to someone who simply gave me a contact for a local Hoover Warranty claims repair location. Before lugging the brand new vacuum to the repair center, I called them to describe my problem (with two brand new vacuum cleaners). I'm glad I called. The repair center stated that if I brought the new portapower vacuum to them, there is NOTHING THEY COULD DO TO FIX THE PROBLEM if that is the way the product is manufactured now by Hoover. Wow, who would have expected Hoover to assume their customers would tolerate such an inferior product.

text:
I really wanted to love this vacuum. It is beautifully designed, at least if you like a rugged, commercial aesthetic. Pieces click to together in a satisfying way, and the chrome gleams against the gray and orange color scheme. I really enjoyed putting it together. I enjoyed the fact that it is not as loud as my previous Hoover, and the children and cats did not flee the room in terror when I turned it on.

However, when it came to using it on our hardwood floors, it did not perform. I felt like I was chasing the dirt around, rather than sucking it up. I had to put my hand over the nozzle to make sure that it really was functioning, and yes, if you place your hand right over the tube, you can feel suction. A moderate amount of suction. I found that if I swept really well ahead of time, it might pick up some of the stray leftover dirt. But forget about anything stuck in the cracks between the floorboards. If I didn't sweep really well, I was on my knees, picking up bits of tissue and stray threads that the vacuum had failed to suck up. With some experimentation, it became clear that the suction was not strong enough to spread over the floor cleaning tools with any effectiveness, and the best result was achieved with the crevice tool or the bare nozzle. Sweeping a 1 inch tube back and forth over the entire surface area of our small home would make vacuuming a long and dull task.

Just so you know, if you are purchasing bags to use with this machine, you also need to purchase an adapter, another $10 or so. The adapter is just a funnel with a little rubber band type thing that you roll onto the neck of the bag. When you replace the bag, you are faced with the gaping maw of funnel as you fumble with the rubber band thingy. This wouldn't be a dealbreaker if the machine actually worked, but I was sort of unhappy that I would be faced with staring at/breathing the stuff I just vacuumed off the floor.

The vacuum that I'm replacing is nothing fancy, just a 10 year old upright hoover, an unglamorous plasticky and clunky machine whose suction has seen better days. This new Hoover has weaker suction than the 10 year old Hoover. It's going back where it came from. I don't really understand how this product has such good reviews-- it doesn't seem like it would be very much help if you have any real dirt to clean. I don't feel like I have especially high expectations for a vacuum, but if this is the story with vacuums at this price range, I might have to double my budget and splurge on an entry level Miele. In fact, I just did.

review_title: Great on carpets, not so great on tile
text:
I purchased this unit because I needed a carpet cleaner and considered it a bonus that it cleaned hard floor as well. It performed great on my carpet - much better than anything I had been doing by hand.

This morning I decided to try cleaning my tile floor. I re-read the instructions to see if anything needed to be done differently. I came across this line: "How to Attach Squeegee for Hard Floor Cleaning (Available on select models only)" Well, my unit didn't have a squeegee which begs the question, "Why would any hard floor cleaner come without a squeegee?". This was a serious drawback as the floor barely dried after going over it several times. There is also considerable air blowing out of the side of the unit, blowing the cleaner solution out to the sides as it is sucking it up. Not a problem - I can catch the extra solution on the next pass UNLESS it is blown someplace that I can't access, like under the refrigerator.

The unit also has an automatic shutoff feature that stops suction when the dirty water tank is full. On tile, the automatic shutoff continued to engage when the tank was barely full. I learned that turning it off and turning back on fixed this problem, but it kept occurring every couple of minutes even after emptying the dirty water tank.

All the features of this machine, including attachments and suction, work wonderfully on carpet. I won't be using it on my tile floor again, though - expecting it to do equally well on both was just wishful thinking.
