text:
I read many reviews before purchasing this about a month ago. I was very excited, I had planned to use this mainly on stairs, a dog bed and fans. I use robot vacuums for most of my flooring. I had hoped to set this on the middle landing of the stairs and vacuum the 4 stairs down and the 4 stairs up. The hose is supper short, which i guess makes sense because they expect you to wear the vacuum. So needless to say I attached the hooks and wore the vacuum which is not heavy but it swings around, it is a hard plastic box and every time I shift it hits into walls or other things. Maybe a back pack where it is more stable vs shifting around all the time would do better but the only option hoover has is another bag that has the same one strap system where it would still swing around. So very disappointed in the hose/ carrying set up (plus I can not find a replacement hose that fits this model even the same length, but i went looking for a long hose)

Power cord, I have already stretched it out straight twice but it is a cheap cord that is prone to get kinks, I have been using it for a few weeks and for commercial grade this is bad. I have now circled the cord up, basically the way it came and clipped it to the vacuum and just use an extension cord so the cord doesn't kink up and break. The funny thing is when I read reviews before someone had complained about the cord saying it was kinking badly and had a picture, the company had responded that he was the first to complain about the cord, so it must have been something he had done, now that I look back I can not find that review?

Overall the vacuum is easy to clean and has good suction. My previous vacuum was a hoover windtunnel air series (which has lasted 9 years) the suction is the same. I was under the impression this would be stronger for 2 reasons, 1st It's commercial grade vs for houses so assumed, 2nd I had always heard a bagged vacuum has better suction than bagless but for all intensive purposes I cleaned half the dog bed with commercial grade and the other half with my 9 yr old vacuum and it took the same amount of work to get the same cleanliness. So yes the suction is good........but I would not say it met my expectations.

I hope a hoover representative reads this and maybe they will come out with a replacement hose, a long replacement hose, a different bag set up that hooks more securely to the human host so it can't swing into things, more attachments and for future vacuums spend a little more and get a good power cord or just make it very short and say buy your own extension cord.

All in all did not hit my expectations and I am disappointed in this purchase plus there are not options available to fix the above issues unless I just buy a whole different vacuum, which I did not want to have to do for another 9 years not a few months after buying this one.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: Never loses suction is 100% true, and how to extend wand and use old attachments,+Cord solution
text:
I am an inventor with many patents. Quite impressed with this design. The screen never gets clogged, they creating a centrifuge that throws even lint away from the screen in center (intake/suction) and it drops it to bottom. First vacuum have ever seen that does not clog. Simple and brilliant, no moving parts.

I asked question about wand not being long enough, the reason was the curtain cleaner works well on wood floors but is angled such that I at 6'-1" have to bend over to get it flat. I then came up with what is in the pic, took old bagged Oreck attachments, 3 wraps of duct tape to shim it up to right diameter, then used angle grinder to notch it for "catcher" hook like the Shark uses and inserted it. Works like a charm as the Oreck swivels so vacuum head can be flat at any angle. BTW the Shark system on snapping various parts of wand, hose , etc together is very nice and solid.

Best vac have ever used. Compared to Hoover Wind Tunnel no comparison, lighter, quieter, more suction and does not clog.

And on the cord being low and tripping people as mentioned here a lot. Easy solution. As you see in photo have a simple loop in cord that matches the top cord wrap post. That makes it a cord to top in a jiffy. If you want to detach as you see in pick just turn the post down, slide off, when done push on and turn post up. It is that easy.

this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

text:
We just had the windows replaced in our house, and as such moved around a lot of furniture. We decided to get one of these rug cleaners to do some deep cleaning since the furniture was already moved. I read the consumer reports article, which recommended the "Hoover Dual V Steam Vac All Terrain w/ Spin Scrub F7452-900". However, when I stopped by the local Walmart, this was the closest model they had so I picked it up.

My first complaint is that the instructions included in the cleaner were very confusing. It was apparently written for multiple models, and had a lot of statements such as "If your model has this, then do this. Otherwise do something else." There didn't seem to be no definitive description of what my model actually had. The video instructions for this model that I found on the Hoover web site were much better. Except they seemed to include features not on my model. The videos, for example, provided instructions for a "Surge" button; which the one I got from Walmart did not have. That was a bit confusing. Are there variations on the same model number?

Anyway, I found the cleaning to be substandard. It definitely sucked up a lot of dirt out of our carpets, but seems to have left just as much behind. The instructions spoke about heating this rug to make drying quicker; but my unit was not doing that and it took >12 hours for my bedroom carpet to dry; with a dehumidifier in it.

One thing I have to say is that the hand tool attachment that this unit comes with seemed to work very well. But, If I'm going to spot clean my whole rug; why pay money for this big heavy machine?

I returned it and am going to try again with the consumer reports recommended model; which is available on Amazon.

text: After having a bissell pro-heat 2x pet for about 3 years, with 3 repairs on the first unit, and having the second and third units completely replaced-- when the most recent one quit working again, we had just been given a gift card for an early Christmas present and decided, after researching a lot- to buy this unit. I used this the day it arrived on my downstairs carpets and was impressed. A few days later, I used it to clean upstairs when the dogs tracked mud down the hall and was again impressed. I just used it this morning and did the entire house and I have to say that my carpets look simply amazing. We live in military base housing and our carpets are on their last year of their lifetime but the carpets look better than they did the day we moved in (aside from some red juice stains that I didn't catch when they happened). After the 3 uses, the stubborn chocolate milk stains I had around are barely noticeable on our light... dirt colored carpet LOL.  The spin brushes really fluff the old matted carpet fibers-- I didn't expect it to really dry so fast as to "eliminate wet socks" as it says on the box-- but to be honest, it really does suction up water very well and dries very quickly... under 2 hours actually which is amazing. Alot of reviews complained about the tank size being "small" but this is way bigger than our bissell's tank was-- and it is consistent-- as soon as the dirty water tank is full, it stops sucking but at the exact same time, the detergent tank and clean water tank are empty-- its not disproportionate. It is also a breeze to clean... the bissell used to feel all slimy and gross in areas where dirt would cake in and you couldn't clean but not with this. No unscrewing to get to the brushes to clean them, everything pops on and off in two seconds. All in all, so long as this continues to work, I have no second thoughts about this purchase! Great machine! I have recommended it to many already!

Clean water goes in, cleans carpets, and goes to dirty water tank. So, you are never just re-using dirty water to go over the carpet.

Cleans carpets, does a great job. I personally don't fill the laundry detergent compartment to the full line, because it seems like it is overkill and leaves a lot of suds in the dirty water tank. However, even using less detergent, you really go through a lot of detergent, so the prices add up there.

The dirty water compartment has to be emptied frequently, and even cleaning one area rug can use 3 containers of water with detergent. However, for the way it cleans and makes everything nice and new and with how good it cleans, I don't mind buying the detergent. I just placed an order for more of it.

A suggestion: put it on rinse only first and go over it with just water. You will get a lot of dirt up that way. Then add the detergent and do the cleaning, and a decent amount of the crud will have already been rinsed away. Carpets stay moist for a little while, but hey have been bone dry the day after.

Great product, can't beat the price, just be prepared to buy detergent. I wish I had bought more than 2 bottles of it when I first ordered the vacuum because I'm currently waiting for my new order to arrive.

review_title: Hoover Max Extract 77 Multi-Surface Pro Carpet & Hard Floor Deep Cleaner, FH50240, Vs. Hoover SteamVac Carpet Cleaner with Clean
text:
s. Hoover SteamVac Carpet Cleaner with Clean Surge, F5914900

First off, for those of you who do not know, Hoover now belongs to a Chinese company. In many reviews I’ve read, people are unhappy about the lose of quality in Hoover products. This most likely is the reason.

This review compares the Hoover SteamVac Carpet Cleaner with Clean Surge, F5914900, with the Hoover Max Extract 77 Multi-Surface Pro Carpet & Hard Floor Deep Cleaner, FH50240.

I purchased a the Hoover Steam Vac from Amazon, but did not use it for more than a year. That was a mistake since it had a one-year warranty on it. Use your machine a lot when you first get it in case it breaks then it should still be under warranty. Also, before purchasing either of the machines, I suggest you check to see where the nearest authorized Hoover repair dealer is. It is a lot easier if you can take the machine to a local repair person, if needed.

The Steam Vac did a great job on carpets and small area rugs and I was very happy with it. It is easy to use and light enough that it is not hard to move back and forth. It got a lot of dirt out of the carpet as I could see by the dirty water I emptied into the sink. The carpets dried within 1.5 hours! I vacuumed the carpets first, then washed them with the Steam Vac, then later went over them again with only water to rinse them.
The rinsing get more of the soap out and the carpets looked fluffier. Then when they were dry, I vacuumed the carpets again to fluff them up more.

The upholstery attachment came with the Steam Vac. It also has a Clean Surge feature which lets you apply more detergent for heavily soiled areas. The Max Extract 77 does not have Clean Surge.

I used the Hoover carpet cleaning solution in the machine as there is a warning to use low-sudsing products, which is of course theirs! I also used Resolve spray and/or Carbona 2 in 1 Oxy-Powered carpet cleaner for the hard-to-remove spots.

This machine has a separate water tank and a separate cleaner/detergent tank. To rinse the carpet, you fill only the water tank, not the detergent tank.

The problems I had with the Steam Vac, are the same as those often mentioned in the Amazon reviews:

First, SteamVac Brush Block containing 5 Brushes doesn’t hold up well. One brush broke away from the block. I believe mine broke the second time I used the machine. However, I could still use it by, prior to turning on the Steam Vac, tilting the vac back a little and placing the brush in the block. It’s not at all ideal, but you can get by with doing that. A new brush block costs about $28.00 here on Amazon - expensive if you have to replace brushes.

Second, I found water leaks onto the floor when you tilt the handle part of the machine back to remove the dirty water tank. So I placed the machine on a tile floor when I was going to empty the machine. The leak comes from some water that remained in the machine after the water left the tank.

When I finished using the Steam Vac, I gave it a thorough cleaning and gave the parts time to dry before I put some of the parts back on. I did not put the brushed on when storing the machine.

Third, I purchased the Hoover SteamVac Bare Floor Cleaning Attachment 48417008 to use the machine on tile floors. So many people were complaining that this piece would not fit or stay on the machine. I found the same problem. The directions and the videos showing how to put it on the machine do not work. I followed those direction. I thought I had the attachment on properly and cleaned a tile floor. But after about 5-10 minutes, the attachment fell off. Finally, after trying to attache it several times, I continued without using the attachment - bad idea. I heard a snap and smelled a slight burning smell and the machine stopped working. I’m assuming water got into an electrical part, but I’m not sure. So my advice is if you buy this product only use it on carpets. If you want to clean hard floors, buy something else.

I took the machine to the local vac shop, which was the authorized Hoover repair place near me. The service man there said there was a problem with these machines and their turbo. The cost of fixing the machine and replacing the brush block would have been almost the price of buying a new machine. I did ask him to show me how to put the bare floor attachment on. He has some trouble getting it on, but eventually pressed on both sides and then it snapped into place. None of the directions stated to also press both sides to get it on.

The service man said a better improved model was the Hoover Max Extract 77 Multi-Surface Pro Carpet & Hard Floor Deep Cleaner, which did not have the turbo problems. Since the Steam Vac did such a good job and it would have cost me about the same price to have someone clean my carpets as to buy the Hoover Max Extract, I opted to buy a reconditioned Max Extract. The reconditioned machine costs about he same price I had paid for the Steam Vac, The reconditioned Max Extract has a 6-month warranty compared with a 2-year warrantee on a new one. If you ever buy a reconditioned machine, be sure to see what attachments come with new machines; you should get all those attachments with the reconditioned. One attachment was missing on the reconditioned, but it was on the Steam Vac so I had the service man take it off my old machine and put it with the reconditioned machine as this attachment fit both models.

The Max Extract also did a good job cleaning the carpets. It has a block of 10 brushes compared to the 5 brushes on the Steam Vac. The Max Extract is heavier than the Steam Vac so pushing it forward and pulling it back takes more strength. It doesn’t seem to work well on smaller area rugs 5 ft X 6 ft (the only size I tried the machine on) because the rug will not stay on the floor when you pull the machine toward you. I think this is because this machine has a strong suction that makes it pull up the smaller carpet, thus it’s name MAX Extract. To clean smaller carpets, you would need to weigh down the ends of the carpet somehow. I was able to clean the 5 X 6 rug by going back and forth with the machine along the short side of the carpet, the 5 foot side. But it was harder to use on the 5X6 rug than on the larger carpets and I found it a pain to do this. If you have a lot of small carpets, I would not recommend this machine.

The Max Extract has a combined water and detergent tank. There is a knob in the front of the tank that you switch to point to wash if you are going to clean the rug. By doing so, the detergent and the water are dispensed onto the carpet at the same time. If you have the knob pointed to rinse, no such mixing takes place when you squeeze the lever to dispense the water. I found it difficult to notice when the machine was out of water. You really have to pay attention to that or you wind up cleaning the carpet with detergent only, which I found myself doing. I did not find this problem with the Steam Vac.

The Max Extract did not leak water when I tilted the handle part slightly back to remove the dirty water tank.

Many people complained that this machine leaked water on the rug while they were cleaning the carpet and their rug was getting soaked. I did not find that problem. The service man from whom I purchased the machine told me that many people forget to put the screw the knob back on that they took off to empty the dirty water compartment. It is easy to do that. I found myself almost doing it once. If it is not on, some water will go on to the floor rather than all of it going into the dirty water tank.

I had asked the service man to show me how to work the machine and how to get the parts on and off. I recored him doing it with my smart phone. I knew I would need to see again how it is done when I was ready to use the machine as some of the parts are tricky at first to get them back on. After using the machine, you know how to do it.

The Bare Floor attachment came with the Max Extract. But the service man at the store where I bought the machine could not get the attachment on. Luckily I had asked him to show me how to get it on. He tried several Bare Floor attachments that he had and none of them would stay on the machine. (Did I mention Hoover was now owned by a Chinese company!) He looked at each bare floor attachment he tried and said they each were missing 2 of the tabs and that he was going to order one for me. To date I have not received it so I will return to the store to ask about it. It could turn out that I will not be using this machine on tile floors, which would not make me happy.

When I finished using the Max Extract, I gave it a thorough cleaning and gave the parts time to dry before I put some of the parts back on. I did not put the brushed on when storing the machine. I have used the Max Extract 2 times as of this writing. Everything seems to be working fine but time will tell. I intend to use this machine a lot during the 6-months it is under warranty so that I can be sure it is going to hold up. And if I get a bare floor attachment, I intend to do a lot of tile-floor cleaning before the 6 months is past. The reason I purchased these machines was to do carpets so I can live without the bare floor attachment work, but I’m not going to tell the service man that!

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: Buy it as a disposable item
text: I waited a year to judge my cleaner, so some of these issues could have been fixed.  I have found appliances like this only reveal themselves as a good or bad investment in the long term.  I shampoo the house and my vehicle upholstery about once a year and enjoy having a machine handy for when the kids or pets make a mess.  I previously owned a Bissel Pro-heat and it lasted about a year before the plastic started cracking and it quit dispensing the cleaning solution.  I kept it going with duct tape and by hand spraying the solution on the carpet ahead of where I was working.  Eventually water just trickled out of it and it was doing nothing but making my floors wet.  I would give that machine one star.  I decided to try the Hoover based on some reviews.  Initially it worked great.  It got lots of dirt out of the carpets and kept the floor reasonably dry.  (Though it requires frequent filling and emptying of the water during a job, one positive is that collection chamber is easy to clean out.)  In less than a year's time I started having trouble with the cleaning wand.  It leaks horribly at the trigger and it won't stop spraying when I release the trigger.  I took it apart and got it working for about 30 minutes more.  It's a really horrible design that was never intentioned to last.  (The water spray width never was a wide as the wand either, which I would have thought would have been sorted out as this thing was designed.  The result is narrow, wet stripes on the upholstery.)  By now the floors are wetter after use also.  It turned out to be another item like so many nowadays:  Built to be disposable and in the landfill in a few years.  I don't know if there is a good alternative in this price range (since I have not found it), but if you buy, expect this one to only last a couple years and factor that into your purchase.

review_title: ... one star just for the fact that it worked great for the three times I used it
text:
It gets one star just for the fact that it worked great for the three times I used it. The last hoover I had worked for 6 years (still worked when we decided to upgrade to this). This is what I wrote to the company about my experience:

Bought a hoover max extract 77, worked for a month and a half or so. Then the power stopped working so I had the power cord replaced at my cost. Then the machine wont spray any water from the clean water tank, it will only spray water from the cleaning solution. Contacted hoover 4 times over the phone. The first time I was told your handle now needs to be fixed, that's not under our warranty, click. Second time, I am told that the warranty only covers the motor so its not their problem. Get that last answer about the warranty another 2 times. Finally I contact them through email and they tell me again that if I would like I can drive an hour and a half away to have it looked at, on my dime, and that if it isn't the motor then its my problem to fix it. I spent almost two months trying to figure this out with them and now the military exchange wont even take it back. I only used it three times in those two months and now it doesn't even work and they refused to do anything about it. This is seriously ridiculous. I am now out on a lot of money that I don't have to waste for a huge piece of plastic that cant even be used as a paper weight. I used to only use hoover and I used to tell everyone about it. Now I will still tell everyone about it but it will be a much different story then before. If you are looking for this machine don't bother. Buy another brand. Now I get to go review my purchase on all the other sites. Thank you hoover for your outstanding help.

September 2,2014
UPDATE:
After writing that on their facebook page, they contacted me and apologized for the misinformation from the customer service people. They said they would have it addressed and sent me a new machine. They said the parts should have been covered under warranty. They were amazing and fixed the problem quickly. Very happy with their help. Hopefully nothing goes wrong with this one. :)

review_title: Great value, easy to clean carpet
text:
I've used this carpet cleaner for over a year and a half and as a whole, I'm very happy with it.

I have off-white carpets with 3 kids and a cat (and a husband who occasionally spills too ;-) ). This cleaner is the only way I can manage the kids + carpet combination. I am constantly disgusted by the grime that comes out of the carpet, but all those feet trekking through the house brings in lots of dirt and spills. I've used this vacuum to clean red Kool-Aid several times, poop ("look mom, I took my diaper off!"), potty-learning accidents, mud, chocolate ice cream syrup, blue popsicle, vomit, and even several stains that were already on the carpet from the previous owner that weren't removed by the hired professional carpet cleaners.

I did use the included carpet soap, though at a much lower concentration than suggested by the "fill" lines on the tank) and haven't bought any additional Hoover soap--I just haven't found it necessary even though the manual/warranty indicates it's necessary to only use Hoover soap. When I am giving the carpets an all-over clean, I either use water alone or water with white vinegar (the vinegar smell will evaporate away very quickly--vinegar is great for freshening/odor removal). For a targeted mess (see the above list of "whoops") I pre-treat the mess by spraying diluted ADVANAGE 20X Multi-Purpose Cleaner (usually lavender, sometimes citrus) directly on the affected area and then use plain hot water in the carpet cleaner to scrub and suck up the mess. I've not had any stains left behind yet.

I clean the carpet by using a quick forward pass while pulsing the water trigger, a quick backward pass without water, a *very* slow forward pass with no additional water to scrub the section of wetted carpet, and a *very* slow reverse pass to suck out all the water. My carpets are barely damp to the touch following this procedure--dry enough to walk on with clean socks but please no dirty shoes!--and dry within 15 minutes. I never hold the water trigger down, only pulse it, and when I say *very* slow, I mean much slower than you would ever use a normal vacuum. Think snail speed.

When I'm done, I try to move the unit onto a solid floor before turning it off so I can use a towel to wipe up the bits of water that will fall out of the unit once suction stops. Always take the clean water tank off if you're going to let the cleaner sit for a while to avoid any leaking. Try to keep the unit upright so the leaks stay in the reservoir. If you are done using it and want to dry it all out, tip it back on a solid surface floor to let any spilled water out and wipe it up with a towel.

Always rinse out the dirty water reservoir when you're done! I let the dirty tank air dry while fully open to keep it fresh and let the seals recover, before I replace the screw and door for storage. I store the vacuum without the tanks attached, and often with some water in the clean water tank so it's ready to go if I have an urgent spill (see: red Kool-Aid).

As many others have mentioned, it's essential to wipe off the mesh filters. I do this every time I am done by just smearing my finger on the mesh to get off as much fiber and dirt as I can. Every few uses I spray out the front piece that makes contact with the floor to suck out the mess (not sure what it's called) to get collected fuzz out, and pull carpet fuzz/hair out of the scrub brushes.

If it seems like you've lost suction, check that the hand attachment hose is firmly seated in its spot on the back of the vacuum. The hose end needs to be covered in order to achieve suction on the floor. Then re-check the mesh filters. Finally re-seat the dirty water tank *firmly.*

The hand unit isn't amazing though I don't use it much. I did use it once to clean vomit out of my almost-new car. In that process, I used auto upholstery cleaner to target the mess (and stink!) and then did lots of rinsing (spray, suck out water, repeat) with the hand unit. After a good drying in the sun with the windows open, the yuck smell was gone and I could tolerate to be in my own car again. Rinse out the hose when you're done! I sucked several gallons of clean, hot, water through the hose (keep an eye on the dirty tank level) to rinse.

I wouldn't buy this cleaner for the exclusive purpose of cleaning hard floors, but I really enjoy using it to clean my kitchen/dining area that is frequently messy/sticky. It's slower (and obviously louder) than a mop, but the fact that it's immediately dry is appealing so kids/husband don't walk through a damp floor with dusty shoes/feet and leave a tracked mess behind right away. I also have a steam mop, which is great for releasing a stuck-on/dried-on mess, but not so great about removing it rather than smearing it across the rest of the floor--this vacuum is nice in that it doesn't just spread the mess across the whole floor.

I haven't tried this on an area rug, only wall-to-wall carpeting.

My only complaints: 1) the tank screws either aren't coated at all or aren't coated well enough, and are corroding a lot. It doesn't impact functionality yet, but I do worry that will be a liability of this carpet cleaner being able to work well for a long time. 2) The brush speed lever isn't attached very well and it's tough to keep it set to power clean. When I remove the dirty tank, I set the brush speed back to #1 and restore it to #3 power clean after installing the empty dirty water tank next time I use the cleaner.

Overall, considering the price and how well it cleans my carpet, these "complaints" seem trivial in comparison. I bought it as a way to tolerate having carpet until we replace the carpet with hardwood because we wanted to do other house projects first, but it works so well that the carpet-to-hardwood replacement keeps sliding down the project list. In that regard, it works TOO well!

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
I wasnt expecting this to perform so well but as a first timer with resin casting, i have to say im impressed! Blanks are crystal clear, resin mixed and poured easy, dyed well, and had low odor

A couple tips for new users tho;

Do NOT get agressive with the mixing! Make sure its thoroughly mixed without introducing too much air. Once mixed, let it sit for 3 to 5 min to let the bubbles rise

The pot time of 40 min is very conservative, i got about a hour of working time myself.

The resin is 1:1 and VERY sensitive to this ratio! If your resin never hardens, or hardens too fast, your mix is not accurate, or not thoroughly mixed!

The resin self levels well and bubbles do rise, but be sure to hit the surface with a torch or heatgun briefly to pop bubbles.

I could be wrong, but i believe the instructions stated this resin is not ideal for very thin coats (2mm?). Ill edit this if i was mistaken.

Finally, temperature is VERY important! 72*F room and resin temperature seemed to be tge sweet spot for me

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text: I absolutely loved this carpet cleaner while it worked. It extracted more water from the carpets than any other I have ever purchased. The rotating brushes did much better than the rollers at cleaning tough stains. However, soon after the warranty expired it stopped spraying water. It turns out the pump went out. I have found this is a very common issue with this model. This repair would cost close to $150 so at this point I find it would be more cost effective to buy a different brand that is more reliable than to spend 1/2 the cost of the machine to repair this one. It is a shame that with this being such a common issue Hoover didn't perform better Quality Assurance testing prior to selling this model or at least offer affordable repairs.  Hoover responded to my review on their website stating "It should hold up better than that" then sent an email stating they want to help and requested my model # and Factory number.  I gave them back that information and never heard from them again.  If you look at this product on the Hoover site it is filled with horror stories of the same issue I have along with constant leaking. I tried calling their customer service number and was told that since it's out of warranty there is nothing they will do.  Even though I have only used this machine 5-6 times over the 2 1/2 years since I purchased it.  I would give this machine zero stars if that was an option.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text: This epoxy resin kit is great for beginners. Really good quality and 40 minutes of working time, and for smaller crafts (I make bookmarks, coasters, clocks, chess sets etc) one gallon gives you plenty to work with. This kit came with the resin and hardener (easy to measure at 1 to 1 ratio), 2 large plastic measuring cups, two mixing wands and a pair of gloves. If you are just starting out I would suggest you also invest in some silicone mixing cups if you want to add several colors to your projects, they are easy to clean (just let the residual epoxy harden, flex the cup, and pop the old resin out) and smaller so you don't have to mix all your resin as the same color. The big cups included with this kit are great for mixing enough clear resin to fill your project, but you will want to separate it into smaller cups if you add micas, dyes, glitter or mix'ins for small portions of the project or to blend several colors into the craft. This kit will definitely be enough for some crafts on its own though (you just need the molds and any decorations you want to add of course). I really enjoy using this resin, my projects come out beautifully! I've included pictures of what came in the package as well as some bookmarks and a clock I've made so far.

review_title: Very Satisfied, Minus One Little Glitch
text:
I have not been pleased with Hoover (vacuum cleaners) the past few years and have even noticed Walmart, Bed Bath & Beyond and some other larger stores are phasing Hoover out of their stores. I replaced a Bissell carpet shampoo/steamer with this Hoover Max Extract 77 a few days ago. I am happy to say that Hoover has put a twinkle back in my eye- at least for this particular product! I bought this on a whim, without reading any reviews, etc. It was out of sheer desperation, as I needed one quickly!

I will be upfront about one thing before I go on... I have not used this as of yet, to clean any of my hard floors, so I apologize, as my review won't cover that.

This was specifically used to deep clean 1500 sq. feet of carpeting through out my home. I had high traffic areas that were extremely filthy, as well as the regular cleaning needed and A LOT of puppy urine accidents, as I have been housebreaking a new pup.

- This machine is the friendliest I have ever encountered as far as accessing the clean water tank to add water and then replace back to the machine, as well as accessing, emptying and replacing the dirty water tank! It is very convenient and easy to access to the soap/solution container, as that is attached/inside of the clean water tank... ALL OF THE ABOVE IS CONVENIENT, EASY AND "NOT" TIME CONSUMING!

- This machine dispenses the soap sparingly, yet effectively, so you are indeed getting your $'s worth!

- This machine was put together smartly, where it is easy to push and pull, the attachment's hose resides in a good place, where it doesn't get in the way or fall off for you to trip over. The power cord is of reasonable length and all of the controls are within reach without being too inconvenient to reach.

- This machine removed many traffic stains as well as some horrific pet accident stains that were almost everywhere throughout my house. I will admit, I didn't take notice to how well or how bad the brushes underneath actually spun, but it was evident they did what they needed to do. The suction as far as sucking up water was excellent- probably the best I have ever experienced and with my ceiling fans on and a few open windows, my carpeting was dry within 3 hours.

- I will suggest if you are dealing with pet urine stains, to definitely use the solution specifically for that. It worked like a charm and also handled my few grease stains as well as regular traffic areas perfectly!

- I do STRONGLY suggest reading the instructions and following them to a "T", so you don't set yourself up for a few minor failures. Following the directions for finding and cleaning out the two lint traps each time you go to empty out the dirty water tank is a must. incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text: If you think once is enough then think again. We live on the big island of hawaii on the Hilo side. We live just south of Hilo (Hawaiian Paradise Park) and have an acre of land that looks like a park. Our roads and driveway is red cinder. We have berber carpeting and two Golden retrivers that are inside/outside dogs. I bought the Hoover from Amazon and went right to work on the very dirty carpet. I broke the living/dining room into three areas. I washed each area three times, rinsed with clear water twice and then set the Hoover to pick up only. The island is not like California with dry air, so removing all possable water is a must. review_title: Excellent carpet cleaner- even a newbie like me got impressive results.
text:
Very impressed with this piece of equipment. I have never owned a carpet cleaner/shampooer in my life. You wouldn't find it hard to believe after you saw my carpets- unshampooed after 11 years, post 2 dogs, one raised from puppyhood (insert "ewwww" here). Not like it was a health hazard, but my light mushroom colored carpets were closer in color to the mud they are grown in (ok, not that bad).

I shampooed the carpet using the cleaner that came with it. I think it was very effective, but too strong of a scent, not unpleasant; the scent faded within a week. It took two cleanings (remember, 11 years, 2 dogs, oh, and I forgot one cat.... plus two kiddos) to get it to look mostly normal, which is quite impressive for the lack of care my carpets had before. The second time around I used Hoover Expert Pet carpet cleaning solution (NOT a concentrate). Very mild odor, just as effective at the concentrate that came with the machine.

My mistake the first carpet, the first time, was probably got the carpet too wet, with too much cleaner. READ the instructions: No more than 4 [consecutive] "wet" passes, then you need to do the wet extraction- which I easily could say would be another 4 extraction passes (a single pass is one way, so a back and forth stroke is 2 passes). I had essentially done 2 application passes and 3-4 rinse passes (=6 passes), followed by 3-4 extraction passes (too much fluid, not enough extraction). The next carpet I did, I revised my technique which included less cleaner, more rinsing and less extractions:
Pass 1: Push: Rotate switch in front to "rinse", press "trigger" on handle. Rinse/water only with a quick stroke; just like you get your hands wet before you add soap, I found it effective with cleaning my carpet (this machine can just do a rinse, very important because too much cleaner residue will attract dirt). ***Fill your rinse chamber with HOT water. My tap water is 125F. Instructions will tell you the temperature limit***
Pass 2: Pull: ends up being some extraction of water.
Pass 3: Push; Rotate switch in front to "wash"; add-cleaner pass.
Pass 4: Pull, rinse
Pass 5-8: (release "trigger") Push/pull/push/pull- extraction passes.
Pass 9 &10: rotate switch in front from wash to rinse, press "trigger"; Push and Pull to rinse again.
Pass 11-14: Release "trigger", Push/pull/push/pull to extract the remaining water.
Dry time is around 8 hours, summer time. - my carpeting is very thick/plush.

This process was necessary to clean my carpets. Maybe you won't need as much, and maybe you'll say that such a process is overkill. I did what I thought needed to be done. The results were astonishing. I'd add before and after photos, but I don't want to be publicly shunned ;-)

Also: maintain your cleaner. Rinsing the tanks are easy. But the tedious thing I felt I needed to do is to pick out the fibers from the cleaning brush. If they are clogged with carpet fiber, they cannot clean as thoroughly.
Why buy my own carpet cleaner instead of hire someone? I don't have to prep the whole room for someone to come in; I can do half a room at a time without displacing all my furniture and not have to take time off work.

Only negative: the wheels are now squeaky. ... and that I didn't buy this sooner!

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text: This shampooer works wonderfully! I have used other in home, and rented Rug Dr in the past, but I am so happy to have this shampooer. I literally got it today and finished cleaning it 10 minutes ago. I had read these reviews before deciding on it, and after using mine I believe many of the poor reviews are stemming from people having little experience with shampooers. The machine did not leak, the accessories worked perfectly, and one hour and a half after shampooing the office the floor is dry (if you are not familiar with shampooers you may think this is a long time... its not). I followed directions included to the T, used hot water, made wet and dry passes, moved SLOWLY, and have great results! Of all the bad reviews I read the only one I don't chalk up to inexperience or operator error is the one person who complained about the wheel squeaking. This seemed like a strange complaint, but after using mine in 3 rooms I found the sound to be incredibly annoying. I still wont be trading this for any other model. I am 100% happy with the results, the ease of operating and taking apart to clean (hands down the easiest, most obvious shampooer I have ever cleaned). *Advise to people new to shampooers, after you shampoo, before cleaning, park the shampooer on a towel, as you take parts out some water will get on the floor. The water tank has twice the capacity of the cleaning solution tank (to allow for rinsing), so if you do not plan to use a rinse only cycle just fill the water tank half way, this way you run out of water and cleaning solution at the same time. The cleaning solution tank is not easily visible while operating, but the water tank is, so if you only fill it half way you will know when you are out of cleaning solution. I did have to refill multiple times, but this is a give and take. If the tanks are big enough to not require refiling the machine becomes really heavy and cumbersome. I would much rather refill often than have a machine so heavy I dread using it. Read the operating directions in full, and follow them, I have yet to hear of a single time where someone got better results doing things differently than the directions with a shampooer.

Overall build quality:
I find Bissell to be of a better build quality and feels more solid and might last longer than Hoover.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]
