this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

text:
I bought the MaxExtract 77 locally at Walmart because they were sold out of the of the Bissell Proheat 2X's. I've had pretty good luck with Hoovers in the past, so I figured this one wouldn't be much different. Packaging seemed decent and all the parts unpacked fine and nothing was broken. Assembly involves just your basic snap-together procedures with the exception of the main handle, which requires you to have a phillips screwdriver for a single machine screw (included).

My problem came when I actually tried to use the 77. It laid down water just fine, and seemed to vacuum it up ok, though it wasn't a 1:1 ratio of water dispensed to water collected, and I wouldn't expect it to be since no carpet cleaner is going to be 100% efficient in that area. But the water actually being collected wasn't nearly as much as I had seen on my other Hoover machines (can't remember the model #s at the moment).

Furthermore, just as I've read in other reviews of this unit, the brushes didn't seem to spin at all. I doubt it was user/setup error since the design is extremely simple and multiple people checked the setup against the instructions multiple times. The brushes are driven off a turbine motor which is itself driven off air flow. While this might work great in cars, either my turbine was seized, or the 3-position switch that adjust the brush speed was stuck on "Off". Everything was seated correctly, but the brushes just plain wouldn't spit. This is precisely why that, when it comes to vacuums, I prefer brushes to be mechanically driven instead of pneumatically driven.

The brushes themselves were very hard to turn. I played with a demo unit in the store and the brushes turned freely by hand. On the unit I actually purchased, it seemed as if somebody spilled Coke in the bushings, it was that hard to turn.

Verdict: Good design, horrible execution.

review_title: Excellent cleaner, but might be more then you need... read to find out :)
text:
With kids, a 120lb dog, and friends/family coming and going frequently the beige carpet in our home needs very frequent cleaning. I already owned (and loved) the Hoover MaxExtract Dual V [[ASIN:B0013YPWE6 Hoover MaxExtract Dual V Carpet Cleaner, Black, F7412900]] and finally decided that I was sick of lugging it up and down to our finished basement (I carpet clean at least monthly) so when I had the chance to try this model I jumped on it. It's everything the Dual V is, and more... meaning that yes I do think it cleans a bit better (it has 2 rows of rotating brushes vs the one in my Dual V) but its also ALOT heavier and harder to push around. I don't think my 60yr old mother would have a problem using the Dual V but I don't think she could use this one for very long, if at all.

Both clean exceptionally well and both are very easy to fill/empty/refill. If you just need a good solid cleaning and don't have a toddler spilling foods or a dog tracking mess I'd save a bit of money and weight and go with the Dual V, if however you need really keep down intense cleaning then I'd absolutely go with the MaxExtract77!

One bit of advice though, don't both buying this thinking you'll use it for hard floors, it's just to heavy and too much of a pain to bother dragging out for your hardwood or tile, what I own and really love is the Hoover FloorMate SpinScrub [[ASIN:B000R5LVVA Hoover FloorMate SpinScrub Wet/Dry Vacuum Cleaner, H3044]] it's worth every penny and you'll be thanking yourself in the long run if you own one machine made for the carpets and another for hardwood/tile. I love Eurekas for dry vacuums but there is nothing better then a Hoover for the wet jobs!

review_title: Restored my three year old carpet to Like New condition!
text:
I had been wanting to buy a carpet cleaner since the moment we purchased our light beige, nylon living room carpet three years ago. My husband is incredibly frugal, so I knew this would be the last carpet we bought for decades and decades to come! Spot cleaning with Z-Lex always did the trick, though the darkening at doorways was becoming worrisome. Well, we hosted a lovely New Year's party last night, replete with young children who were unfortunately tracking muddy footprints across the carpet for most of the evening. I tell you, after CAREFULLY reading the full length instructions, I assembled the unit and put it straight to work. Every last stain, new and old, came out with little effort with the push/pull process and the carpet was dry within 4 hours!

Please note a few important user instructions:
1. Squeeze the trigger only during the first two sets of passes (pushing and then pulling comprises a single set of passes) on a select area of carpet as this is how the detergent/water combination and then rinse water are released. If you squeeze the trigger during three or more sets of passes, you're going to risk over saturating that area. It's possible that one or more buyers may have thought they needed to squeeze the trigger throughout the entire cleaning process and, as a result, ended up with a miniature lake in their living rooms!
2. The unit auto-rinses when you you are squeezing the trigger while pulling back towards yourself. You can always switch to the Rinse-only mode, but it's worth mentioning the auto-rinse feature since this is a selling point for many!
3. Pay attention to the orientation of the caps on the clean water tank and dirty water tanks. When replacing them after filling the tank with hot water and detergent, it is easy to put them on in the wrong direction (a simple mistake) that permits water to leak out. Once installed correctly, no water leaked out of the unit while held in the recommended upright position. (The instruction manual repeatedly states that these two tanks should be removed and set aside in the upright position if you are laying the unit down for some reason.)
4. There are two small filters (not just one), so be sure to clean off both. This step is very quick and very easy (faster than cleaning your dryer's filter, to give you an idea).

That's it for now! I haven't cleaned my ceramic kitchen tiles with the unit yet, so I'll post an update once I do.

Happy cleaning!

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: This really is a great little vacuum
text:
This really is a great little vacuum, if you know it's quirks. When used for the first time its suction is incredible, you can easily suck up change, screws, glass, etc.. The problem is that some things get stuck in the hose, usually at the collar that attaches to the vacuum body. You may not even realize it at first because there is still some suction, but only a fraction of an unclogged hose. One tip is to get to know what the motor sounds like fully unclogged, then you can hear what it sounds like when it begins to clog (it whines at a higher pitch). I sometimes throw a penny on the floor and attempt to vacuum it as a test; if it doesn't rush through the tube into the vacuum, your hose is clogged. What I do is take my broom with the longest handle and unscrew the hose, check if there's a blockage at the hose's collar where it meets the vacuum housing (sometimes you can just pick out the blockage with your fingers), hold the hose over the toilet or trash bag, and shove the broom stick through the hose. This relieves any blockage I've come across. Some things that cause blockages I've run across are little bits of cellophane, twigs, twist-ties, Q-Tips, and the like. I just pick up those objects by hand when possible. The other cause of poor suction is a dirty filter. If you don't use the bags, the filter gets packed with dirt quickly. It takes some effort to clean it thoroughly under running water, but it's worth it (let it dry for a day afterward). If you mind these two problems, you'll likely keep the very powerful suction this vacuum initially has...

P.S. I bought a vacuum brush attachment - http://www.amazon.com/Attachments-Replacement-Dusting-Brush/dp/B0016PS0JQ/ref=sr_1_1?ie=UTF8&qid=1404455722&sr=8-1&keywords=vacuum+brush+attachment - which fits nicely. It works beautifully with this vacuum and is my favorite attachment. Great for quickly dusting the walls, ceilings, and floorboards :)

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
I confess that I bought this mostly because I made the mistake of purchasing a home with large tiles with huge grout lines. I had tried all kinds of methods to get them clean with little success. The Swiffer mop didn't get into the nooks in the tile - never mind the grout - and I often had this ... residue left streaking the surface. Then I tried the steam mops with micro-fiber pads. The grout and tiles tore up those pads quicker than I could replace them -- and I had only slightly better results.

I was excited when I saw this machine could do tile floors. Finally I had hope. I bought it and immediately wanted hearing protection. This is a super LOUD machine. Having said that, it works on the tile (most of the time). There are still some stubborn places in the grout that require personal attention -- and this is obviously a big machine that can't fit in small spaces. You can try using the attachments, but I usually don't want to slow down my momentum to do that. I just use the smaller steam mop on those areas when I'm done.

I loved the settings allowing you to scrub more or less, use more or less soap ... It's wonderful. Make sure you do a good sweeping beforehand, and check the filters for anything clogging it. So far I haven't had any problems.

I have yet to use it on my carpets. After I do that a couple times, I'll try and remember to update this review. So far I'm very pleased.

I will NEVER buy a more expensive brand of Hoover again.

That being said, my daughter bought one of those Bissell steam cleaners a few years back, and that one was horrible also. Moral of the story - expensive isn't always best.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

Cons: no headlight (a must for bare floor owners with pets), wobbles and not well balanced, clever but just not well made.

The decent suction with the small head really grab carpets. Aggressive beater bar contributes. The suction bypass helps but I cannot get a smooth roll on my closed loop or my pile carpets. The suction is great on hardwood but with no headlight you cannot see the dust.

One of the latches (where the removable hose mounts to main vac) requires several tries to latch (maybe why it is refurb) . The chord is on the right, which may be fine for lefties .

The unit I bought was refurbished and it looked new out of the original box (there was a little dust in the bin) - no problem there for those concerned.

I am returning and continue looking for a better quality machine.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
This is my second Hoover, the first one didn't survive lending it to my girlfriend. She took it apart to clean it and never could get it back together again. Oh well, it was about 20 years old and probably would be fine if I were to fix it.

As for this one, it works as well as the first one. I just cleaned my beige carpet which hadn't been cleaned in at least 5 years. It looks almost new. Also I've been doing some landscaping and had tracked a lot of mud across the carpet and you would never know.

I also used it to clean my ceramic kitchen floor and it did a pretty good job. It didn't get a few small spots (got most of them) where spills had been on the tile for a long time and it didn't get the grout between the tiles. To be fair, in the past I had clean those spots with a scratch pad and the grout had to be cleaned with a brush. Still, it was much faster and did a better job than I achieved by hand. I didn't use the squeegee because the grout lines negated the usefulness of it and it picked the water up fairly well.
________________________________________

On the downside, the brushes quit spinning shortly after I first used it or perhaps not at all, I'm not sure about that. I was going to return it, but figured it wouldn't hurt to see if I could find the problem and fix it. The fix was very simple.

First you need to remove the dirty water tank. Under the tank near the front of the machine there is a impeller unit housed in a black irregularly shaped part with a screen facing the front of the machine. You can see it on the first picture posted here by "Peggles". It's just behind the yellow spray bar in the front.

First remove the front (suction guide) of the machine. It is the piece with the lettering on the front of it. Near the top (under the water tank) there is a plastic tab that you pull on and rotate the piece forward. It will come right off. This is the same piece that you need to remove to get access to the front screen.

Next, Remove the 2 front screws and the 2 back screws (not the 2 middle screws) on the impeller unit and it will lift off the machine. On the side of the impeller unit you will see a number of tabs holding the top and bottom together. Carefully pry the tabs out (a little) and pull the top and bottom of the unit apart. Once that is done, turn the unit over and you will see the impeller.

On my machine the impeller would not turn, so I rocked it back and forth until it did. Once I did this, the impeller would spin freely. I put everything back together and it has been working fine ever since.

________________________________________

These misgivings aside, this is a nice machine.

What I like about this machine over my older one is that the tanks are easier to remove and dump, especially the dirty water tank. I also like the separate tanks for the cleaning solvent and water.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
Had some bookshelves installed in the kitchen 4 years ago, but about 9 months ago, one these just pulled out of the wall. Appears it wasn't screwed into a stud, and neither was a heavy duty anchor used.,

Reinstalled it using toggle bolts and it was holding fine. Bu shelves got taken down as part of kitchen remodel, new toggle bolts not fit and old ones had been threaded. Wife did not new holes as that would have meant whole repainting.

Found these at HD, but they were only available online (not true), but they wouldn't have arrived in time, so back to trusty AMZ. Next day delivery.

These are big solid anchors, that have a weight rating of 300lbs, which is HUGE for drywall. Installation was easy, and so far everything is holding up, although going lighter on numbers of books to start.

I've deducted 1 * as these do require a 3/4" hole which is huge and may show outside the bracket, and the set I received had 2 screws missing. Called their customer service, and 2 new screws dispatched on same day.

These look to be great anchors, and customer service was great. Will update if they pull out.

text:
After my crappy Bissell problems, I was so worried about what machine to try. I did so much research because I didn't know whether to fix my newer Bissell or call it quits and buy a Hoover. I called the local vacuum store (certified Bissell repair place in my area). I was surprised to learn (because Bissell is such a well known, major producing company) that they spend a lot of time fixing Bissell machines. They said they fix Hoover too but they see an immense amount of Bissells. OK...so which Hoover to buy? I actually called Hoover because the reviews all over the internet made me question what I wanted. The Hoover customer service rep compared the products I was interested in, explained the differences in some of the features and was able to answer my questions. In the end, I am very happy with my purchase! Here are a couple key notes to remember: 1) Read the directions. Even if it is not your first rodeo, the intruction books are there for a reason and give important tips for optimal use. 2) Always vacuum your carpet before you clean it. I have 3 dogs and my house gets vacuumed daily but I still vacuum twice and in multiple directions before a cleaning. 3) When you put the clean water tank on the machine, it is time to work. Don't insert the tank and go piddle around in the other room. incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
I'm giving the Hoover MaxExtract 77 Multi-Surface Pro Carpet Cleaner only 4 stars because it uses a lot of cleaning solution. This was no surprise since we read this in other reviews before purchasing it. The MaxExtract is easy to operate and does a good job of cleaning and extracting. The carpets dry in 2 - 3 hours as opposed to our old cleaner which took 6 - 8 hours to dry, so that is a plus. With two small dogs and two cats we're constantly cleaning the carpets and the Hoover is a definite improvement over our 3 year old Bissell. The free delivery to our door in two days made us realize how much easier and more convenient it is to buy certain products using Amazon Prime. It's something we certainly will not forget in the future.

Now if someone could come up with a product that actually completely removes set-in dried, yellow urine stains on light tan carpets, we would be thrilled. Nothing we've tried in the past 10 years has been able to get the dried yellow stains out of the carpet. Since my previous home's carpets were very old and almost white in color, I started using a very diluted solution of bleach and water. I'd spray it over the stain, let it sit for a few seconds and then go over it with the cleaner. It definitely helped to lighten the stain, but it was tricky and sometimes the carpets would get bleached so I don't recommend doing it. I guess the best thing to do is avoid light colored carpets.

text:
This unit is not as powerful as some upright vacuums, but it is strong enough to get the job done.

Typically, I have the unit strapped around my shoulder and neck, with the unit actually lying against my back. The cord is long enough that I can vacuum a significant area without re-plugging. Further if I need to move furniture while vacuuming, I can hang the hose over my neck, leaving both of my hands free--never having to but the unit down.
The unit is not much louder than some battery operated vacuums, but is significantly more powerful. Probably one of the few vacuums I have used where I was not bothered by the noise.

All of the attachments lock into each other, and can be quickly connected and disconnected. I have primarily used the vacuum on hard floors and low pile commercial carpets, and it performs as wells as I could hope. However, I do suspect that this unit would be out performed by a unit with rotating brushes on a high pile carpet.

There is no special area on the unit to wrap the cord, instead the unit comes with a buttoned strap which will hold the cord after you have manually wrapped it. For me, this was not an inconvenience, since it makes releasing the cord very quick, and wrapping the cord around my elbow and hand is easy enough.

One of the primary reasons I bought this unit is because of the lack of filters. The washable bag acts as a filter, and there are two other filters on the unit which appear to be easy to clean. The bag is not as large as the canisters in some upright units, but so far it has allowed me to vacuum multiple rooms without needing to be emptied.

The only complaint I have for this unit is that there is no accessory attachment area. There is a bag for the unit which can be purchased separately which presumably solves this problem.

All in all, the unit is designed for commercial purposes. Easy to disassemble, comes with a parts manual, and has a general no frills design which just works.

review_title: Very convenient, but clearly not as strong as a full size
text:
Very handy, especially for vacuuming around furniture, etc. Using the shoulder strap sounds like a burden, but it's actually very useful. I'm not sure if it's more cumbersome for smaller/shorter body types. I'm 5'10".

The machine is better for hard surfaces and dust-vacuuming than carpeting, even through it includes a carpet attachment. The strength is only okay, at least compared to a full size canister or upright vacuum cleaner. It will pick up small particles with no problem. But larger objects don't get sucked in right away like would using a full-size.

I'm using the disposable filter bags. They're pretty small, for obvious reasons. If you use this as your primary vacuum cleaner, you may go through a lot of these bags per month/year. They're cheap enough, but you'll need to stock up.

Attachments are very easy to use and put together. Very durable, too, even though they're mostly plastic.

I'd recommend it, depending on your usage needs.

text:
About a year or so ago, I purchased another Hoover that is labeled as "powerscrub", but I'm not 100% sure that is the official name. Honestly, I thought it was a different brand, or I would never have bought this. It barely scrubbed my carpets, and I honestly thought that it was normal. A month ago, I noticed my carpets getting really gross to step on, so I brought it out again in hopes of reclaiming not-so-gorgeous apartment-quality carpets only to find out that the unit would no longer suck up the water it dispensed. So I took apart the machine best as I could, gave it a thorough cleaning, rinsed the filters, etc. and started it up again, and it still wouldn't work. I'm not a handyman, and if I cant fix something by common sense alone it's a lost cause.
So I scrolled through Amazon looking for a new carpet cleaner that would actually work, and this one was decently priced and had good reviews. I bought it, but when it arrived and I took a look at my old machine vs new and found out that they were the same brand, I swore under my breath. In my mind, I had just basically re-bought the machine that didn't work and broke down after only a year. My immediate instinct was to send it back, but but a really busy schedule held me back, and my carpet got to the point of being absolutely disgusting to walk on, so I cracked the box open and set it up (which took barely two minutes), and was impressed with the simplicity compared to my other model. You can take apart the machine very easily, and it looks like a breeze to maintain.
When I turned the machine on for the first time, I was startled. I had it on the highest setting, and when I turned it on, the machine actually cleaned!! The scrubbers went right to work (leading me to question whether my other one had ever worked at all, or simply dispensed water and then sucked it back up) and got into my heavily-trafficked carpet. In one pass, I could see the difference in quality. The water went down powder white (I /really/ needed to clean them, so I dissolved some oxiclean and added it to the water tank for extra oompf) and came out a (frankly disgusting) green-brown. The power scrub pulled up the carpet from its compacted state due to foot traffic, and now they are soft and look nearly as good as new! I finished up the area of concern without actually finishing, because it was 10pm when I got this sudden burst of energy and I have downstairs neighbors, so I didn't want them to be woken up by the sound. But for only 10 minutes of work I am thoroughly impressed, and will be doing the rest of the carpets (and maybe test it out on hard floors) today! I'm actually very excited and impressed.

TLDR: Awesome, powerful machine that actually scrubs the carpets and restores stained and heavily-trafficked carpet!

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
I purchased this after scouring the internet for reviews on different makes and models of carpet cleaners. I must say, the reviews do not lie. It does a wonderful job of cleaning - gets out stains, leaves the carpet soft and clean, and has fabulous suction so the carpets are quick to dry. I primarily purchased this because we got a puppy who has had her share of accidents - but once I began cleaning, I was obsessed! I am completely disgusted at the amount of dirt that came out of my carpets! Ugh! They didn't look that bad, but even places like bedrooms that get very little foot traffic were filthy (this is based on the dirty water in tank - sooo gross!)

I have yet to use it on hard surfaces, so I can't comment on how it does there. The hand held attachments work well, though. I did the stairs with the hose and spinning brush head and they are much cleaner, though not nearly as clean as places done by the full sized unit. It is so easy to put together, fill the tanks, empty and clean - even the brushes just pop right out (although I did have to work rather hard to get all the carpet fibers out of the brush heads). My only complaint is the cleaning solutions do not go very far. The bottle of 2x cleaner only did two rooms (and I have a small house) so using this on a regular basis will require quite a bit of solution to do the whole house. Still, it saves a ton of money over having your carpets done professionally and I think they look and feel just as good (if not better, because I always feel like something is cleaner when I clean it myself!). It is a bit heavy to lug up and down the stairs, but just make sure the tanks are empty and it isn't quite so bad. Overall, a terrific purchase! Highly recommend!

review_title: Barely Adequate -- And Here Are the Reasons
text: I have had the Portapower for over two years and feel that I have now had adequate experience to reflect on its good and bad points.  I have also had a Miele canister and can compare it to another albeit far more expensive vacuum.  In short, I think you get what you pay for.  Here are the major problems of the Portapower.  1.  The Portapower does not come delivered with the ability to dispose of the bag.  Really, you have to purchase an additional piece of plastic that converts the round mouth to a square mouth in order to then use disposable bags.  The vacuum comes with a single fabric bag that is not easy to empty or clean.  It is best done outside and with a perfect knowledge of where the wind will blow the bag contents.  2.  The Portapower has virtually no filter for retainer fine dust.  Absolutely no ability for a hepa or similar filter, unlike the Miele.  When you turn on the Portapower you should expect that the room will start having a stale smell, which is from the expulsion of fine dust out the back of the vacuum.  The Miele does not have that problem.  3.  The Portapower does not have a retractable power cord.  The Miele has one that you can activate with your foot.  This difference might seem trivial but becomes a hassle.  It comes with a band that is intended to tie the folded cord (about 30 feet), but it is so flimsy that it amazes me that any thought was given to its adequacy.  Even a velcro strap would have been a better solution.  4.  The power of the Powerpack is not going to blow you socks off.  Instead, I think you will find that it is barely adequate.  5.  By no means is this vacuum designed to commercial specifications.  Aside from the tube, there are no metal parts.  The latch to open the canister to access the aforementioned dust bag is incredibly flimsy.  The accessory fittings are noticeably cheap plastic that are not designed with a goal of minimizing clogging.  For the Miele the plastic seems much more substantial and the tube diameter is noticeably larger, clearly designed to make sure that clogging is minimized.  Moreover, the Miele canister has a compartment for the accessories, while the Portapower has no such feature.  On the good side is that the Powerpack has not failed in two years of light use.  If I were in a position of purchasing a vacuum today, I would spring for the extra cash and purchase a bare bones Miele for $300.  I know that it is unfair to compare the Portapower to a vacuum that is more than twice as expensive, but I do it only to let the prospective purchaser know that s/he has not yet reached the price point of marginal diminishing returns.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

I have owned a Hoover in the past (last one lasted 23 years). As the old one wore out I considered many products but chose this one because it really had every feature.

-Using hand tools is super easy with the auto conversion
-The Dual row brushes get out almost every stain
-The wash rinse selector is awesome because when you rinse the carpets there isn't that "sticky" feeling on the carpets after
-The heaters blows tons of air and it does reduce dry time.
-the separate solution tank saves you money because you don't have to dumb valuable shampoo every time you use.
-Everything can be removed easily which helps cleaning

The Cons
-Takes 3+ hours to dry
-The cord is SUPER short
-Hard floor attachment is flimsy and doesn't really work

review_title: This model replaced my Hoover Steamvac Model F8100-900
text: I bought the Hoover Steamvac, Platinum Collection, Model F8100-900 before there were too many reviews out there on it.  I had read that it leaks, but I read that about several other steamvacs.  I figured if I had a problem, it would be covered under its six-year warranty.  When I first starting using it, it worked wonders on my carpets.  Stains were no match, and I was pleased.  Unfortunately, not long after I had it, it started to leak.  I called Hoover's customer Service and I was referred to Cathy's Sewing and Vacuum in Tucson, about an hour and a half north of me.  They took it in without question when I described how the tanks have been rapidly leaking out water and soap.  The salesman there told me they had lots of problems with the model and the only thing good about it was the warranty.  About a year later, I borrowed it to a friend, and her son broke the latching mechanism that keeps it in the upright position.  Then I noticed it was leaking again.  To avoid a trip to Tucson, as I live 80 miles south of there, I attempted to fix it myself.  When I unscrewed and opened it, several pieces inside came falling down.  At this point, my husband told me I probably voided the warranty.  I decided to bring it to Cathy's Sewing and Vacuum anyhow.  I was honest about what I did.  They told me I may have voided the warranty, but took it in anyhow.  About a week and a half later, they called me and told me I can pick from one of two other models, because they will no longer support the model I had, since it had so many problems.  I was very pleased to hear that, and I chose the MaxExtract 77.  They put it under the remaining warranty.  It's a great model with less bells and whistles, but more brushes.  I'm not sure which actually cleaned better--they seem to work about the same.  The MaxExtract 77 has a shorter cord, so as I started to steam clean my carpets, it unplugged.  The tank is designed so that it's one tank that mixes water with the solution.  Although this design prevents functioning problems, the water depletes quickly before you have a chance to finish half of the room.  The dirty water reservoir on the MaxExtract77 is also easier to pull out and empty than the former.  I have two dogs, no kids, and live in a dry-dusty climate, so I'm vacuum at least once-twice a week with my Dyson Animal vacuum.  I've steam cleaned three rooms so far, and it worked very well.  The reservoir tank contained some very, very dirty water.  Stains came out with little effort.  I can't seem to get the high traffic areas very clean, but maybe I need a better soap.  I'll try again.  I do like that the bumpers are made of rubber as to prevent nicks and scratches when bumping into furniture or baseboards.  That was a smart design idea.  I'm pleased over all that Hoover and Cathy's Sewing and Vacuum were able to stand behind their products and services.  I hope this review has been helpful.

text:
This is a mixed review because the first machine failed practically out of the box. I used it once, removed the waste water bin to empty it, put it back in to continue cleaning -- and the motor did nothing but make a high pitched whine. I checked everything you could check, then called Hoover. Here's the good part. I told them what had happened, turned it on so they could hear the noise it was making, and they immediately said they would ship me a new one right away. I had the replacement in a few days. I had an older Hoover carpet cleaner that failed after a few years of heavy use, as I foster dogs for a rescue group and have a few of my own, and the floors really suffer from it. I like this new version much better for a few reasons:
1. The detergent is in a separate compartment from the water, so one fill of concentrated detergent lasts for several water fills, and if you have some left over it can just wait for the next use.
2. The waste water container is MUCH easier to remove, replace and clean. You simply lift it out (nothing to unlatch) and open a cap to empty it, then replace the cap and drop it back into place. With my old one you had to fiddle with the lid to make sure it was absolutely sealed or it would not work. That is not an issue with this one. When you are done and want to clean it out, then you remove the lid for a thorough cleaning, and it has an easy-to-use latch to seal it shut properly.
3. It does a great job of cleaning! I used it right away on a rug in a very high traffic area where the dogs track in a lot of dirt from the back yard, plus normal kitchen traffic. The difference between the clean and uncleaned areas was startling.
Despite my initial issue, I was very happy with Hoover's customer service and am happy with the machine.

text:
I was looking for something to clean the rug, not just a pass of steam, but really clean it, when I found this one. I looked at all of the possibilities and decided that it was worth it to spend a little more and get something that multi-tasks.

First- the thing itself. Comes apart easily, puts back together fairly easily. The plastic means you have to be careful and not force anything into place. The two tanks hold plenty of water, but I think the dirty tank hold a little less than the clean tank. Easy to fill, easy to clean. Love that the dirty tank comes apart so you can clean the inside. Easy to roll, but a bit heavy to carry. Easy to set up. I wish the cord was about 5 feet longer.

Second- the rugs. In my dreams, the spots on the carpet disappear. Not the case, but they are noticeably lighter. Perhaps over time, they will be gone. There were some age ugly spots on the upstairs carpet. We didn't replace the rug when we moved in, 6 years ago, but probably should have. I have rented a cleaner and did what I could. IT was ok. I used this and the rest of the carpet looks great. Almost brand new. The heavy traffic spots look tons better, but not perfect. I do not think it was the machine, though. It also did a great job on the grease spots the air conditioner guy left on the rug in the basement. They are almost gone. One is still there, but it was pretty bad. Again, not the fault of the machine that they are not gone, but so much better than they were. The area rug in the living room gets used by the cat as a little box. Between what is left behind and the residue of the spot cleaners, the carpet was not as soft, smelled a little and I wasn't quite sure what I was going to do with it. This picked up all the residue and the carpet looks and feels like it has been restored. No complaints about this part.

Third- the hard floors. I have white ceramic tile in the kitchen, with grout lines as thick as my little finger in some places. The surface of the tiles traps dirt. I clean the floor every day, but mop about once a week. It has been about that long when I cleaned the floor. It scrubbed and did an ok job with the grout. Nothing gets in there better than a toothbrush, but it did fine. It did NOT get up all the stuck on stuff. There were brownie crumbs and they were still stuck to the floor. A little disappointing, but had I swept better, it may have beeb better. Also, it did not suck up all the water. But, the part where I started was dry by the time I got to the end, so no big deal. What i really didn't like was when the dirty tank was full, all of the previously sucked up water ran out and all over the floor and I had to redo it. That was annoying, but I suppose if the tank is full, the tank is full.

Overall, it met my expectations and I am happy so far.
