text:
The MaxExtract was supposed to be a replacement for my not too old Hoover SteamVac that the neighbor keeps borrowing. Right now, I don't think I'll be parting with the SteamVac. Here are the pros and cons of the new MaxExtract as I see them.

Pros:
* Wider cleaning. The Max has a wider head and there should cover more area at a faster pace.
* More bristles. Lots more cleaning bristles and a beefy axle connecting them to the motor so it should last.
* Super easy to clean. Yes, the dirty water tank has all kinds of weird crevices but since the lid comes right off it is super easy to clean and addtitionally doesn't have the large sponge filter to clean that the SteamVac does.
* Super Easy to empty. Much easier to remove and empty the dirty tank than the SteamVac
* "Active" tool wand. Just set the MaxExtract upright and remove the wand from it's storage holster and it's ready to go. Unlike the SteamVac you don't to to manually plug anything in. Very nice.
* Great cleaning performance. worked great on my carpet.
* Wash vs. Rinse selector. No more having to throw out unused solution mix because you've reached the end of the wash cycle.
* Quieter. Noticeably quieter in operation than the SteamVac.

Cons:
* Left carpet wetter than my SteamVac.
* Absolutely tore through cleaning solution. Easily used 2 - 3 times more solution than the SteamVac. It was crazy how much I used in such a little space.
* Heavy. Unfortunately all the above pros come at a cost in weight. This thing is a beast to push around.

Summary:
While my pros significantly outnumber my cons, the cons are very important. The fact that the unit is heavier and more burdensome to push around AND leaves my carpet wetter all while costing a fortune to operate in cleaning solution leaves me seriously considering that all the very worthwhile improvements aren't worth the added hassle.

Note: Be sure to clean the small filter under the dirty water tank at the end of each use in order to not lose suction. Simple remove and run under water to clean and then replace.

review_title: I am very happy with this vacuum
text:
While this is a fairly recent purchase, I feel I’ve used it enough to share my opinion. I am very happy with this vacuum, here’s why:

• The cord is long enough that when plugged into a centrally located outlet I can vacuum my whole condo (1,200 sq. ft) with out having to unplug/replug in.

• The edger works far better than any upright I’ve ever used and the head swivels easily enough to get under furniture- I can vacuum completely under my sofa without having to move it, scaring my cat out of his hiding place.

• IT SUCKS! Works wonderfully well on both the carpet and ceramic tile floors. And, it vacuums up without problem scattered litter on a plush bathroom rug without sucking up the rug, unlike uprights I’ve had which then jammed, sometimes breaking the belt as well as just scattering the litter.

• A cloth, reusable bag large enough to do several complete vacuums without having to empty it. When I do empty it, I vacuum it out with my shop vac and it’s as good as new.

• Its small size- in a condo where closet space is at a premium its small footprint is appreciated.

So why just four stars? Design flaws which I think merit at least a one star demerit:

• The handle just isn’t ergonomically designed causing hand fatigue. My girlfriend claims my hands are excessively large (although my urologist would probably respectfully disagree), so if my hands get tired, imagine poor Donald J., although I suspect he’s never touched a vacuum in his life.

• Wrapping the cord around the handle it’s iffy if it will stay in place. Extending the top of the handle would solve this.

• No pad on the shoulder strap.

Bottom line, for the price, this vacuum performs exceptionally well.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
I haven't written a review in a while. A lot of the reviews which I have read aren't helpful. I figured it was time to make a contribution.

No regrets. It's a good machine. The price makes it a no-brainer.

Every comment about the strap failing is right-on. Now you know. So plan ahead, before using the machine. I reinforced the stitching with 3-0 Silk. I didn't want to let the cannister fall upon my first go of it. I have the strap let all the way out and wear it like a sash. The straps lies between my neck and right shoulder. The cannister is slung above my left hip. As such, it's not going to fall off of my shoulder if I lean or bend. The clips which attack the strap to the housing are secure. They're not going to fail.

I'm tall. I always improvise to lengthen a vacuum cleaner's wand. This vacuum cleaner's wand length is above average. Nevertheless, I added an extra 13" section from my Stanley Wet-Dry Shop Vac. If fit well on the far end. This made the wand length ideal.

This vacuum cleaner's bag does not need replacing.

If you wind the cord tightly it probably will kink. I don't think that the cord will kink much if you treat it right.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: Cleans puppy stains and everything else!
text:
This is my second carpet shampooer. The first one was a [[ASIN:B00009R66F Hoover SteamVac Carpet Cleaner with Clean Surge, F5914-900]], and it worked so well that I wanted to try this one because it's supposed to do hard floors too. We have a puppy who is doing really well with potty training, but he still has accidents, and this has worked great on carpets.

It was easy to assemble-- almost too easy. The chamber on the bottom that collects dirty water just sort of sits in the space. It doesn't lock in place and it doesn't feel sealed to me. It doesn't leak but I was afraid to use it at first because of this. The dirty water never goes back onto the carpet. I don't like the way the tank is structured. The top comes off as a large square so you can rinse it out well, but I'm always wondering if the seal will fail and if I will have the dirty tank come apart when I take it out. You do NOT want dirty carpet water all over your floor. Even if you don't have pets and it's brand new, that dirty water smells terrible. You need to make sure you empty the tank every time. It's super easy to clean, and it only takes a couple of minutes.

It has a separate tank for clean water. Inside that tank is a separate container for cleaning solution. This way you can choose how concentrated you want the solution to be, and you can use plain water on an area without having to empty the tank. The other cleaner had a single tank for clean water and cleaning solution. With this, if you forget and put in cleaning solution first, it doesn't foam up when you fill the tank.

I tried the attachment on my couch and sofa, and it seemed to remove a lot of dirt without leaving things too damp. The carpets don't take forever to dry either, and it has great suction. It's easy to use the heated cleaning feature. I don't know if it's really killing germs in the carpet or not. I wonder if it isn't just heating it up enough to actually encourage bacteria growth, but like the number of licks it takes to get to the center of a Tootsie Roll Pop, the world may never know.

I did not try it on bare floors. It's heavier than my other carpet cleaner, and I was actually concerned that it might damage the floors with all that weight and moving around. It just doesn't seem like something I would want to scoot back & forth multiple times over a hardwood floor. Tile may be different.

The bottom line is that we replaced our old cleaner with this one because of the clean water tank, and ease of cleaning the unit. It's overall a better design if you can afford it, and we love the way it works. It has certainly kept odors at a minimum and kept the carpet fresh looking. If you intend to use this on bare floors, you should go see one in person before you buy it just to see how heavy it is and how it will roll on your floor. The puppy does not like this big noisy thing, but it works well on his accidents.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

But, it's still a far cry better than the other portables that I've tried.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: Excellent, versatile tool that performs really well on hard floors, carpet and upholstery.
text:
I am in LOVE with this machine. It's so not like me to get excited about any cleaning tool or product, but the Hoover Multi-Surface Pro Carpet and Floor Cleaner has changed my experience with my hardwood floors. I live in an historic building from the 1930's, with original albeit resurfaced hardwood floors. I'm in an urban area, have dogs and a bird, so the dirt and pet dander can be really disheartening. I was noticing that when I mopped up spills on my floor the day after I'd had the housecleaner vacuum and steam mop all floors, dirt would still show on the paper towels. Not since buying and using the Hoover Max Extract though.

This machine got my hardwood floors beautifully clean and is relatively easy to use in spite of the heavy weight. The brushes and strong suction really lifted all dirt that hot steam mopping couldn't. As other reviewers have noted, the squeegee attachment is a completely useless bit of nonsense. Just throw it in the trash. It does nothing but cause 20 minutes of consternation as you attempt to get it to "snap" on as the instructions say, start to feel like a clumsy dimwit because you can't figure out how to get it on there, finally realize that the best it's going to do is rest on the front edge, then waste another 20 minutes trying to keep it on the machine while you clean your first hard floor. Finally, you realize that the suction on the machine is so good that a squeegee is unnecessary. I can only assume they had to get the product released and didn't have time to fix this ridiculous part, but they'd do well not to advertise it.

The large wheels make the machine easy to maneuver. Even just using very hot water in the machine gives a good clean. If using the included floor cleaner I would strongly recommend taking the time to switch to the rinse cycle afterward. It avoids any dullness on the floors afterward and pulls up even more dirt. It's kind of disturbing to empty the tank afterward because it pulls up dirt you wouldn't have thought was there. Separate clean and dirty water tanks are easy to remove, empty and replace. The dirty water compartment needs to be emptied with some frequency, but it's a quick thing to do.

I've also used it on wool throw rugs. It does a much better job of cleaning than my old machine that had brushes that rotated vertically instead of horizontally. I'd be a bit cautious with it though--most of my rugs came out looking great but one looked like I'd cleaned it a little too deeply and the nap is still getting back to normal. I used the deep cleaning tool on portions of that rug so I'm thinking it was a bit too forceful. Great little tool for stains or ground in dirt though. Keep in mind I'm using it on rugs that are generally hand washed. For regular carpet it would be great.

This review is too long, but I also did use the upholstery tool as well. Didn't really expect it to do much but it actually did a fabulous job on an antique chair I had bought and planned to re-upholster. It revived the fabric and cleaned it deeply. I didn't have the same luck with some stains on an off-white stool but that's to be expected. For in between steam cleaner appointments it does a good job on furniture.

This is a great, versatile tool that's very easy to use in spite of its weight. Highly recommend. I shop as much as possible online to save time, and rely heavily on others' reviews to make purchasing decisions so try to be descriptive in my own. If this was helpful please click yes below.

review_title: Most likely an impostor! Not like the original!!
text: This particular product, from this company, at least, must be an imitation. This is the second of this style that I've owned, the first one being stolen. I currently clean houses professionally for a living and had my first one of these for two years before it was taken. I LOVED it!! It had the professional suction that I needed to do great detailing work, with a long, industrial cord that allowed me to do distance cleaning from the outlet, and the attachments were a snap to exchange. Never had a problem with any of it.And I was hard on it!!  After it was stolen, just had to get me another. Was thrilled to be able to get it for such a great price here on Amazon. Three days on the job (equivalent to vacuuming one's home for three days), however, and the cord at the base of the vacuum already became exposed. Additionally, although the cord is nice and long like my other one, it's inferiority shows through by how tangled it gets, and stays. A real hassle. Another thing that keeps me from falling in love with this vacuum like my first one is that there's a little hinge that keeps the flap to the bag closed (and where the hose attaches) that is incredibly cheap, causing me to have to constantly close it during each job. At times the flap has even opened extensively, making it seem like it was going to break off when trying to close. My other one was much more solid. The last disappointing feature about this vacuum compared to my original one, is with regards to the attachments. First off, the two long metal hose extensions do not come apart easily. If I need to shorten the hose to do certain detailing, I have to just use the accordion part of hose itself. And, additionally, two of the attachment end pieces are very lose when I attach them, punctuating just how inferior of a quality this vacuum really is to the original.  As far as the motor goes, it still does seem to have strong suction and I haven't had any issues with overheating or suction waning. So, if you're just wanting this for light home use, it might do the job for you. But if you're needing it for more professional work, spend the extra and get the original. Wherever that may be?!

review_title: One Of My Best "Responsible" Decisions Ever
text:
I'm now pretty much middle-aged, so a lot of my attitude about things has changed. I've never been a particularly organized or clean person - always had more important things to concern myself with - but recently I find I'm increasingly aggravated by mess. One big source of mess in my home is my beloved cat, Desi, who while basically a very good boy in terms of personality, has taken up a very bad habit of messing on the carpet. SO, in recent times, I've been thinking more and more about cleaning my floors, and I'd been debating in my head whether to rent a carpet cleaning machine or buy one. I finally settled on buying because then I can clean on my time and my terms. I did a little bit of homework on which to get, and then settled on the Hoover MaxExtract 77. Please note, I bought mine at Wal Mart, so this review will focus on strictly my opinion of the machine and how to use it, rather than anything to do with an Amazon purchase experience. For the record, I ADORE Amazon and have had nothing but dozens of good experiences. It's just that it was cheaper to buy it at Wally World at the time, so there you go.

First off... My unit appeared to have been opened and partially assembled (one of the bad things about Wally World) and then half-a** packed back in the box. Everything looked clean, nothing broken, nothing missing, so I put it all together and gave it a try anyways. Assembly was dead easy, and I didn't even look at the manual before my first use because frankly a child could figure this one out. That's why I went through so much cleaning solution on the first go, lol. More on that later.

For my first attack on soiled carpet, I picked the worst spot in the house, where my... cough... beloved a**-cat had been urinating frequently when I wasn't home. The carpet in that small spot was a deep brown (normally gray) and dense with it. I knew this would make or break my opinion of the machine straight away, and plus that spot's been ticking me off for a long time now, and I wanted it gone. In retrospect, I should have shelved some of my other expenses and done this a LOT sooner.

I filled the cleaning solution part of the tank (it's molded together as one tank) and the water part with full hot water from the tap, then threw everything together and went at it. I didn't realize you don't hold the trigger down continuously (ooops) which keeps spraying cleaning solution into the carpet, so in one go I way oversoaked the carpet and ran through water and solution like mad bananas. Maybe it's not that bad a thing - it was a BAD spot. It was during this first mission that I learned three things:

1) The machine is heavy. You will get a good workout while cleaning your floors, and you do need to go back and forth over each strip of floor quite a lot, first to soak and scrub, and then to continue scrubbing while pulling dirty solution out of the carpet or off the flooring. Make one or two back and forth passes over the area with the trigger pressed, then back and forth a bunch of times without it pressed until you stop seeing lots of foamy water coming back into the waste tank.

2) Don't smell the waste water as you pour it outside or down your toilet, especially if you're cleaning up pet mess. O M G... there is nothing nastier on the planet, I'm sure. As much solution as I went through on that small patch of floor, it kept coming and coming like an army of psychopaths - UGLY brown. I just got done doing another larger patch of the floor, in fact, and though I thought that area was fairly clean, still very dark wastewater. This means it works and works well, obviously. Point is, expect it to gross you out, badly. Just remember, this is why you made the purchase.

3) There's really no such thing as sucking the carpeting dry, so just do the best you can and then put a fan on it. Air conditioning and/or a very low humidity day will really help move it along toward dry. If you want to really impress yourself, in this early stage, try touching it barefoot when doing carpet, and you'll be delighted at how soft it feels on your feet. My carpeting is very dense low pile, and still... that first spot felt so fluffy I was amazed.

There were two bad spots on that small patch of floor, and the basic stain didn't fully come out, but I'm not surprised - considering the severity especially of the one spot, I'd probably need a very strong, pet-specialized solution to really wipe the spot out. In general the machine did VERY well on it.

After you're done with a patch of carpet and you've run through a tankful of solution, give yourself a break and a pat on the back, empty out the wastewater tank, and if you're going to hang it up for the day, then break the machine down and clean it up and leave everything to dry. The waste tank opens up in two pieces for good rinsing, thankfully, and all you need to do with the solution tank is just rinse each of the two sides out and put all the plastic parts out on someplace to air dry. Don't forget, there's a screen filter on the machine itself, toward the handle side on the right. Make sure you clean it out well because hair and particles will clog it up eventually. Vacuuming the floor first is a NECESSITY, but still.. this machine will pick up things the vacuum won't. Again, that's why you got it.

I conclude with this:

I'm very glad I got this machine, SO FAR. They say that all such machines will break, and most likely in a relatively short time. I'll come back to add to this review some months down the road to give an update on that situation since two days of use is NOT enough time to give all the good and bad points of hardly anything.

The machine is apparently very thorough. It has five little rotary brushes that seem to do a fantastic job on carpet, and as an added bonus it's good for hard flooring as well. It appears to vacuum up its own water very well... No leaks so far except for the wastewater tank - DON'T tip it forward when carrying it to the sink (mine may have a small crack at the front, haven't investigated that yet). It appears to clean REALLY well, because damn, there's no end to the dirty water coming out of my carpets. I'm SO impressed with that, I'm just like "Riiiiiick.... why didn't you do this sooner?" It is heavy, unwieldy, and quite a workout, but that's physics, bro. If you want a good cleaning, then you need downpressure, and machines full of water are pretty much going to weigh a lot. Be a sissy, suck it up (ha ha... score a pun point!) and be clean, or have someone that isn't a sissy do it for you. In the end it is pretty rewarding. Oh and it also has a hose and a handheld attachment for doing hard to access areas like car upholstery and etc, that's a BIG bonus going for it.

Easy enough to set up and use, easy to break down and clean and store, does a nice job, cleaning solution gets used up fast so get a lot and btw it is a bit pricey. All in all, I'm happy I got it and happy I settled on this Hoover model rather than one of the many Bissel alternatives. This could quite possibly be the best $230 I've ever spent on my home and "responsible" personal life. :-)

As for dear, sweet, innocent Desi.... Within this fuzzy lump of cute lays the heart of a vengeful, destructive demon. Beware, no carpet is safe!

[...]

Update, 2-14-14: Valentine's Day and still in love with my machine, almost a year after buying her. Still running strong, and as effective as ever, though I have noticed a couple of drip-leaks along the top edge of the wastewater tank. I just hold it level when full of icky s***, and everything's fine. What I really wanted to pop in here to say is that I have a little interesting research data from recent carpet cleanings - water reclamation estimates! First, I found that to do really bad spots, the handheld hose attachment WITHOUT the rotating brush is my definite weapon of choice. Just work it hard, and it'll pull up dirt like you won't believe. By comparison, using the machine in normal mode claims a LOT less crud, so to get the same level of cleaning, you have to do it much more often.

What's really interesting is when I did the water reclamation tests today. First, I filled the cleaning solution tank with pure hot tap water (I don't use actual cleaning solutions and you'll soon see why), and then I ran the machine over a section of carpet like I usually do. While doing it, I thought to myself, "Hey, I should see how much water I claim back from the carpeting!". SO, when I was done and I took the wastewater tank to the toilet, I sat it down for a moment and made a mental note of how full it was vs. how full the cleaning solution tank still was. I cleaned out the wastewater tank, refilled the cleaning solution tank, and then poured water from the cleaning solution tank straight into the wastewater tank until it was as full as it had been after doing the carpeting. WOW, what a result. The machine was only about 50% efficient at pulling up the water out of the carpets... that's not great, but not terribly surprising.

What WAS terribly surprising was when I ran the same tests using that handheld attachment and elbow grease. AMAZING. The reclamation appears to be more like 80 - 90%! In fact, it was so good that I had a hard time seeing any loss at all. To confirm this, I ran another test - I *poured* a full 12 oz bottle of water right onto the carpet in a spiral patch and then sucked it up with the handheld attachment. Again, so high a percentile of reclaimed water I was amazed and had a hard time seeing a loss. I'll estimate about 85% until I can do better testing with a good scale to measure the actual water weights, but hell and damn am I impressed by that. Also, just in general, the cleaning job of the handheld non-rotor brush is just amazing. If you need deep cleaning, boy that's how you get it done. NICE.

Some little things to note: I did some additional reclamation testing with just the machine in normal "vacuum cleaner" style use, and now I have better methods figured out because of it. When you're working carpeting, do ONE pass on each area with the cleaning solution spraying out. Just ONE, and then several passes without it spraying to pick the water back up, moving rapidly backward and SLOWLY forward because forward motion is where you get all your pulling power. Because the reclamation isn't the best, any more water applied and you're just making a puddle down at the base of the floor that will not get pulled back up, and much of the ick goes down there with it to stay. Spray light, and the water won't be able to penetrate too deeply, and your reclamation will go way up as will your cleaning efficiency. If you really need to go deep down, then use the handheld, DO NOT use the machine in vacuum cleaner mode! Better yet, soak the holy CRAP out of the spot and then use the handheld, and it should really impress you with a great deep cleaning. Save the vacuum cleaner mode for large area, more superficial type cleaning.

Minor update, 7-18-13: The machine works as well as ever, and I continue to wage war on my evil yet deceptively cute and fluffy cat (he will use any means to convince me that he is innocent at heart!). Every so often, say a month or two apart, I haul out the machine and go to town on a swath of carpet, and I am still rewarded with filthy waste water. Here's the most interesting part about that - I long ago stopped using any kind of cleaning solution. Yep, I just use straight water now. It's WAY cheaper, obviously, and with the filthyness of the waste water I certainly can't claim that it isn't still cleaning. One of the other reasons I went to straight water is to avoid leaving any residue in the carpeting, after reading a lot about such issues on the 'Net. So there you have that. One last thing before I go for another long while - DO NOT GET LAZY AND LEAVE THE WASTE TANK FULL OF WATER! The screws that hold it all together are unprotected steel, and they will rust like freaking crazy! All four or so of the screws in the hatch part of my tank are now badly rusted because I left the machine sitting with water in the waste tank. This is not a design flaw, really, though I'm sure they could have used a better screw material had they wanted to. Rather, it's MY fault for getting lazy. Lazy has NO place in the use of this machine!

Rick NR417

review_title: I don't OWN it yet, but have used one extensively
text:
I am getting ready to order one of these vacuums. I owned the previous non-commercial version and it was amazing. It draws 7.4 amps someone said. That equals 1.18 HP/880 watts; APPROXIMATELY. There are many variables in vacuums other than the electrical draw. The volume of air moved, the suction reading from a water column will give you the actual "sucking" power. The silver non-commercial version was so good that they made it commercial. My hose parts broke, and there are NO replacements. Their vacuum itself works as well as the day I got it over 10 years ago I think. I HIGHLY recommend this. Oreck's portable has less than 1/2 the power at 0.58 HP. If a vacuum was to have a DC power supply and a BLDC motor then you are talking about a much more efficient motor, but none of these have that. It would be prohibitively expensive. (think Dyson possibly) I still have the upright that was of the same model, like a pair. The amazing thing is that the bags were 100% Hepa material. No small filter that gets clogged after a couple of minutes then the air just flows around it. The bags are like felt or a sweater almost, lol.
Well, I highly recommend this and will be ordering it as soon as I finish this.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

When I was in college I worked for a residential cleaning company during the summer and winter breaks. The company had a fleet of these Portapower vacuums and I loved how great they worked. They were easy to carry around and had tremendous power for the compact size. I recently purchased my first home that has hardwood flooring throughout and I had to find this vacuum to keep it clean.

I've owned the vacuum for about 18 months now and I have to say that it's not like I remember. It still does a tremendous job cleaning hardwood floors but the quality seems inferior to what I remember a few years ago. I remember this unit standing up to an environment that treated it very poorly. It was constantly thrown in and out of cars, dropped on driveways, drug through whatever, and cleaned some unspeakable things. All of this without problem. The vacuum kept on running like it was supposed to.

Fast forward a few years and things have changed. First, the cord tangles extremely too easily. I'm not talking about a little tangle where you can straighten it or hold it over a stairwell and it straightens itself out. This unit tangles and coils up permanently and doesn't come undone. I assume it's partly due to the cord being a thicker gauge industrial cord but it is very difficult to work with.

My second complaint is the hose. We use our vacuum once a week for light cleaning in our home. We don't take it outside to clean the cars or anything like that. We have no pets so there is little hair or dust that it sucks up. In short, our vacuum doesn't take much abuse. The other day the hose just split in two. There is no way to tape the hose together so we were forced to purchase a new hose for another $20.00. I understand things wear out but this should not have happened after this short of a time with such light use. Very big disappointment.

In conclusion, this is still one of the best vacuums on the market for cleaning hardwood and tile floors. However, the materials being used on the units today seem much cheaper than what was being used a few years back. Hopefully my new hose will last longer than the first. If another hose goes, then so does the unit.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
I do not own this newer version of the PortaPower. My mom had one of these when I was a kid, and i remember us using it a lot. I bought one of these for myself around 1989, and I still use it to this very day, about 26 years later! Its model number was S7065-060, and it looks exactly the same (shape, hose, attachments) other than the body color, which is orange on mine

I recall my little orange Hoover once having some Good suction power (definitely not as strong as my 6 amp Rigid shop vac, whose suction is excellent), but now I would have to rate its suction as only Fair. I'M fully to blame though: NOT the product. Mine was still working normally until 2008, when I used it to clean up a lot of drywall dust during a remodel that summer, which took a significant toll on its motor.

Even having abused my Hoover (at one point I thought I'd completely ruined it), it survived. I've continued to use it for light duty cleaning around the house (dusting, cat hair, dirt on the entry rug, etc), though it now has trouble picking-up anything much heavier than a standard paper clip.

I'm pretty picky, but this is a solid product. The attachments are great. The hose is thick, heavy & durable, and the body is rugged (hopefully the newer models have not been made TOO lightweight, i.e. easily broken/cracked). And I also love the re-usable bag. If you DON'T use it for drywall dust cleanup (or for anything else that's too fine, such as diatomaceous earth) & you clean the bag often, this thing should last you forever. I would definitely buy another PortaPower (and I may, if mine eventually ends up dying on me -- again, due to nobody's fault but my own).

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

There were ample attachments for all jobs.So much for the good, now the bad: the bag is very small (although it holds more than you might think). The floor cleaning attachment is not well made or well engineered. Now for the ugly: The floor cleaning attachment has 4 small plastic wheels on the bottom of it, these wheels have a propensity for getting dog or humane hair wrapped around them and is almost impossible to remove. If you have a pet who sheds a lot, this is not the vacuum for you.

Long cord

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
I am a professional residential cleaner and ordered this portable vacuum only because I assumed it would be similar to the Platinum portable canister model that was an add-on with purchase of an upright. There are zero similarities! The Platinum is very lightweight and sleek! It has simple construction and is easy to use, no frills, bells, whistles. Even the powerful suction of the Platinum is better than this PortaPower model.

This PortaPower has an extra long heavy gauge cord that weighs too much, with a cheesy snap-strap that won't really stay closed on the heavy cord. The PortaPower has multiple heavy metal extension wand parts, adding to the weight, where the Platinum has a single retractable plastic wand part. I have used my Platinum portable vac for 5 years and it is going strong, so I don't understand why the PortaPower has all the supposedly more durable metal parts. The PortaPower has a thin strap that cuts into one's shoulder, with a cheesy buckle the strap slips right out of. The catch bag that came with the PortaPower is cloth, and has to be dumped out and reused, what a dirty hassle! I purchased separately the plastic funnel and round gasket that secure an optional disposable paper bag, but even this would be a mess to switch out. The styling on the PortaPower is completely lacking.

I want to return this PortaPower model, but the return date has passed while I've been busy. I hope the Seller sees this review and contacts me with a return offer....

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

text: I have had this for a little over a year and I should have returned it right away. It was my second Hoover and the first lasted over 10 years. This one was suspect from the beginning. I am going to be leaving my house for at least a couple hours today so I do not have a problem with this. My carpet is clean. That was my intention upon purchasing and using this machine and that is what I got. Thank you Hoover for a wonderfully clean carpet :)

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: Hard to push, poor cleaning,  Leaks from the dispensing tank.
text: I only used my Max Extract 77 twice.  Once was on a linoleum floor.  It did not clean it any better than I could do with a sponge mop and left puddles of water whenever I stopped to empty the tank.  I recently used it to do my medium pile wall to wall carpet.  It went through two full bottles of 2x cleaner solution in less than 350 square feet of carpet.  I could not understand why it was dispensing the cleaning solution so fast but after a while realized that once I pulled the dispensing trigger once, it kept dispensing, even after the trigger was released.  According to the manual, this is not how it is supposed to operate.  In addition to washing with the cleaning solution, I also rinsed with fresh water.  The dirt in the recovery tank indicated that it had, indeed, drawn a lot of dirt out of the carpet.  Once the carpet was dried I notices numerous large blotches which I think corresponded to where I was when I emptied the recovery tank.  I went back over those areas the next day with fresh water but the blotches remain.  Warning- on carpet, the cleaner is very hard to push.  It should have a handle designed for two hand operation.  Results- lightly soiled areas looks good.  High traffic areas not so good.  Blotches everywhere.

review_title: Carpet cleaner pairs well with a good vac.
text:
The Hoover MaxExtract 77 is everything that all of the other reviews have already said, it is powerful, the attachments are nice, and the separate tanks for cleaning solution & water make cleaning floors so much easier.
I will say this: Get a good vacuum cleaner as well! I was using an older vacuum that was not working that well and the MaxExtract was working overtime in picking up dirt. The brushes became very dirty and required quite a bit of cleaning. I was doing 2-3 passes on the carpet just to get all of the dirt out.

I would imagine that this scenario would have not happened had I had a better vac.

UPDATE 12/11/2013:
I bought a Hoover Windtunnel Upright UH72400 ([[ASIN:B00B7871DS Hoover WindTunnel Air Steerable Upright Vacuum, UH72400]] right after my first review and vacuumed the entire house then used the MaxExtract again. A single pass on the floors did the trick and I am happy with my combination.

text:
This is my first carpet cleaner and I had misgivings after reading so many reviews of so many machines, since it didn't seem to matter which machine I read about - there were plenty of problems. But I went with the MaxExtract and am glad I did. I've used the machine twice, once to clean the living room/dining room/hallway and the next week to clean both bedrooms on my wall to wall carpet in a two bedroom apartment. We hadn't cleaned the carpet in 4 years and decided it was time. I like the idea of doing the carpet myself, when I want to, rather than having to call in a professional. I also can get the machine for about the price of a cleaning or two so why not?

The MaxExtract was easy to put together. It is all plastic, but seems pretty solid to me. It was easy to use and did a great job. My carpet looks new. Yes you have to fill the water container a lot, but if it was any bigger the machine would be too heavy and bulky - same with the dirty water container. The machine is kind of heavy, with larger containers it would be too much for the average person to handle. So just put in your mind that you have to fill it up alot and get into how clean your carpet will be!

I will most likely clean the carpets once a year so hopefully everything will still be working fine a year from now. I'll let you know. Meanwhile, enjoy your new MaxExtract. I did.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]
