text: Had some fresh flowers I wanted to preserve. Comes with two spatulas, two larger measuring cups, a yellow level thing. Workstation is everything, need a thick table cover preferably two or more layers. Set everything up before getting started, make sure its all in arms reach and change out gloves multiple times. I mixed, poured then changed gloves. Resin and hardener are very sticky. Can use a Lava pumice soap bar if any Resin gets on hands. My flowers intact floated to the top as I did not sink them in Resin and let them dry first. I wanted the layered look some depth and the flowers floating to the top changed that as the glitter, shells and glass bits all floated with the flowers. Lesson learned to do one layer, let it dry, do another. Was worried i did not mix exactly half Resin half hardener but all three molds hardened right away. Process takes time and lots of bending over the project, standing. Have about 40 minutes to decorate arrange before hardening starts. I put old boxes on top of the molds as they hardened to avoid and dust dog dander. My three molds equaled about 90 ounces. These two jugs just barely filled to the top all 3 molds. Also, i used plastic cups for mica colors and different colors of glass vs using a wood stick and trying to fish some out with sticky hands. Then threw away the cups. Wood sticks, glitter from dollar tree, sadly DT does not have shells anymore. :-( Cleanup was easy i threw away the brown paper packing in two layers i laid down before, the cups, sticks. Tried to wash out the measuring cups but hot water does nothing for the resin left behind. Lots of lessons learned in my first pour.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: Overall, good machine, needs a few tweaks.
text:
My old faithful spinscrub widepath finally died after many years of great service. Needed something to replace it and after much looking decided on this machine since I liked the fact it could also do carpets. The "replacement" for the old machine was is the spinscrub deluxe which is not nearly as wide but does ok at cleaning. Yes, I own this one also. The 77 will do a great job on carpets, but she ain't perfect. I like the tanks on the machine since they are pretty large and hold a lot of cleaner/ detergent/dirty water, but don't think that means cleaning a lot of area without emptying and refilling. I think that's part of the reason it does clean so well is that it drowns the carpet, agitates the heck out out of the carpet fibers and the redeeming quality, it has AMAZING suction. I would have to guess it reclaims at least 85 to 90 percent of what it dumps out and what's it sucks back up is horrifying even when the carpet doesn't look that bad. If you understand that part going in you'll probably be happy with the machine on carpet. On hard floors, it dumps way too much water/cleaner. Again, does a great job cleaning the floor(mainly tile and laminate) and the suction again redeems itself. It would really be nice if you could control the amount of water/soap the machine dispensed, but you can't. My old widepath did a great job on hard floors and probably used 1/4 of the water/ soap. It also had much smaller clean/dirty water tanks. Seems on hard floors, best method is to move very quickly. Brushes are moving very fast, so not sacrificing cleanliness.
Pros: great suction(really, really great!)
Light
Large tanks
Easy to clean machine
Not overly noisy
Great results

Cons:
Way too much water used for hard floors
**** Hoover pay attention to this****
You morons used zinc plated screws on the INSIDE of the dirty water collection tank. This is completely STUPID and whomever at your company made this decision to save a few cents should be terminated immediately. After 6 months of use with approved Hoover cleaners used, I noticed these screws were rusted so bad they appeared ready to fall off. In actuality they weren't as bad as they looked, but were in really bad shape for only being 6 months old. I went to a bolt supply company and bought enough stainless steel screws to replace them all for 19 cents. On a $299 machine you couldn't put 19 cents worth of stainless screws where they were needed to ensure a long life for the machine???? If these screws rust through, the lid on the dirty water tank would fall off leaving no way to reattach at that point. That was a really bad idea.

Tips: dilute your cleaners way beyond what the bottle says to. Especially on carpets. On the hard surface cleaner, I use 2 capfuls per fill and still does a great job with no sticky feel. On my bottle of Hoover carpet cleaner it says for machines with separate soap bins not to dilute cleaner, follow this and you will have way, way, way too much soap in your carpets. I use an old gallon water jug and put maybe 6 oz of cleaner and fill the rest with water. Fill the soap bin with this solution and have had great results without over soaping the carpet.
Even though I am critical of this machine on a few aspects(sorry for my rant, paid $224 for the machine, shouldn't have to replace screws) it does a really good job. Overall I am happy with it and the results are awesome. I cannot say enough how powerful the suction is on this machine.

And as other reviews stated, the squeegee works really well, until it falls off. Haven't used it in a while and still pulls water off hard surfaces with ease. I'll over look that since it has enough suction to overcome that.

review_title: This might be a great machine, if it worked
text:
This might be a great machine, if it worked. The 2 star rating is mostly due to the poor customer service and difficulty of returning/exchanging the product.

I used it one time (after reading the instructions carefully) and it broke after 2 minutes of use.

The customer service number was completely unhelpful. I need to package it up and pay for the return shipping, and they will decide if it should be fixed or replaced. Instead, I opted for taking it to a warranty service center and was told the PC board was fried. While they are willing to fix it, they cautioned me that whatever caused the problem initially would probably fry the new board as well.

I would recommend a different brand, simply to avoid the hassle of dealing with Hoover's customer service if you have a problem. Also, purchasing this from a local store would have given me the option of returning it without paying more for shipping a defective unit back to Amazon. For now I will have the warranty center repair my damaged PC board and hope it does not happen again. If it does break again, I will by another brand from some where other than Amazon.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

Was a little worried about a seeming lack of pickup of dirty water, but then realized I was just using the product incorrectly - unlike some other cleaners I'd used, the dirty water pickup happens when the trigger is NOT pulled (whether you're going in forward or reverse).  The other cleaners I'd used picked up only on the reverse stroke, so I just naturally followed the same pattern when using this cleaner and as a result was only picking up dirty water on the "reverse" passes.  Read the manual (always a good idea to RTFM), adjusted what I was doing, and the cleaner began picking up much more dirty water.  LUV it.

review_title: Third times the charm?  Powerful yet short-lived carpet cleaner
text: As so many have said, when it works the machine is incredible.  We have had three machines in the last ten years and they all worked very well until they failed.  The main issue is that the parts degrade from contact with water/cleaning solution.  This is made worse by things like pet hair making their way into the internal cog work.  The hose attachment began leaking on all three machines and the rubber becomes tough and brittle.  This makes for likely rips when using any attachments.  The loss of suction causes water to back up in the system and furthers the breakdown of component parts.  While I like the carpet cleaner, I really can not recommend it for the cost, longevity, the waste of cleaning solution, the breakdown of seams leading to internal leakage (such as between the cleaning solution and clean water chambers),and complete lack of customer service on these issues.

review_title: Hoover vs. Bissel vs. Rainbow shootout
text:
Edit: After less than a year, the mixing valve failed, the dirty tank top cover warped and no longer seals properly, and finally, the clean water tank valve failed. Hoover's customer service is less than helpful, claiming (falsely) that I used 3rd party detergent, and that is the reason for the failures. I have been using a variety of tactics to make this machine work: rinsing out the detergent tank between washing and rinsing, taping around the dirty tank seal (otherwise the extracted water quickly foams up, gets sucked into the blower, and sprayed back onto the carpet), making a final pass with my Rainbow to extract more dirty water, and now running really fast from the sink to the machine before all the water leaks out. It was great when new, but I have used it less than a dozen times. My old Bissel lasted for a decade. I will be going back to Bissel, and now profoundly regret getting rid of my old one.

--original review--

TLDR: I'm happy with this carpet cleaner. It does a good job, has its standout features, as well as its quirks, just like any other machine. I would buy it again, but would probably be equally happy with a Bissel.
Since I have these 3 here simultaneously, a shootout is in order. I have a Bissel ProHeat 7950 (purchased 2000, no longer available), Rainbow Aquamate 3 (purchased 2011), and this Hoover (purchased 2014).
First, overall impression of the Hoover. It seems to be well put together. I like the idea of the separate tanks for clean water, dirty water, and detergent. The spin scrub brushes seem like they would clean the carpet fibers better, by brushing them from different angles. The design is aesthetically pleasing, and all the accessories stay onboard. I'm not a fan of the turbine-driven brushes, though it seems to work okay.
Pretreating: I'm of the school of thought that believes in giving the cleaning solution time to do all the work. I generally pretreat, wait 5-15 minutes, then come back and do the water extraction. It gives the expensive cleaning solution time to work and pull up some of that deep dirt. The Bissel actually has a Pretreat/ Tools setting, which diverts the suction away to the accessory hose. This allows the cleaning solution to be sprayed onto the carpet with the brush rolling, and seems to do a good job of loosening ground in dirt. The Hoover has no such option, probably the biggest flaw in the machine. Removing the dirty water tank and placing a gym sock over the screen allowed me to pretreat with the Hoover. However, without the dirty water tank installed, the machine is incredibly loud. Since more of the suction is directed to the turbine, this might shorten the life of the turbine and brushes. The Rainbow similarly does not have a pretreat function, but I simply removed the clear front panel to pretreat. Sometimes the Rainbow doesn't want to spray without sensing suction, but momentarily placing your hand over the suction hole usually fixes it. If not, a ping pong ball worked to block it off while pretreating. Furthermore, the Bissel has the motor toward the front of the nose, which puts a little weight on the brushes. The Rainbow doesn't lose but an ounce or 2 with the plastic shield off, so no degradation in performance. The Hoover has the motor near the wheels, so with the tank off there is no weight on the brushes to help them scrub the carpet. Scoring: Bissel, Rainbow, Hoover.
Water spray: The Hoover has 5 spray jets, compared to 2 on the Bissel and the Rainbow. The 5 spray jets put a good amount of water down, and do it evenly. The Hoover's spray is anemic, though that could be due to many years of abuse. The two nozzles also spray unevenly when they work, leaving wetter and drier stripes. The Rainbow doesn't suffer that problem, probably due in part to its narrower 10" brush (vs the Bissel's 12" and Hoover's 13"). The Hoover's clean tank seems about the same capacity as the dirty tank. The Bissel's bladder-in-tank design means that the clean and dirty water capacities are about equal as well. The Rainbow has a significantly smaller clean water tank, probably around 2 qts. All 3 auto-mix the detergent (though Rainbow requires you to add some water to the detergent tank), but only Bissel allows you to adjust the mix strength. Scoring: Hoover, Rainbow, Bissel.
Extraction: The Hoover got the carpets nearly dry, and within 3 hours they were dry. The Rainbow did almost as well as the Hoover, requiring 4-5 hours to dry completely, but still dry enough to walk on and even lie on. The Bissel was by far the worst, requiring 12+ hours to dry. The Hoover picked up a small amount of water droplets after the Rainbow, about the same as going over a rinsed section a second time. It picked up a significant amount of water after the Bissel- not as much as the first pass after a rinse, but a lot more than the Rainbow. Scoring: Hoover, Rainbow, Bissel.
Maneuverability: The Hoover is a beast to push around. I'm a guy in fairly good shape, and my arms and back were starting to tire after cleaning about 1000 sq. ft. The machine itself weighs 22 lbs, plus add another 8 pounds for the clean water tank and potentially 8 more in the dirty tank, and you could be pushing around 40 lbs. That's not even counting the additional resistance from it sucking itself to the carpet. The Rainbow is light and easy to maneuver, thanks to the vacuum motor being housed in the canister part. The Bissel is the easiest, being self-propelled. Turning the self propelled function off, however, puts it nearly on par with the Hoover. Scoring: Bissel, Rainbow, Hoover.
Emptying: Each design has a pretty ingenious solution, and this is where they differ most. The Hoover's dirty tank slides off an on easily, even with the machine locked standing. It has an emptying hole with a removable cap, and the entire top removes for cleaning with a pop latch. The emptying hole makes it easy to drain, but the design of the tank means you have to shake it around to get the last dirty water out. Furthermore, there are lots of corners and crevices for dirt to hide. The Rainbow has the standard 2 qt and optional 4 qt tanks, which sit below the vacuum motor unit. They are both easy to clean.The Bissel's bladder in tank is also easy to remove, with a handle built into the tank lid, though there is no handle to aid in emptying. The dirty water does pour out of the back easily. It's a nightmare to clean, as the bladder cannot easily be removed, and neither can the plastic top piece. Furthermore, it makes more of a mess if there is any clean water left in the tank, as it pours out while you're emptying the dirty water. Scoring: Rainbow, Hoover, Bissel.
Brushes: The Bissel and Rainbow have traditional roller brushes. The Bissel is activated by the handle tilt, while the Rainbow's is activated by the handle trigger. Bissel is run off the vacuum motor, while Rainbow has its own small brush motor. The Hoover's spin scrub brushes are run off of a turbine, similar to the way the spin scrub hand tool works, or even the Bissel's power brush hand tool. Overall, I just don't feel this design has as much power. Scoring: Rainbow, Bissel, Hoover.
Cleaning: The Hoover's dirty tank is difficult to clean. It's also difficult to empty any leftover detergent back into the bottle. However, the spin scrub brush rack removes easily, as does the front suction plate. Both are relatively easy to rinse clean. The Rainbow's front plate snaps off and wipes clean, and the dirty tank wipes clean as well. The brush is more difficult to remove and clean, though. The Bissel... forget about cleaning it unless you're ready to take it apart with a screwdriver. There is a tiny mesh screen that has to be removed and cleaned periodically. Scoring:Rainbow, Hoover, Bissel.
Repairability: Eventually, any of these machines will need some repairs to keep running. I'm not the type to throw out a several hundred dollar machine if I can fix it. Though I have not taken it apart, everything on the Hoover seems easily accessible and well laid out. The Bissel is fairly straighforward, but has a lot of parts. In addition, the water runs up to the handle to be heated, then back down to the head unit. The Rainbow was designed for ease of manufacturing, and everything snaps together. It's difficult to take apart, and never seems to work the same after being put back together. It's more of a disposable unit... sad, because it costs nearly the same as the others. Scoring: Hoover, Bissel, Rainbow.
Other comments: I LOVE Hoover's self propelled feature. However, it seems that they no longer sell anything that is self propelled. I also like Bissel's heated water feature. I'm not sure if it makes a difference, but it stands to reason that hot water would be better for cleaning. There is one section of carpet that was treated with some spot remover, and it always foamed up with the Bissel or Rainbow; the Hoover, however, didn't cause it to foam up. This leads me to believe that though I really want to like the spin scrub brushes, they're not as effective as the roller brushes. However, they did seem to get up all the other stains, so their performance can't be that far off. Though the Rainbow seemed to do well on paper, it (the Aquamate 3 attachment) has been a regretful purchase. It has been the most troublesome in its short life. The shorter width also means it takes longer to cover a given area. The Hoover's dirty tank was not sealed well from the factory, and has a small drip. The Bissel and Rainbow will both leak any leftover water or cleaner into a puddle on your floor if left alone for a period of time (few days?). I don't think that will be a problem with the way the Hoover is designed. Furthermore, the Bissel's detergent tank cap is easy to overtighten (as are the Rainbow's detergent and clean water caps), which creates a leak. The Bissel's tank gasket got pinched one time, so it drips clean water onto the floor.
Overall, I think the Hoover and Bissel are worthy competitors: both good machines, but neither perfect. I hope this review helps you sort out the features that are important to you. Though the Bissel I own is no longer available, it is very similar to current models. The Rainbow simply isn't up to the task of heavy duty whole house carpet cleaning. It's more of a spot or room machine, and a dainty one at that. I cannot recommend it outside of those limited uses.
The Bissel has stood up well to abuse. I bought it in college to clean up after parties (and get my rental deposit back, which I did!). It was replaced 3 times under the store's 4-year extended warranty program. We used it at least weekly, and frequently lent it out to friends. I think the Hoover should do as well.

text:
I wanted to like this machine but I do not.
Cons:
--You MUST carry the thing on your shoulder because:
--(a) There are no wheels. I put felt sliders on the bottom of the can to help protect floors when I set it down.
--(b) The short springy hose just pulls the vacuum on its side, upside down, whatever.
--The bag is easily clogged. We have one cat and a 2000-sq foot house with all wood floors, and I have to empty at least once to vacuum the entire house.
--And the bag is not so easy to clean. You have to actually pull out the dust bunnies, then bang the bag on the side of the trashcan a bunch of times, and every other time you have to actually rinse it out and wait for it to dry.
--So I'm going to have to buy some extra bags.
--The suction is okay but not fabulous.
Pros:
--The cord is very long. Nice!
--The attachments attach with an easy twist lock, so they stay on. Nice!
In summary: Shop around. You need wheels, a non-springy hose, and a bag that doesn't clog so easily.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: Works GREAT except wheels on the bus don't go round n round
text:
Bought this to replace Hoover Steam Vac that essentially died after 6 arduous years of use and good service. While it's still a big bulky plastic-y thing that looks a bit like an oversized Mattel Transformer, I expect it to be as sturdy as its predecessor, off which not a single thing broke, cracked, or came off in 6 years of furniture and wall-bumping use, despite all my initial doubts and trepidations. After 60 days with the Max, I continue to be impressed with it's cleaning performance, including water extraction, from both carpet and hard surfaces (as long as I have that squeegee attachment in place for hard floor cleaning), and how radically much easier it is to clean than the Steam Vac, which was a pain in that regard. Having finally taken opportunity to use upholstery cleaning attachment, I found that worked very well too.

My one and only complaint at 60 days, is that the wheels squeak and creak, and one sticks. I notice sometimes one wheel does not turn at all on part of either the forward or back stroke, and it's slow and reluctant to turn by hand as well. As a cleaner I love it and can't say enough about how well it performs, but I paid too much (significantly more than the prices listed here) for the wheels on the bus to not go round n round. It will be back to the dealer for a check on that as I can see no means of adjustment, but that's the only bar to the 5th star from me as I've experienced none of the problems expressed in the significant number of negative reviews - at least not if I: 1. Had the hard floor squeegee attachment in place, and 2. Cleaned the 2 filter screens.

review_title: Great quality, but lacks manual settings
text:
This little thing really is an incredible incubator. It's dependable and simple to use, but it does have two minor drawbacks: It's noisy, and it has no manual settings. Unlike other high-quality mini bators like the Brinsea mini advance, you cannot control the temp or humidity. You just select the bird species from its menu and it does the rest. The other problem is that it beeps. A lot. It beeps when you turn it on, it beeps when it turns the eggs every two hours, and it beeps when the water reservoir is low!

Those complaints aside though, I've had excellent results with it: 100% hatch rate for chicken eggs and 70% for my call ducks, which is quite high since they are notoriously difficult to hatch! If I had to do it all over again I'd probably drop the extra $60 and get the Brinsea, but if you're a first-time hatcher or perhaps a teacher who wants to hatch eggs easily for the classroom with a "set it and forget" incubator, then the rcom is definitely the best choice.

text: Bought it because of a positive experience with what seemed like an equivalent model bought 25 years ago. This model is much worse. I have used it three times on light duty jobs and it is already clogged. I tried to use it to clean out my car and it picked up the pebbles from the floor and the suction is so weak it, it spit the pebbles back out on to the seat when the position of the hose changed slightly. Also, the old version of this had a nice long hose so you could put the canister on the ground and reach into a car or into cushion. This vacuum's hose does not extend anything like the picture suggests. The hose has a lot of tension so if you extend it more than a few inches, the canister slides along and bumps into things. To prevent this snaking action you have to wear the vacuum. Poor suction and poor usability make me regret this purchase quickly after buying it.

I wouldn't want it in my bedroom. incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: Very Good but Room for Improvement
text:
Overall I give this vacuum 4 stars, but there are a few of items I really don't like about it.

1. It always falls off your shoulder anytime you bend down. And, even though it weighs only 8 pounds, after a little while it can get uncomfortable hanging on your shoulder. I ended up buying a small backpack at the local Goodwill. I cut holes in each side of the backpack, one for the hose and the other for the exhaust. Another plus with the backpack is I have a place to store the tools. It works great.

2. The hard floor attachment (floor brush) is way too small at 9 inches. Why is the carpet attachment 2 1/2 inches wider?

3. The cord is too stiff. It's like bending a wire coat hanger. Well, that's a bit of an exaggeration, but it does tend to hold its shape. This causes the cord to get caught on furniture and corners when you're moving around a room. I've never had a vacuum with a cord this stiff before.

3. Speaking about the cord, it's long, like 33 feet long. This is great when you're vacuuming the whole house. It's not so great when you want to do a quick pickup as you have the long cord to roll up. A great idea would be a cord that detached from the vacuum (like my electric leaf blower and string trimmer). This way you could have both a short cord and a long cord. Update: I ended up cutting mine and adding the necessary male/female plugs. Wouldn't advise you do this while it's under warranty. If you do cut it, consider what is your longest room before you clip.

4. The upholstery tool is hard plastic with rubber on one side. This works great for pulling pet hair off the furniture. However, the rubber on the tool makes it a pain to use on loose upholstery as it causes the material to bunch up. You cannot "glide" it across the furniture.

Other comments/observations:

Several reviewers commented on the noise. I think it's quieter than my Shop Vac and old upright Panasonic. So, I have no complaint there.

Cleaning out the cloth bag is messy. Pet hairs really stick to it. As another reviewer suggested, I've washed the bags in the washing machine several times now without any problems. I haven't tried the disposable bags, but due to the small size, I think you'd be buying a lot of them.

If you have mostly hardwood, laminate or tile floors in your house, this vacuum really is better than trying to maneuver around a canister vacuum. And, uprights are best left for carpets.

text:
I bought this cleaner after steam vac from another brand died on me. I can't tell you how happy I am with this carpet cleaner. It really gets DEEP down to bring the dirt out of carpet. And not just dirt, I find chunks of rocks and other sediment that it pulls out from deep down.
I was shocked to see how much dirt it pulled out of my seemingly clean carpets.
CLEANING the tank is a cinch! You can empty it through the screw off hole, or unlatch it to pull the top completely off. (The bissel I had, had a bladder inside and cleaning it was sick and never complete, and it would start smelling, so this is much nicer).
It has a motorized brush hand cleaner to do stair etc. I do wish it had the same pressurized water technology on this.
I have not yet used it on hard surfaces.
TIP: Make sure when you empty the tank to clean the little screen under where the tank is, it fills up with carpet fibers and doesn't funciton properly if the screen is full of lint/carpet fibers. I found another screen when you flip open the front, but it doesn't get full as often.
I would buy it again and it definitely out performs my prior unit. Worth the $$$

review_title: After two warranty service visits still doesn't work properly
text:
This machine is a great disappointment. I would give it 0 stars if possible. We purchased this Max Extract 77 to replace a MaxExtract all terrain which is starting to fall apart after about 4 years of good service. I noticed that the Max Extract 77 failed to dry the carpet after using it about 10 minutes. I pulled the old machine out to pick up the remaining water, which it did without a problem. After 30 minutes of trouble shooting with the Hoover rep, they told me to take the machine to a service center. Two weeks later, I picked up the machine and it still not picking up water as it should. It also still leaking large amounts of water out the back when moved in the upright position After another 30 minutes with the Hoover rep I was told that I should not expect the machine to pick up more than 1/3 of the water it puts out. Are you kidding??? Well, if I had known that I would have never bought it. The Hoover rep suggested that I try another service center. I'll update this review after I get it back. I did not know that companies actually produce new models which are inferior to the old ones on purpose!!
Update.. the second service center (3 hour round trip drive) suggested that the water tank was leaking because the caps were not sealing. A new water tank was supplied. The new tank also leaked, however, I fixed the problem by taking the seals off the first tank and adding them to the seals on the new tank. OK now the tank does not leak, but the machine still does not pick up enough water to make it useful. My biggest mistake was discarding the packaging so I can't send it back. This machine was manufactured in Mexico and after looking at the tops of both water tanks I can clearly see the same defect, causing the tank not to seal.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
I had two Bissell ProHeat machines in the past ten years. I thought it did a good job of cleaning the carpets, but as another poster says, it leaves behind bits and pieces of the carpet in large fuzzballs. The second Bissell finally died, and I'm laying hardwood in part of my house. I wanted a machine that could clean the hardwood and the carpets in the rest of the house. For that reason, the MaxExtract was very attractive. Once I got it home, I used it on the carpets for its first action. I am so happy I got this machine! Just as a comparison to the Bissell, there are no fuzzballs after using it. And, the water/cleaning fluid tank is so much more ergonomic. It's vertically positioned, so the weight is distributed better when you're carrying it. The Bissell was more horizontal, making it bulky, swinging back and forth more. The Hoover carries more like a bucket. Also, with the Bissell, the dirty and clean water tanks were stored with the clean water being in a plastic sac inside the dirty water. Cleaning it out after dumping out the dirty water was difficult, and filling it back up with clean water took some positioning in the sink. With the Hoover, the clean water and cleaning solution are in tank together. The dirty water tank is completely separate. This makes much more sense, and everything is vastly easier to fill up/clean out than the Bissell. This machine has a much better design and is more user friendly than the Bissell. I wish I had known this before I bought the second Bissell.

The only thing I don't like about it is the cheap plastic tool carrier that I had to attach to the back. The tools don't fit all that well, and the long hose used for manual cleaning doesn't really fit around the carrier very well, causing the ose to fall off while I'm using the machine to clean the floor. I ended up taking the hose off and storing it until I need it.

I have not yet used it for hard floor cleaning because the hardwood floors are still being installed, and it requires that I change the cleaning brushes on the bottom of the machine. I fully expect it to be as user friendly as everything else, and I'll update this post to provide some feedback, especially if it's not easy to use.

I thought there must be something I'm doing wrong but then I found a video on youtube which this man shows the same problem--his experience was identical to mine. Other people left comments as well about the issue. To make matters worse--all my floors are laminate and tile with an exception of one small area rug. And even worse yet--I'm past my return date. The fact that Hoover knows about this problem, has done nothing to resolve it and continues to sell it makes me livid.

review_title: not useable on tile; perhaps will work on carpet
text:
After wearing out my third Hoover hard floor/carpet cleaner I was quite happy to try this one. Unfortunately the squeegie (essential for hard floor cleaning) would not even attach. A call to Hoover brought a quick response that they would send a new squeegie. It arrived eight days later and did attach, but not with a "snap" as mentioned in the manual and the Hoover site video. I began to clean the tile floor; after a few swipes the squeegie came off. Tried several times with the same outcome. I had a prolonged call with the Hoover support line; the agent kept indicating I hadn't put the squeegie on correctly. She suggested that I should take the machine to the service center (70 miles away, I turned that idea down), and then said I could take it to a local appliance dealer to have them show me how to attach the squeegie. After telling her I had read the manual twice and watched the Hoover how-to video, plus had my engineer husband read the manual and watch the video, and he had no better luck attaching the squeegie so that it would stay on. She then told me she would transfer me to someone that would give me further assistance. When the new person got online, she not only did not know anything about the situation but said she asked if I was a dealer because that was who she works with. She transferred me back to customer assistance and another agent who offered to send a new squeegie. I did not want to go past the 30 day return period, and did not have any hope that a third squeegie would solve the problem, so declined that offer. I asked if they had any clips or other means of keeping the squeegie attached and got a negative reply. I told her I would be giving up and returning the product.
Amazon made it very simple to return the product; they deserve a five star review for that process.
Addendum: About 30 minutes after completing the customer support phone conversations, the first agent called to let me know Hoover would replace the appliance. I did not take advantage of their offer, but instead gave up on a hard floor cleaner/carpet cleaner and purchased a different brand vacuum/steam mop....which does work.

review_title: A Tale of Two Poorly Housebroken Dogs, Hoover vs. Bissell and a Beige Berber Carpet.
text:
We have two rescue dogs. Cute little girls, but poorly housetrained. If someone is around, they'll ask to go out. If no one is nearby... Well, let's say two dogs and a light beige, Berber carpet is not a good mix. For years, we depended on our Bissell ProHeat Upright Cleaner until a key component failed. (A gear broke off.) While it had been a good workhorse for about five years, it was time for a change. I had been intrigued by the Hoover spinning brush design and dual tank system over Bissell's spinning roller and single bucket with a bladder inside. I read favorable reviews and I guess it's only right that I add mine.

I love the dual tank design of the Hoover vs. the singe tank with a bladder of many Bissell models. The two tanks of the Hoover pull out of the machine very easily. To be fair, the single tank of the Bissell was easy to remove and replace, too. However, Hoover includes a removable top to the dirty water tank to facilitate cleaning. The problem I had with Bissell's bladder system was trying to clean the darn thing after using it. I never felt as if I could clean its unexposed nooks and crannies.

As far as pushing and pulling the machine across the carpet, I prefer the Bissell over the Hoover. The Bissell does its work on the back stroke, as you pull it towards you. The Hoover MaxExtract 77 uses a push and pull system. The push movement cleans while the pull stroke rinses. Having a Berber carpet means having a very low pile carpet. I was surprised how much effort it took pushing the machine forward. Remember, once filled with water, both of these devices are hefty. They're sucking and scrubbing your carpet as you move it. I'm a big guy (over 6 feet tall and 200 pounds), but using either of these machines will wear you out by the time your done.

As for how well it cleaned and dried the carpet? I think it's a toss up. I remember being impressed with the Bissell when we first bought it. I am very impressed with the Hoover, too. It removed lots of nasty, puddle stains. I think the Hoover left the carpet drier than the Bissell and equally clean. I've also used the big cleaners you can rent from the grocery store. Both the Bissell and Hoover give equal or better results. Both of the home models are easier to use than the rental units.

Water and soap use. I felt as if I was changing the water more often with the Hoover than with the Bissell; though this is arbitrary. If you don't use the CleanSurge on every cleaning stroke, the soap reservoir seemed to last for two complete tank fills. I used the 32 oz. bottle that came with the cleaner. It was a 2x concentrate that loads into the clean water tub. It was very simple and accessible to fill the soap reservoir and clearly marked with where to fill with cleaner and water. It holds 16 oz. of 2x cleaner per filling. Our Bissell model had a separate container for the soap. I like Hoover's method better. Easier to fill. The caps are easy to screw on and off.

On each filling of the wash tank, without using the CleanSurge, I was able to clean a 4' x 4' square area. Then I had to stop, empty the dirty water tank and refill the wash tank. After two tank fillings, it's time to refill the soap. I cannot say one model uses more or less soap than the other. With either one, you go through LOTS of soap!

Spinning brushes versus a roller brush, which is better? You got me. Both seemed effective. I am very impressed with the Hoover's spinning brushes and do not regret the change in technology. I think the best guidance is to consider other factors.

ProHeat Bissell versus Hoover's MaxExtract. With Bissell, the instructions said to fill the reservoir with hot water, then start the unit for two minutes to give the heater a chance to warm up before using. It would leave the carpet moist and warm. I didn't see where the Hoover recommended a water temperature. I used hot water and I was happy with the results.

All-in-all, the Hoover MaxExtract 77 met or exceeded my expectations. It's dual tank design is very simply and much preferred over the Bissell's single tank with a bladder design. As for durability, I can't rate that yet. I've only used the Hoover twice. If it lasts as long as the Bissell did, I'll be happy. The MaxExtract has extra features I haven't tried yet. I haven't tried the detachable hose yet or its spinning brush. It won't need to do much to work better than the Bissell. I found the Bissell hose system worthless and ineffective. Also, the Bissell model I owned wasn't designed for tile or hardwood floors while the Hoover was. I haven't tested this aspect yet, but I'm looking forward to giving it a go soon.

One additional note about this particular model, the MaxExtract 77 appears to have more spinning brushes than other models. Look carefully at the photographs of this model vs other models. The MaxExtract 77 has a front row of six spinning brushes and a second row of five brushes.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
I bought my first one of these as a present for my wife. It steam-cleaned the carpet and didn't cost $40 to rent. After two months, I'd have given it 5 stars. Then it started breaking. We use it maybe 6-8 times per year, so it's not due to overuse.

It first broke down after six months. I took it in to a local warranty dealer, who fixed the clogged tube (while complaining loudly that Hoover had started producing really cheap machines in recent years). It broke down again after another 9 months (15 months total) for undetermined reasons and was no longer under warranty. Before I could stop her, my wife went out and bought another (same model).

That one lasted 9 months before breaking down. Different vendor told me my mother board was fried (and also complained loudly that Hoover had started producing really cheap machines in recent years). A local warranty dealer confirmed that and Hoover sent me a replacement (refurbished, not new). 5 months later, that unit is now no longer picking up water and I am beyond the warranty period.

These are cheap, but the breakdowns are maddeningly frequent. I think I'm going to make my next try an upscale brand (Riccar, etc.).

The reality: Two days later, the WingIts arrived. "WingIt," of course being an idiom for "hastily executed with little to no planning." Product is starting to become more in line with its namesake than description.
These plastic anchors have to be "assembled" before they go into a wall. Also beware, they need a 3/4" drill bit. While "assembling" them (which consists of sliding one plastic hexagonal rod into its corresponding plastic sheath) TWO of my six INDESTRUCTIBLE, NEVER HAD A FAILURE EVER, STRONGEST DRYWALL ANCHOR EVER CONCEIVED cracked. The plastic cracked. Who could have seen that coming?

The result: As these Wingits couldn't even stand the blistering force that is popping them together, I was not going to trust them to anchor half my TV's weight to the wall. They have been reboxed and the return shipping label is printing as I type.
0/10, I am less than thrilled.

text: I bought this Hoover MaxExtract 77 to replace my old Hoover carpet shampooer which still works, but is tired after 15 years.  At first I mistakenly bought a Bissel, but after putting it together and seeing how cheaply built it was, I took it back.  I bought this Hoover Maxextract 77 directly from Hoover.  It is not quite as heavy duty as my old one (which was built in the US!), but it is impressive.  I just finished making some of my old 1980's wool area rugs look like new.  After pouring out the licorice water I realized I had it set to "rinse."  Imagine what I can do using carpet shampoo!  It has some nice features that my old one did not.  You put the detergent in a separate compartment and you can then switch back and forth between "clean" and "rinse" without having to change the water bottle.  I don't know why they make the collection bucket so bumpy but surprisingly, it is easier to clean out than my old one, using a sink sprayer.  It feels like a nice heavy duty machine and seems to get stains out pretty well.  You will never get rugs as clean as sending them out but most rugs get to the point where it is more expensive to send them out than the rug is worth.  That's where this DYI machine comes in handy.  One of the reasons I bought this model was for the rotating upholstery cleaner which I used all the time on my old machine. It does an OK job on tile floors but does not clean the grout.  I use a Black & Decker scrub buster on the long stick to scrub the grout, then go over it with this machine to suck up the dirt & water.  I would not use this machine on my hardwood floors--I don't care how much they are sealed.  It does NOT do rug fringe, but it does not choke on it like a vacuum (I duct tape rug fringe under the rug anyway). Some helpful advice:  1.DO vacuum your rugs before you use this machine.  Don't use the shampooer as a general vacuum.  2.Put some fans in the room and rugs & carpets will dry quicker, even without a heater. 3.  Lay small area rugs on top of bigger rugs that you are about to clean and they will not scoot around so much.  4.  I clean the tops of area rugs, then flip them over and do the back, if they do not have a rubber backing, then I do the top again. 5. Pour the waste water down the toilet or outside, not the sink, unless you want to do a plumbing job.

You may have to go over the wet area a couple times to get it completely dry, but it does get dry.  Bottom line is, FOR ME, this thing works.  I have no problem with having a mop that I paid $250 for...as long as it keeps the floors clean.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]
