review_title: no issues yet, but some minor concerns
text:
this is the 2nd steam cleaner i've owned and for the most part, i'm pleased with it.

out of the box it was fairly simple to assemble. i noticed right away, however, that the plastic water holder was pretty carelessly glued together. there were gobs of dried glue at some of the plastic seams.

i had a lot of trouble getting the plastic water holder snapped in to place. it wasn't until it was filled with a couple gallons of water that snapped in to place. that's fine while you're steam cleaning, but during storage it's not so efficient.

as far as cleaning, it appears to do a good job. even though i steam cleaned my carpets about four months ago, the hoover max extract still pulled up some unholy gunk out out my carpet. the suction, in my estimation, left a bit to be desired (my carpets were wet -- yes, i read the instructions -- after several dry passes). but it was a fairly warm day they dried in a couple of hours.

in short, it did the job, but closer attention in the manufacturing and a better wet suction system would go a long way.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text: As a multi-tenant property owner for over 18 years, I was looking forward to having a machine that could easily clean both hard floors and carpets. This machine was easy to assemble and I had it up and running within minutes, but.....it does not vacuum up most of the water. It leaves about 2/3rd of the water on the floor. Fortunately, I tested it on resilient flooring first and so was able to mop up the water with towels.  Thank goodness I didn't use it on a carpet - it would have been ruined by that much water. I called  customer service and they walked me through a set of diagnostics. We confirmed that the machine was working properly - it was pulling vacuum, the valves were properly positioned, etc. My overall opinion? This machine is outperformed by a mop and bucket.  Very disappointed.

I love the features that make it easy to clean/rinse after use, like the waste tank that comes apart and the removable nozzle. The auto rinse function is great, too. It would be nicer to have a longer cord, but no big deal.

I don't get the complaints of other users who say the machine leaks. I had to problem. Just make sure both tanks are properly placed and secure...

A TIP: If you have a water softener like I do, DO NOT use as much Hoover cleaner as recommended. You will end up with WAY too much foam in the waste water tank, and suction will stop when its only half full or so because the suds raise the float. I recommend maybe 2 tablespoons, if that. Soft water will probably do a decent job without any shampoo...

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

..before purchasing this vacuum, I read the reviews. They did not do this little vacuum justice. I just unpacked this little guy and cleaned the whole house in 2 hours (4 bedrooms)!, from chairs, lamp shades, table tops, floors, stairs and throw rugs.

Carpeted stairs – this zoomed though the chore, and admit it they are a chore!!
Dusting – had to hold at a slight angle because it has so much suction.
Floors – the device was the right size for breezing though the bathroom floors, which I hate to do!
Blinds – zipped though them no issues.
Rugs – great on throw rugs and small area carpets. I have one of those dirt catcher rugs by the back door, it is a pain to clean, not any more.

Every once in awhile you’ll say this is the best money I’ve ever spent, this qualifies!! I loved it so much I bought my best friend one. Now I know she’s going to think I’m crazy until she uses it!! : )

The only downside is I tried to trip over the cord a couple of times, until I figured out to throw it over my back. The vacuum does get heavy after awhile, definitely use the hip strap(bought the separate carry bag). The other positive – the cord is long, I plugged it into a central location upstairs/downstairs and didn’t need to move it to clean the entire 2nd/1st floor. Now that was nice!! I can’t wait to try it on the car interior. : ) Really, I don’t think you’ll be disappointed in this vacuum.

Should mention I own a canister and an upright Aerus vacuum (the original Electrolux (now Aerus), not the current Electrolux brand). They clean well but if you own them you know they are heavy and it takes some effort to drag them out for cleaning. This will be a joy to grab, and it does just as good a job cleaning. Yes, I take cleaning seriously!! : )

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,

review_title: A wonderful investment if you have carpet(s) and you’re a dog owner.
text:
My dogs are 11 and 14 years old - with one having accidents almost weekly on my cream carpet.

That being said, I use this vacuum on the reg, quarterly, to clean cream carpet which covers my entire apartment. I’m also very allergic to my dogs (found out after I adopted them, don’t judge), so I have to constantly suck up the dust and dander.

I was tired of renting a disgusting and dirty carpet cleaner machine from Safeway and then rolling it four blocks to my building in the middle of downtown DC (I don’t own a car). After two years of renting the big large red machine, I decided to invest in my own carpet cleaner vacuum. I was initially hesitant to buy my own vacuum because I live in a 700 sq ft apartment with limited closet space to store this machine. However, 4 years later, I have no regrets.

That’s right, I’m writing this review four years later because my neighbor borrowed my vacuum and then asked for me to send him the link bc it worked so well. When I visited the “My Orders” section I saw I ordered this machine in 2017 and it’s still working like new. If anything, I use it more now because of my dogs’ aging, resulting in inconstance and a lot of “surprises”. I thought this called for a rightfully due positive review.

To confirm, I clean it after every use, I wipe clean the filters and make sure I clean the brushes, removing as much debris and dog fur (and my long black hair!) as possible, which my regular vacuum can miss when I dry vacuum before shampooing the carpets. I love the attachment to spot clean and have not used the squeegee attachment for my tiled kitchen floors.

Again, I’m writing this review four years later because it is truly tried and tested for cream carpets with one 14 yo Golden Retriever mix and one 11 yo German Shepherd mix. Happy cleaning!

review_title: Super vacuum with one minor complaint
text: Super vacuum with one minor complaint. Comes only with a reusable cloth bag, which must be emptied and cleaned often, depending on your usage. If you want to use disposable paper bags (type N), as we do, you have to order the plastic adapter and rubber ring/belt separately. IMHO, Hoover should include the adapter and rubber ring/belt with the vacuum, giving the customer the option of using a reusable cloth bag or disposable paper bags. The parts show on the included parts list, but must be ordered separately. Otherwise... a really super, powerful, lightweight vacuum (8.3 pounds). Highly recommended for dusting, since the vacuum can be carried using the shoulder strap, freeing both hands to reach high up to clean book shelves, etc. I strongly recommend purchasing the Hoover carrying case with the vacuum, as it has a padded shoulder strap for more carrying comfort and a nylon mesh bag to store accessory parts. Another plus with this vacuum is the approx. 30-foot long power cable so you don't have to unplug and replug from room to room. We first used one of these Hoover PortaPower vacuums (nearly identical to our new one) over 40 years ago. Hoover still makes and sells them, proving true the old adage: If it ain't broke, don't fix it!

I've had the Hoover V-2 for quite a while and it finally gave out. The V-2 was a very good machine, but this one is far better. The only downside is that the recovery tank has to be changed more often with the auto-rinse feature, but that is a small inconvenience considering how well this machine works. It cleans extremely well, no doubt due in part to the new pressurized detergent delivery and forced heat features.

Unlike the V-2 and other older models, this one cleans on the forward stroke. It then automatically rinses on the backward stroke as you keep the trigger pressed down. For tougher spots, there is a second "power boost" button which you can push with your thumb while holding the other trigger on the forward stroke to put more detergent into the mix. It works well, but if you use it a lot, you'll want to alternate thumbs as it takes a fair amount of pressure to hold it down. Detergent use is far more efficient than with the older models, even with frequent use of the "power boost" button.

Cleaning upholstery and smaller carpet areas with the V-2 was a nuisance, because the separate hose and its power cord both had to be attached to the unit. For this model, Hoover has kept the hose "on board," so it can be used simply by attaching the scrub brush and pulling the trigger on the attachment. This is a major plus. The hose delivers a lot more cleaning solution than the old models. I was initially concerned that it was oversaturating upholstery, but it actually did a very good job. If possible, leave a ceiling fan going to speed drying and use several "dry" strokes after applying the solution.

This machine is well worth its price. Highly recommended!

review_title: A portable, versatile, and reliable Hoover vacuum cleaner
text:
Our overall rating on this product is higher than the features in this review, because we value this cleaner for applications that need portability.............such as vacuuming a car, vacuuming the inside of an air handler, vacuuming hard to reach areas in a garage, cleaning the inside of our heat pump, and cleaning up after completing home projects. We also value it for its reliability and long life. This is the second Hoover portable vacuum we have purchased. The first, which was nearly identical to this one, lasted more than 25 years. As you know, not many products last that long these days.

This vacuum has better suction power than many portable vacuums, and is very versatile with the variety of attachments that come with it. It complements our floor vacuum, which we use inside our home.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: Not as happy as I would hope.
text:
I was replacing a Bissell Pro-Heat with this Hoover MaxExtact77. The reason I changed to Hoover was that I hate the bladder system that Bissell uses and my Pro-Heat was a bit bulky and heavy for me to use. I prefer to have my clean water and dirty water completely separate. Also do not like to mix my detergent directly in with clean water because I want to be able to run a rinse pass easily. After much research, I decided on the MaxExtract 77 because I could use it on my tile floor as well and it met all my requirements.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: Started out great - broke after a few uses
text:
NOTE: I wrote the original review (immediately below) in January, 2013. SEE UPDATE AT THE BOTTOM OF THIS REVIEW.

Bought this machine at Wal-Mart this week for $219. I've cleaned two carpeted rooms (closed loop, low pile carpets), my couch, and a padded rocking chair so far. Overall, I'm very pleased. Definitely worth the investment.

I live in an old house in the country with two kids, six cats, and a husband that works outside a lot. They all track in dirt, mud, and sweat. We eat and drink on the furniture daily. You can imagine the condition.

The carpet is 20 years old and had been steam cleaned only once years ago, so I didn't expect miracles. The machine pulled up more stains than I anticipated (carpet is dark blue). It didn't fully remove the toughest stains, but this is to be expected. Maybe a second pass with the machine will help those. No doubt, my carpet looks and smells MUCH better.

The couch and beige padding on the rocker hadn't been "shampooed" in their 12 years of existence. The arms of the couch and rocker were especially filthy. I was amazed at how much of the dirt the machine pulled out. Again, I wouldn't call them "like new", but the arms and cushions look far better. If I'd been using this machine from day one of getting the furniture and cleaning stains regularly, I feel sure that the couch and rocker could well be in "like new" condition today.

PROS:

--Easy to assemble
--Easy to operate
--Good job extracting dirt and stains
--Uses tap water (not distilled like my Steamfast brand portable cleaner)
--Comes with handheld tools for upholstery, stairs, and spot cleaning--LOVE these
--Hose length is good for doing upholstery
--Vacuum handle can extend down low when reaching carpet in awkward places (e.g., under a low table)

CONS (these don't bother me, but might prohibit others from buying):

--Machine is lighter than I expected when it contains water (1 gallon), but still a lot of stress on your back when you push and pull.
--Water needs changing more often than I expected, but I move slowly and that makes a difference. For an 8'x8' carpet, I changed the water about 7 times. I just poured it outside, as I have exterior doors in every room of my old country house.
--Plastic parts on the machine do seem rather fragile. I wouldn't get rough with it.
--Clean water tank must be inserted just right to prevent it from leaking. Sometimes requires multiple attempts. A bit of a hassle, but "do-able". If not for this, I'd give the machine 5 stars.

TIPS:

--Buy a bottle of cleaning solution with the machine. The solution that comes in the box is really just a sample. Doesn't go far.
--I bought Bissell 2x Professional cleaner because I didn't see the Hoover solution at the store. Realized after I used the Hoover sample solution and the Bissell solution that the machine requires only about half the amount of the Bissell solution per gallon of water as compared to the Hoover 2x Professional solution. Both appear to work equally well.

Bottom line: I definitely recommend this machine to others. Just be sure that the cons don't pose major problems for you, especially if you have physical limitations.

UPDATE AS OF JUNE, 2014:

--DO NOT PURCHASE this machine

--The vacuum started out great. After a few uses, I noticed the clean water tank leaking. Initially, I blamed myself, assuming I must have incorrectly inserted the tank onto the machine. When readjustments didn't help, I thought I must be overfilling the clean water tank. Wrong. Now, the soap dispenser leaks uncontrollably. I've used this machine about 15 times in 18 months, taking good care of it throughout that time and using it according to instructions.

DON'T WASTE YOUR MONEY

review_title: What a disappointment!  Leaves carpet so wet that mildew has set in after 5 days. Also leaks a lot of water on carpet when off.
text:
My older Bissell unit finally broke down after many years of faithful service. I checked out Consumer Reports and found the Hoover to be one of the top rated models, so I bought the most current Hoover model the MaxExtract77. I didn't get it out of the box and set it up till this last week. We tried to do the carpet downstairs. What a joke! The carpet is a low pile, level loop commercial glue down. With the Bissell it always was dry in a few hours, but this HOOVER left the carpet soaked. Even though it does pick up some water,, it leaves the carpet way too wet to dry in a timely fashion. We went over and over the carpet to try to pick up all we could. Now, 5 days later it is still wet and the smell of mildew has set in. I called Hoover. nice CSR lady but she said "if it picks up any water at all, it must be working correctly". SHe told me to take it to a Hoover repair center. She also said the slide switch with settings "1,2,3" is labeled wrong. Don't know if that's true. but?? Since I didn't open the box till 3 weeks past the 30day Amazon return policy, Amazon Customer Serivce was very nice and sent me an RMA without any hassle! Thank you Amazon! I though I was going to be stuck with a LEMON. I would definitely NOT recommend this product.. Unfortunately I still need a carpet cleaner, but I don't know which one to buy.

UPDATE: Another reader felt that perhaps we did not have the height adjustment set correctly. There is NO height adjustment. Check out the users manual on this point.
As a follow up, I was able to buy for $16 including shipping from AMAZON the broken part for my old Bissell ProHeat 2X. I put the new part on and I am back in business. I cleaned the living room deep pile carpet, it came out great, and was dry in 8 hours. Again very happy with AMAZON.

text: Solid construction, very tight, no leaks.  This item is designed as a flow diverter, but works equally well as a source switch (similar in function to an A/B switch in electronics).  This can be plumbed to either have a single source that can be diverted into one of two outlets or you can create a reverse flow: having two sources from which you can choose one or the other for a single outlet.  I'm using it this latter way.  I have town water and well water plumbed to the back of my house for outside use.  With this valve I can have the town water through the hose for filling the dogs' drinking dishes and other potable uses and then switch to the well for volume uses like watering the lawn.

text:
I have had a Hoover Wide Path 6500 for 10+ years. It has never been repaired. It was an Awesome steam cleaner. I just knew it was nearing its end. I wanted to buy a new model and did a lot of research online first. I thought for the money and good reviews this was the best choice. I used it for the first time this weekend to clean the carpets. It did a better job the the old model. The brush heads spin way faster. The tanks for the cleaner/water & dirty water are very easy to remove and reinstall. The machine is much lighter than the old model. The plastic is also much thinner and isn't as wide as the old unit. That way it is much lighter and easier to use. I can see how some reviews say they broke something plastic on the vacuum. If you take your time and don't rush this should last a very long time? If you are careless and try to throw the tanks on or hit the walls. I can see something plastic breaking off. The only 2 things I can say bad about the cleaner is. The power cord is shorter than the old model. So you will have to unplug it and use another outlet for the other side of the house. The instructions say to press the trigger on the front pass then on the pull back. This is putting water/cleaner down on both strokes. The old one was only on the front stroke and extracted on the pull back. I did as instructed and the carpets were wet a lot longer than the old model. Next time I will try pulling the trigger only on the front stroke to see of they dry faster. The carpet took about 8 hours to dry completely with my dehumidifier on. They look great for 8 years old and furry kids.

***1-7-2014 UPDATE***

Well the first one lasted less than a year and now the second one broke down 1 year & 4 months later. I just replaced it with a different brand. So everything I said above is true it does a good job cleaning the carpets but isn't made to last. So if you decide to buy this model and keep it over a year? I would definitely buy the extended warranty like I did.

text:
I bought this product years ago. I needed something for my first house to help keep the hardwood floors clean and the carpets nice and tidy. I had the unfortunate luck to find this product, and Hoover. When the time came to finally use it, imagine my happiness when, on its maiden voyage, it begins leaking water EVERYWHERE. The spinning brushes weren't working, so the suction wasn't properly working either--and I was left to soak up water from the floor towels and a mop. As annoyed as this was, I called customer service. They were quick to offer a replacement. I shipped this lug out and waited patiently for the new one. It came--and is only a carpet cleaner. I wasn't provided the same product I initially purchased, and I certainly don't have enough carpet to spend this much money on ONLY a carpet cleaner. I wasn't asked if there was a different product I'd want and certainly wasn't offered cash or credit to getting something else.

This was last year. I wasn't going to post a review--but now I'm finding myself having to buy another product to keep my floors cleaned. Their initial product is what I wanted, and it failed. Then they shipped me a different product that I didn't want or have a real use for. And now I'm having to spend more money for a hard-floor cleaning. I haven't bought Hoover many times in my life, and I doubt I ever will again. Too shady a product and company.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: Where Have You Been All My Life, Portapower?
text:
I've been putting up with minorly-irritating problems with my somewhat similar vac from another manufacturer for the last 25 years or so. The old one (joyfully!) just went in the trash. The Portapower won't win any beauty contests, but it's such an infinitely better product I can't say enough good things about it.

First of all, let me explain that I have almost all bare floors -- linoleum in the kitchen and bathroom, and wood everywhere else. This style of vac is the best choice for my house. It works quite well on the small portion of kitchen carpet I've placed over the linoleum, but its real strength is on bare floors, upholstery, etc. This might work fine in a house with more carpets, but think a beater-bar type floor tool would be better for large expanses of carpet, which this vac doesn't have.

Here are the reasons I like the Portapower vac so much:

1. Inexpensive. Forget Dyson, et al. Why pay for huge advertising campaigns and snob appeal? Totally functional in appearance.
2. Lightweight and easily portable. Weighs about half of what my old vac did, and is comfortable to use with the shoulder strap. I can finally do my stairways without risking life and limb. The only thing that would improve the function would be if it were battery-powered, but I'm sure the suction couldn't be as powerful if it were. The cord (which is bright orange and VERY visible for safety -- a touch that I also appreciate) isn't overly long, but it should be adequate for most uses.
3. Powerful. Must have at least twice the suction that my old vac did. This does cause a little bit of trouble with my old, limp throw rugs, but I'll get over it. Either that I'll get new *stiff* throw rugs.
4. Well-designed. Tools lock to wand, wand locks to hose. My old vac had tools and wand that held together by friction, and I was constantly having to put them back together. NO MORE! Hooray! The combination of the better-designed tools and greater suction means I'm pulling cat hair out of my furniture that's been all but woven into the fabric for 20 years and more.
5. Paper dust bags are optional. A converter kit to use paper bags is available, but not required. I haven't decided if I'm going to going to get one or not -- luckily the kit is not expensive.

THANK YOU, HOOVER! I'm looking forward to a long, clean relationship!

text:
I'm an owner of a small cleaning service. We needed a small mobile lightweight vacuum that our workers could bring to work traveling by public transport. We chose CH30000 Porta Power and it generally met our expectations. It is compact, has an enough suction power, a few nozzles for different surfaces, a lightweight metal tube that is easy to assemble and which could be placed in a backpack. The bag for collecting dust is small, 1 quart, but very capacious, it is enough to vacuum for two 2-3 bedroom apartments a day, and this bag is easy to clean or wash. It's very economical. A 30-foot power cord is very convenient.
Disadvantages:
1. Low efficiency for cleaning carpets with long nap. For this we carry with us a more powerful vacuum cleaner. But if we go to order not by car, then we have to use this one. It work for vacuuming if you make an effort. Also it is low efficiency for cleaning bare floors. We stopped using the carpet/bare floor nozzle from the first days. It is cumbersome. Generally speaking - it works, but not perfect, because the design of the nozzles is not too successful.
2. The attachment of the vacuum cleaner belt to its handle is awful. For a commercial product, this is unacceptable. The belt broke off in the first few days and the vacuum fell to my feet. I just tied it to the handle and now I'm waiting for the belt to come off again and the vacuum cleaner will kill a bone on my leg. Then I'll file a lawsuit against the manufacturer and become a billionaire)))
3. The power cord of this vacuum is simply wound on the handle of the vacuum and fixed with a small strap. This is a very inconvenient and poor attachment that destroys the idea of ​​mobility.
4. One of the biggest drawbacks is that the vacuum cleaner blows out with such force that it disperses all the dust in the room. That is, you vacuum in front of you and behind you a vacuum cleaner raises dust clouds into the air.
Resume: This vacuum cleaner is intended for commercial use, that is, it must be thought through to the smallest detail and as ergonomic as possible. But the creators of this vacuum cleaner failed this task. However, in general, it works for us and we can forgive a lot for its light weight.
UPD The belt is constantly torn. The hose burst at the attachment point to the metal tube. We had to buy a new hose. Nozzles have a plastic mount and broke in the place of attachment to the metal tube. All nozzles have a bristle that wears off over time. Now almost all nozzles are bald and can scratch the floor. That is, after six months of use, you will have to replace the hose, nozzles and a worn bag to collect dust and spend about half the cost of this vacuum cleaner ($ 50). Disappointed in general. Such a product can not be called a professional.

review_title: I've had my Hoover Portapower for 30 years
text:
Like Georgia Girl, I've had the same Hoover Portapower since the early 80's. I really just want a new one because my old one is so scrappy looking, and I've had to repair the little plastic buttons that click the attachments in place, etc. I looked at new ones in the 90's (before such easy on-line research and shopping) but I didn't like the model they had out then -- I think it was orange and goony looking. It's funny that the Portapower now looks exactly like the one from 1981, but black instead of beige.

But I'm disappointed in what James said, about the springy short hose. That sounds like a new feature that they should have more thoroughly vetted. (And I'm disappointed that Hoover was unresponsive to James' input about it.) But I wouldn't really love putting my old hose on my nice new vacuum. Does anyone think it would be possible to clamp the ends of the hose from here to there and stretch it out? Or is it an unmalleable material?

I think I will still get this one. I saw there is a home model (C2094) but it seems to not be very readily available on-line or elsewhere, where this "commercial" model, 3000, is all over the place.

Glad I read the reviews, everyone -- thanks.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: This resin is very finicky!! Edit: I fixed the issue I was having, it was my fault!!
text:
I can mix up a batch and pour it into a mold that has several pieces to it that are all the same thickness and some will cure within the 3 hours I have them on the heating mat and then there are other pieces that stay gooey. The pieces I am trying to cast are not thick, maybe about 1/2cm so this shouldn't be happening and I am always super careful to make sure my mixture is exactly 1:1. I've tried curing without using the heating mat and I get the same results. I would understand if it was poured from a separate batch but it's not. I'm not sure if this resin is just that sensitive or if I'm doing something wrong with it. I make sure not to add to much colorant to the mix also because I know that can cause it not to cure properly. I've had to scrap so many items because even after sitting for almost a week now some of them are set on top but gooey inside the mold and I don't think it's ever going to set. I've wasted so much resin in this past week when I decided to try this brand, I don't think I'll ever buy it again because I feel like I have had to throw more away than I have actually gotten good results from. When I do get it to set, it sets beautifully, but the issue is actually getting it to set and then not knowing if I'm going to end up having a good outcome or having to re-pour it. It's costing me both time and money because I have customers waiting on items and when I have waited days for it to cure and it doesn't, then that sets me back even more because I have to recast it again. I'm at a loss as to where to go from here with resin. I still have almost a gallon of it but I don't want to keep wasting my time not getting a good outcome.

Edit: i changed my review to 5 stars because I read some other reviews and googled some about this particular resin and realized I was the one making the mistake, I tried again and this time instead of mixing my hand for like 2 mins, I used my drill with the mixing paddle and I mixed for about 10 mins and this morning woke up to some absolutely perfect castings, that are all nice and solid and very very few tiny bubbles. I spritz my pieces with 91% isopropyl alcohol(rubbing alcohol) and it makes bubbles almost immediately pop, it doesn't completely get them all out on some bigger items, but my smaller ones hardly ever have any bubbles and if they do it's usually my fault for not making sure that all the tiny small corners or points are fully filled.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
I purchased this little vac for our cabin in N.H. We have 2 dogs, one of which has an undercoat which is constantly shedding! I had previously purchased 2 vacuums that never really picked up the fur. I resorted to sweeping and dust mopping all of the time. Needless to say that mode of cleaning is very time consuming! After reading EVERY review on this vacuum and several other vacs I decided to purchase this one mostly because I could sling it over my shoulder and it supposedly had a very strong suction. I must say, after only one time using it that it lives up to all of the positive comments I have read and possibly more.

I can't believe the quality of the attachments and how easily and smoothly they attach. We have a central vac in our present home and the suction on this little vac is as strong as the suction on our central vac. It attended to the edges very well and to our wood and tile floors. We also have scatter rugs with a very low pile and the vac sucked up all of the dog hair without a problem.
I realize that this is a very early review, but at this point in time I am very pleased! I will write back in a year to let readers know if it has lived up to my expectations! So far, this little vac has exceeded my expectations.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: Beware!  There are to many issues with this model.
text:
Having owned a Hoover carpet cleaner years ago, I took most reviews with a grain of salt. I am giving an honest review after purchasing and using the product.

PROS:
* Has great suction for water pickup.
* Performed great when used for carpet cleaning.

CONS:
* The hard floor squeegee will not stay attached. Each time a grout line is passed as you pull the machine, it pops off.
* The dirty water tank has a two piece design for easy cleaning. Beware, it leaks if you tip it off of a horizontal plane, and drips dirty water all over your freshly cleaned carpet. If it leaks water, it leaks vacuum also.
* The latch that holds the handle in the upright position works its way to the right and has to be pushed back to the left to engage the latch.
* The clean water and cleaning solution tanks are extremely small, and require constant refilling. (I was cleaning an 8 * 12 area rug and it took 4 refills to complete. Imagine cleaning 4000 sq. ft. house that was all carpet!)
* The hard surface cleaning aspect of this is the worst.
** It does NOT clean the grout at all.
** It leaves a sticky residue on the tile.
** It leaves a tremendous amount of water on the surface.
** It SHOULD NEVER be used on wood flooring, even if it is sealed. The amount of water delivered and NOT picked up would cause warping on any wood surface.
* Very loud, but it is a vacuum that's designed to pickup water.

All in all, Hoover works great at cleaning carpets, minus the issues listed above. Save your money and buy a simple Hoover Carpet cleaner and forget about cleaning hard surfaces (Tile and Hardwood) with this or any other advertised multi surface cleaner.

I will be returning this product.

UPDATE! Even though this was purchased as a PRIME item, it is NOT RETURNABLE! How Amazon can sell a defective product and not accept the item for return is ludicrous! In the future, I will be making large item purchase like this from the big box stores that allow returns.

went out in the trash 6 months ago.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

Fast forward to a year later when I was ready to replace the carpet cleaner with only one pet of course I bought a Hoover.

I would never be able to clean the area rugs over the wood floors as it would damage them. Think twice, no three times before you purchase this product. There has to be a better one out there. And shame on Hoover for not standing behind their name with superior products and selling out.

I forgot to mention that is leaking out the back now which it has not done in the prior 2 1/2 months.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]
