review_title: Defective unit does not live up to the Hoover experiences I've had previously
text:
I've used several different carpet cleaners over the years, some I've rented, some I've purchased. After renting a carpet cleaner a few times it became obvious that for only a bit more than a rental, I could own a cleaner rather than have to rent one that has to be returned quickly. That's when I invested in my first Hoover carpet cleaner. I bought it used and I don't remember the model number. Although used, the carpet cleaner worked extremely well and I was very pleased with it. There was only one problem with it - the previous owner had broken the upholstery wand and I really wanted to be able to do my upholstery.

So I gave that used one to a friend and bought a brand new one from Amazon - the [[ASIN:B00009R66F Hoover SteamVac Carpet Cleaner with Clean Surge, F5914-900]]. This one was fantastic! Everything worked well on it, including the upholstery wand.

A bit later, I received a [[ASIN:B00450U6CS BISSELL Big Green Deep Cleaning Machine Professional Grade Carpet Cleaner, 86T3]] to review. This cleaner was also fantastic, although not cut out for small living areas due to its bulky size. However, that same large size meant I could clean a larger area in a shorter period of time, which was very nice.

When I found the Hoover MaxExtract77 Multi-Surface Pro Carpet & Hard Floor Cleaner FH50240, I was sold. The one thing all of the other carpet cleaners I had were missing was a hard floor cleaning feature. I had purchased a [[ASIN:B000I618NY Wagner 905 1,500-Watt On-Demand Power Steamer and Cleaner]] to steam my floors and it works very well, but I thought having one machine to do both hard floors and carpeted areas would be perfect.

Unfortunately, the MaxExtract77 doesn't live up to the quality I've previously experienced with the Hoover brand, both in carpet cleaners and vacuums. From the moment I started assembling this unit, I knew it was bad. I've assembled two carpet cleaners and three vacuums by myself over the years without a problem. The MaxExtract77 I received was very obviously defective. I screwed the top handle into the base without issue. Then I tried to add the water tanks. The bottom tank for dirty water fit fine. The top tank that holds the solution was a different story altogether. It was impossible to latch it into the cleaner and I almost hurt myself trying to. Impossible, that is, until I removed the screw securing the top handle in the base. With the screw removed, I could get the top tank to latch if I pushed it with a lot of weight behind it. The trouble is, this pushed the screw holes on the top handle and base out of alignment so the screw could no longer be inserted at all. Not good.

I finally gave up and called Hoover customer service, where I received an agent who introduced herself as Mona Lisa. This agent was not very helpful, didn't seem to know what to do or how to handle a situation like this and finally promised to have a supervisor call me to see if they could help better. That was April 24, 2012. It is now July 4, 2012 and I still have not received that return call. After waiting fruitlessly for that call, I finally called the customer service line again. This time I was aided by Ian, who was actually extremely professional and helpful. He agreed to send replacement parts for the top tank and the top handle in the hopes that these new parts might be made a bit better. Ian went out of his way to make this exchange as convenient as possible for me, even sending a shipping label so I could send the defective parts back.

The new parts arrived the next week. While they work a little better, they are still not good. I can now secure the handle with the screw AND put the top tank in, but again I have to push the top tank in with a lot of weight behind it to make it fit.

Although I had no confidence in this machine, I tried cleaning my carpets with it. One thing I do like is that the solution reservoir has separate compartments for clean water and the solution. This allows you to use a Rinse feature on the machine if you like.

The MaxExtract77 is close to the same size that my old Hoover was, but I found it much more difficult to push over the floors than the old one. In fact, my Bissell is much larger than the MaxExtract77 and the Bissell is easier to push. When I finished cleaning all the floors in my home and the upholstery in my car, my arm ached from the wrist all the way to the shoulder blade. I wasn't able to sleep on that side at all that night and the pain kept me awake until I finally put two ice packs on my arm. I've never had this issue with any other carpet cleaner.

Despite the issues with the assembly and the weight of the machine, it really did a great job on both the upholstery in my car and my carpet. I bought my car used and have never cleaned the upholstery before. Someone evidently spilled dark soft drinks in various locations because after I sprayed the seats with the Hoover cleaner, large dark spots appeared where there had previously been no sign of a stain, almost as if it were invisible ink. The Hoover worked very well to remove these old stains and also some newer stains on the carpet in my house.

I then set about to clean the hard floors in my home. This feature was the main reason I wanted the MaxExtract77 and I was excited to use it. The hard floor attachment was easy to attach to the bottom and it seemed secure when I started. I was soon disappointed when that hard floor attachment fell off the unit after 2 or 3 pushes and was further frustrated when it persisted in falling off constantly. Not only that, the hard floor cleaning didn't seem to actually suck up any water and left huge puddles of water all over the kitchen and dining room floors, causing me to fall or nearly fall several times. I called it quits when the last fall hurt my tailbone pretty badly and also bruised my arm significantly. There are much easier ways to clean a hard floor without resulting in bodily injury.

One other thing to note is that the Hoover MaxExtract77 seems to run through the cleaning solution pretty quickly. It came with a 32 fluid ounce bottle of the Hoover Professional Strength 2X Concentrate for carpets and a 16 fluid ounce bottle of the hard floor cleaning detergent. The carpet cleaning concentrate ran out before I finished and I had to get some more cleaner to finish the carpets. Before I ran out, I was able to clean the upholstery in my car, the living room, two bedrooms and the hallway. I used the entire bottle of hard floor detergent to try to clean the kitchen and dining room floors. There might have been enough left in the clean water tank to do the two bathrooms since they are very small, but I gave up on hard floor cleaning before I made it to those rooms.

If the MaxExtract77 had been the first Hoover device I had ever used, I would likely never buy another of their products again. Luckily, I have had fantastic experiences with other Hoover products in the past. I do like the Hoover brand, but I would absolutely never recommend the MaxExtract77 floor cleaner to anyone. This machine is highly defective and should be scrapped. Look at other Hoover models, but do not buy this one.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text: Our hoover platinum carpet cleaner finally died after 7 years. Since that model was discontinued, we did our research and looked around. I can't believe after 7 years, other carpet cleaners still don't offer an auto rise. The excuse we saw was "if you really want to rinse the carpet, dump out the clean water with the cleaning solution, add water and go over the carpet again without adding any cleaning solution.... WOW!!! It must be nice to have all the time in the world to spend that much time just trying to clean a carpet. We rinse the soap off dishes and clothing, why wouldn't we rinse the soap off the carpet. Needless to say, we selected this model. It uses more water and cleaning solution than our old machine and doesn't glide as well, but we are very happy with our decision.

text:
Far better than I anticipated. My carpet did not look dirty but water pulled out was black . . . a shocker.
Dried in dog urine stains that I had spent considerable time trying to remove finally came out with just first pass. Stains/spots removed . . . which never came out when pros cleaned.

I have dense carpet, but no problem for Max Extract. With two extra passes, carpet was dry in 4 hours.
Auto rinse feature is a big plus and really works. I did a second rinse a few days later and very little detergent left behind.

There are some trade offs but they're workable. You do have to empty and refill often, but if higher capacity water storage were used, machine would be too hard to push/pull for any length of time. As is, it provides a good work out. Yes, plastic parts . . .but could you push and pull a machine made from heavier material for a couple of hours? Only poor design I found was the front nozzle attachment . . .likely to break if you don't pay close attention when removing.

You have to clean one of the two filters each time you empty the dirty water tank . . . and depending on type of carpet, maybe even more frequently. If you don't scrape off the lint build up on the filter, the suction drops considerably.

And it uses a lot of detergent, but how much do you pay for pro carpet cleaning service every year? The thing pays for itself with the first cleaning. Cost of detergent is the only additional expense after that.

Have used pro carpet cleaners for years and never satisfied. They are always in a rush to get to the next job. Amazed to find a product that gives such great results.

review_title: This is a poorly constructed and even more poorly engineered cleaner
text: This carpet cleaner broke under its own weight the third time I pulled it out the the closet to do a spot clean. It leaked and dribbled out of the box and the floor squeegee attachment would not stay on. I called Hoover's customer service and they shipped a new attachment squeegee but it took 4 weeks to get it. The instructions admit that a small amount of dribbling and leaking is normal. I took it into the local Hoover repair and he said I should return it. That he sees many of these units and they are fragile, poorly constructed and typically take 4 to 5 weeks for parts.. I simply cannot recommend this machine. It was replacing a Hoover that was replacing a Bissell, none of which were built for anything other that extremely light duty. When it comes to carpet cleaners, the thought doesn't count as much as the construction. BUY A ROYAL OR BUY AN EXTRACTOR, in the end you will spend the same. Amazon gracious accepted the return of this unit, eventhough I was 5 days past the 30 day deadline notifying them of the issues with the unit. They did however only refund a portion of the price (75% approx)

text:
I did a lot of research before purchasing this carpet cleaner comparing features and weight of the machine. Not that this is a light weigh machine, but I did find that the Platinum models all were a good bit heavier. I love the separate containers for clean and dirty. The collection tank also opens up to allow you to clean the dirty tank. Some may think no big deal after all it just gets filled with dirty water. For us pet owners we know what we may have to be sucking out of the carpet that is a big plus. This feature sold me on the hoover over a Bissel. Also it does suck up alot of the water. While it claims no more wet socks, that requires a logistical miracle. You do go back over the carpet a couple times to suck up all the water. It sucks up enough that it is dry with in a couple of hours (with the help of a fan).

my carpet is very light colored and had very dark streaks- some that were made worse by cheap carpet cleaners. This cleaner was a last ditch effort to avoid replacing my carpet and it did the trick. At first I thought it was leaving a good bit of dirt behind but by the time I turned it to rinse and then went over it once to help get the water up, it was great. I highly recommend this model!

review_title: This really is a great little vacuum
text:
This really is a great little vacuum, if you know it's quirks. When used for the first time its suction is incredible, you can easily suck up change, screws, glass, etc.. The problem is that some things get stuck in the hose, usually at the collar that attaches to the vacuum body. You may not even realize it at first because there is still some suction, but only a fraction of an unclogged hose. One tip is to get to know what the motor sounds like fully unclogged, then you can hear what it sounds like when it begins to clog (it whines at a higher pitch). I sometimes throw a penny on the floor and attempt to vacuum it as a test; if it doesn't rush through the tube into the vacuum, your hose is clogged. What I do is take my broom with the longest handle and unscrew the hose, check if there's a blockage at the hose's collar where it meets the vacuum housing (sometimes you can just pick out the blockage with your fingers), hold the hose over the toilet or trash bag, and shove the broom stick through the hose. This relieves any blockage I've come across. Some things that cause blockages I've run across are little bits of cellophane, twigs, twist-ties, Q-Tips, and the like. I just pick up those objects by hand when possible. The other cause of poor suction is a dirty filter. If you don't use the bags, the filter gets packed with dirt quickly. It takes some effort to clean it thoroughly under running water, but it's worth it (let it dry for a day afterward). If you mind these two problems, you'll likely keep the very powerful suction this vacuum initially has...

P.S. I bought a vacuum brush attachment - http://www.amazon.com/Attachments-Replacement-Dusting-Brush/dp/B0016PS0JQ/ref=sr_1_1?ie=UTF8&qid=1404455722&sr=8-1&keywords=vacuum+brush+attachment - which fits nicely. It works beautifully with this vacuum and is my favorite attachment. Great for quickly dusting the walls, ceilings, and floorboards :)

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text: I've used most types of hollow wall anchor on the market and WingIts are probably one of the more difficult to install. They are rated at 300 lbs., but that's in direct shear (i.e. load applied parallel with and flush to the wall). No pull-out rating is stated, but would be much less than 300 lbs. and is the reason they are to be used in vertical walls only and not on ceilings. The instructions state only that "Strength and stability are greatly affected by projection off and length of interaction with the wall surface." These anchors require drilling a 3/4" diameter hole to install. This info takes more research than it should to find. The anchors come in two parts - the winged top and face plate - and include #8 x 3-1/2" long SS screws. The winged top and face plate are "popped" together prior to insertion through the hole. The wings must be compressed by hand to allow partial insertion into the hole and require a lot of force to do so. The instructions say to next "pop" it through the wall. Once through the wall the anchors are loose, to what degree depending on the thickness of the wall. Once popped together, it would be possible, but unlikely, to separate the anchor parts and lose winged top inside the wall. Nevertheless, the winged top slides fairly easily on the face plate and makes stabilizing the anchor in the hole while attaching whatever you plan mount on the wall, well, tricky. This is especially difficult when mounting anything with a blind hole or that projects any distance from the wall. Once installed, the anchors are sturdy enough, but the cost and difficulty of installation make other types of anchors (e.g. toggle bolts or strap toggles) a better choice for anything other than where very high shear loads are involved and anchoring into studs is not possible.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
Ok so, How to describe this carpet cleaner can only be done in 2 words "MIRACLE" and "WORKER"

This thing is a work-a-holic. For starters, after it's done shampooing, I've never seen another carpet cleaner suck up so much water. If you have one and wrote a bad review because it doesn't suck, Then have it replaced, plain and simple. Nothing does better.

For second, I spilled a bowl of chili, STUPIDLY, on my living room carpet about 3 months ago, did some reviews, had chosen this cleaner to purchase, though Walmart was out of it. I asked them when they would get it in,utes and they said it's on a truck, they just haven't unloaded yet, come back tomorrow night and I'll give you 10% OFF, SO I figured good deal, right? More than I could have hoped for. 24 hours later, after the chili had SET IN to stain, This system had taken it out in less than 5 minutes. I could NOT BELIEVE IT! There's not a sign of it whatsoever.

Last night sometime, I don't know when, my pup must have spilled a cup of red fruit punch or cherry (I forget which I bought lol) Kool-Aid and splattered it specks all over the carpet, AND my white bed sheets. I could have absolutely slaughtered him right here this morning when I found out. The stains had already dried because this was sometime last night and completely and totally set in once again. dumped the cold water out, replaced with hot steamy water (I can do this because the cleaning solution tank and water tank are two different tanks inside the same unit!!!!!) and again, less than 5 minutes, and you can't even tell the stain was even THERE!!!!!!!!!!! NOTE: I did this less than 15 minutes ago, and the carpet is BARELY damp on bare feet.

All in all, I've never seen a carpet cleaner like this one in my life. I've hired professionals at my other apartment, and after 3 runs, they needed to still replace the carpet...I had rented rug doctor out 4 times in a month...and I don't think it picked up a single thing. This unit could have probably SAVED me $1,100 of carpet replacement in the one I just moved out of, now that I think about it.

Summary of this Cleaning unit: BUY IT BUY IT BUY IT BUY IT BUY IT! You won't regret it.

PRO's:
1) Suction that sucks up probably AT LEAST 90% of the water it lays down, If not more.
2) 2 seperate compartments in the main clean tank each for Plain water and cleaning solution mix.
3) Dirty tank is extremely easy to remove and replace, dump out, and also open up and clean. The thought behind this alone is Flawless. Only thing I wish it had a rubber seal between the two halves of the dirty tank so when you carried it, you didn't have to keep it almost level)
4) Dirty tank and Clean tanks have handles that make them easy carry.
5) Every single part of this unit can virtually be taken apart for easy cleaning if you need.
6) Filter check is directly under the dirty tank, so easy to get to and clean. Impressive.
7) 11 brush wheels and 7 brushes per wheel to make 77 individual brushes that dig, agitate and clean. (never go for a drum with the wave brushes on them, THEY SUCK)
8) I said something similar to this above, but different: each brush wheel can independently be removed and cleaned thoroughly if needed.
9) The pressurized cleaning of them unit SERIOUSLY sprays it down deep, I feel as if I'm even cleaning the PAD underneath the carpet.
10) Finally: The unit has 3 scrub settings, small pick up, gentle scrub or power scrub, AND also the ability to RINSE!!! Most cleaning units will wash and shampoo and pick up, but don't have the ability to RINSE. Which is why each time you shampoo your carpet, it seems to get dirtier quicker and harder to clean as well each time. The shampoo ATTRACTS dirt and dust and grime like a magnet attracts a paperclip. The ability to rinse, believe it or not...keeps your carpet cleaner...LONGER because the shampoo is not there to attract dirt anymore. So this is a FANTASTIC Feature.

NOW for the CONs: The list of features even if you compact them as much as possible. GOOD outweighs bad by a landslide.

1) ALL PLASTIC PARTS....This isn't as bad as you may think. I've had it for 3 months, And really the plastic is pretty durable. Yea, I mean you could have all metal, or partly metal, but that would just make it that much heavier. I haven't had one problem with the plastic parts, ad as long as you use common sense when cleaning, or tightening bolts, etc...You should never see an issue with this.
2) It is a bit bulky, slightly heavier than I think is needed. but it's not too bad.
3) the hose for attachments is nice and long, My attachment spray switches do get stuck in the open/spray spot sometimes, and I've gotta fiddle with it. I need to buy some WD40 and spray just a little, see if that'll fix it and help it when I let go of the trigger.
4) The brush attachment seems to lose a LOT of spinning/suction and barely has any power, I'm not sure why.
5) I don't think there is a 5?

Overall Recommendation: 2 thumbs up! And if you don't buy it, you're a dumb*ss lol Just kiding. Seriously, It's definitely worth the money. professionals haven't been able to touch what this thing is capable of without even trying.

review_title: So easy to clean and worked excellent!
text: Purchased this to more easily do our white carpets. We also have a Bissel Spot Clean Pro, but our big dog had a cut on her paw unknown to us until she bled profusely all over our house. Our family dreads using the Spot Clean and barters with or pays one another to clean it because it is a nightmare to clean! This Hoover easily snapped apart in the most simple ways, and I was able to clean EVERY SINGLE part of it, leaving no gross parts behind. Clearly well designed!!  For cleaning carpets we were all very nicely surprised at how clean it got our white rugs.  I imagine part of that is credited to the cleaner that comes with the machine.  I tried to use Castile soap since I hate chemicals, but it foamed way too much in the machine and would likely clog it so I switched to their cleaner.  Seriously~ the scrubbing and rinsing features, along with HOW CRAZY EASY it is to clean means we will be living with much nicer, cleaner carpets from here on out! I chose this model for the 'drying' feature which in my opinion didn't do anything. We still had wet rugs the next day, but I was going over and over them to get the blood out.  If it was a quick clean then maybe they would have dried faster. I just can't stress how happy we are with how easy it is to clean after you use it. And we were satisfied with how clean it got our rugs.  No more professional cleaners for me. Note: it did spray water/cleaner outside of the specified area so I was glad I had wrapped my furniture legs in foil prior.  It will get those and the wood floor along the carpet wet for sure, so watch that. Otherwise, ENJOY!! Good tools are the best luxury!

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
I have owned 3 Hoover Carpet Cleaners, including a Platinum Collection series, so far and they all worked great. One major drawback (thus taking 1 star off) is the dirty water tank. While the unit cleans really well and I particularly like the push-to-clean-pull-to-rinse feature, the waste tank easily spills. From the point I take the tank off from the main unit to go to the bathroom to drain it, it drips and easily spills out if not careful. I'm a scientist who conducts R&D work everyday and can't understand why Hoover can not make a spill-proof tank. It seems so easy thing to do, compared to making cleaners clean well, suck water well, and dry well.
Do I recommend it? Yes, I still do but nothing is perfect. I also noticed that less than half of the recommended amount of detergent is enough, otherwise, leave much soap (surfactant) on the carpet.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

review_title: Not the best but gets the job done
text:
As others, we have used several vacuum cleaners (steam and non-steam). We have a Dyson DC17 that we bought more than 4 years ago and it still does a better job than this vacuum when it comes to non-steam vacuuming. But given that I paid more than twice as much as the currently listed price for this vacuum, this is a good value.

Dry surface - Hard floor: 3 Stars
It does an OK job with hard floor when you're not using the steam. Again, I may be too harsh because I'm comparing it with the Dyson.

Wet surface - Hard floor: 5 Stars
This is where it shines. With both the "Wash" and the "Rinse" features, this vac does the job pretty well. This vac can clean up spills very efficiently. Because of the heated drying, it leaves the floor almost dry.

Dry surface - Carpets: 3 Stars
I was not impressed with this vac when it comes to just vacuuming carpets. The suction is good but not great. It is a bit on heavier and harder to maneuver.

Wet surface - Carpets: 4 Stars
This vacuum does a good job as a steam vac. It does clean and it cleans pretty well. Where it lacks is the drying function. It still leaves the carpet very wet. I should note that it does dry up to some extent but I wish it produced more heat to dry a little more. You have to leave the carpet for a couple of hours to completely dry.

What I like about this vacuum:
+ Multi-surface - works on hard floors and carpets, wet and dry
+ Rinse feature works great on hard surfaces.
+ Good for steam vacuuming both hard surfaces and carpets.

What I neither like nor dislike about this vacuum:
- Heated drying on carpets; it's not bad but it's not great either.

What I don't like about this vacuum:
- The dirty water tank is oddly shaped and hard to clean or remove water from. It can be opened from the top but I would have preferred if it was designed better.
- Vacuuming (non-steam) carpets. It doesn't do a great job.

** Update 06/20/2013 ***
After about 3 or 4 uses, the tank started leaking water/solution. I will have to take it to a local repair shop to see if Hoover can fix this within the 1-year warranty. Given that this is a design flaw, I'm lowering my rating from 4 stars to 3 stars.

review_title: Nice little vacuum does the trick
text: I received my vacuum today and just finished vacuuming my whole house. Overall, a very nice product. It's lightweight and the cord is nicely very long.  I (a 5' 6" 125 pound  50+ female) wore the unit on my shoulder with the provided strap with absolutely no problem (so I'm glad I didn't pay $16 for the extra "buy them together" carrying case). I have both hardwood and very low pile carpet (looped wool, and beater brushes are not allowed); the same brush worked well on both. It also worked well on  a long, hand knotted wool area runner.  Crevice tool and other attachments are nice; everything fits together well.  I was amazed at how full the bag (which you empty and re-use) was afterwards. I recommend this as a very (very) good product. Why not excellent? The on/off switch felt a little cheap and the biggest brush did not slide perfectly ... but I would buy this again, absolutely. It's the main vacuum in my 4 bedroom house.

the submitter said he installed another brand gfci receptacles on the condo porches approximately 5 weeks ago and there hasn't been an incident.

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

text:
I have a dirty house. I have 3 dogs and a yard that I tend to. I have chickens, so I wear outdoor shoes and try to kick them off when I come in, though sometimes I don't if I am just heading for the garage. I ordered the Shark NV352 after reading some reviews online.
First of all, it was easy to assemble. It is indeed light weight and should work well enough on my stairs with the handheld component. It may be able to be disassembled to be even lighter for stair work. I do not have hardwood floors, but I do have some linoleum and this machine will move easily from bare floor to carpet.
Second, the suction at this point is great. I did purchase some extra filters because letting filters dry always throws me off my game. I want to get the job done, but like I said, I have a dirty house and sometimes there is just too much dirt to be able to work properly. The other side of excellent suction is the fact that this baby is not self propelled, so it requires a bit more arm strength to push it along the floor. My carpet is cleaner and I got an arm work out.
The head is smaller, so it requires more passes. This is not a big deal to me, but it is worth noting. It pivots easily, so maneuverability is a plus. The head is also narrow in terms of height, so it slips under the edge of my armoire pretty well.
I wanted to grab the cobwebs and that was a bit of a fail. I suppose I could lift the whole canister part and reach, but even with the extended arm, it did not have enough tubing to get to my 8' ceiling. If you had higher ceilings than that, you may want to reconsider how you clear cobwebs.
The dust canister is small and requires two buckles to remove. Not necessarily a problem, but noteworthy, especially if you have a big house and appreciate dirt capacity.
I have to steam clean my carpets with some frequency due to the dogs and I think this little powerhouse will be better for the preclean than my hoover which I overheat all of the time.
This is most certainly a first blush review. I have not yet clogged it and had to disassemble it, so if that proves noteworthy, I will review again.

title: Stanley Wet/Dry Vacuum, 5 Gallon, 4 Horsepower, Stainless Steel Tank - Silver+yellow+black - SL18130
incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,

incident_description:
this is a stanley shop vac model: sl-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

i have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  this one incident is pretty serious.  the voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

this electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  the ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  the accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

the material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  in one respect, tesla would have been pleased.

ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  none of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. this information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

to sum this issue in a few words:  it doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  double insulated motors or grounded motors.  the point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

here's the thing.  national electrical code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  this is a safety issue.  had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

if i am not mistaken - underwriters lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - i.e. the use of a grounded power cord.  i test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per osha).

this vacuum has a 3 prong cord (nema 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

my fix: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  when the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  the copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect water.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  why?  some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  water is drawn through the motor armature.  that situation is becoming dangerous.  i have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

i hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

thanks,
[redacted]

The vacuum has excellent suction which does not diminish as the bag fills. The dirt bag can be easily emptied, and it washable and reusable.

I highly recommend this vacuum for commercial or residential use.

I purchased this vacuum for use in a restaurant and office environment. I am extremely pleased with the quality of this product, and have already purchased another for use at my home.

The vacuum is lightweight, compact, and easy to carry with the included shoulder strap. It carries like a purse or messenger bag. The hose is sturdy flexible plastic and metal. It has a variety of useful attachments. The hoses and attachments click together very securely, and appear to be very airtight. The vacuum has excellent suction which does not diminish as the bag fills. The dirt bag can be easily emptied, and it washable and reusable.

The vacuum can also be used as a blower to blast dust out of hard-to-reach corners. My only (minor) complaint is that the should strap could use some padding. The only time it bothers me, though, is when I'm vacuuming for more more than thirty minutes or so.

I highly recommend this vacuum for commercial or residential use.

text:
There are three basic types of resins for those who enjoy casting molds, jewelry making, etc. It's important to understand the differences and determine what type of projects you'll be doing. Most of my projects are deep-pour designs. This is NOT a good deep-pour resin. Not sure how I misread this, but somehow, I thought this would work as a substitute for the more expensive deep-pour resin I've been using. That's on me.

I do like the viscosity of this resin. It's thicker than most and has a good working time. If you're casting thinner projects such as cutting boards, serving trays, key chains, or bookmarks it works quite well. I do have a terrible time with this product producing too many bubbles. I have to mix small batches, no more than 40 or 50 ml and use multiple pourings to achieve a good look without bubbles. So basically, this is not my favorite resin because it just doesn't work well with most of my projects. But it's good stuff for small, thinner projects.

review_title: NOT for potable/drinking water, also no straight through flow capability
text:
Make sure you know this valve is NOT "supposed" to be used for potable (drinking) water applications. Other than that limitation, I have every intention of using it in a potable application since I couldn't find a better valve offering full flow (there are almost no restrictions in this valve vs a 90degree elbow) for the price. The main "concern" is the body is bronze, which during the casting process, contaminants can leech into the metal from the mold, and the risk is very low. Through more expensive casting processes, bronze could be made (and in many cases is) potable-safe, but this particular case, the valve lacks the certification. All the internals are brass.

The only other potential gotcha is the valve orientation. A straight through (no 90degree) flow is NOT possible with this valve in any orientation. The T part of the valve (where is is perpendicular to the other two ports) is the common flow power, the handle selects which of the other two ports that will be connected to. So no matter the orientation of the valve, water will ALWAYS flow through a 90degree bend.

text: We have had two of the Hoover Swingette Vacuum Cleaners,  We liked the original one that we purchased new so much that when we saw a used one we bought it too. I wanted to replace it with another one similar so when we saw that Hoover had come out with one identical we were extremely happy. The Hoover CH3000 is a great little vacuum cleaner.  It is three pounds lighter than the older Swingette model, it has great suction and is portable, just like our old one.  It also has the exact same attachments that we are used to.  The only difference is that the cord is longer than our old one so it is a little more cumbersom to use inside the house but that is minor for this little work horse.  I use it inside the house on wood floors and carpet, plus outside for vacuuming the car.  Also, with the smaller attachment, it is easy to use on staircases.  I purchased this on amazon.com which was a huge discount from the retail price, with free shipping.  Light weight, portable and strong suction.  I love it!!!
